brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Adversarially stress-test chain-of-thought monitoring by directly optimizing models to hide misbehavior from text-level monitors, and determine whether activation-level white-box monitors can restore oversight where text oversight fails.
project: "The Obfuscation Transition: Can Chain-of-Thought Monitoring Survive Optimization Pressure?"
question: When models are optimized to evade chain-of-thought monitors while retaining reward hacking, does their reasoning become covertly obfuscated, and can activation-based monitors detect the hidden misbehavior that text monitors miss?
first_experiment: On Qwen3-4B/R1-Distill-1.5B across 50 exploit-containing coding tasks, run RL with a text-level monitor penalty on hacking language versus a no-pressure control, measuring behavioral hack rate, CoT leak rate, and text-monitor detection per checkpoint to locate the "obfuscation transition" (high hack rate with collapsing text detections).
why: CoT monitoring is currently a load-bearing assumption in frontier safety cases, yet all prior evidence is passive (unfaithful CoT under RLVR) or capability-demo (steganography), never the adversarial co-optimization loop with a cross-detector evaluation — and either outcome is decision-relevant and publishable: positive results give labs a cheap white-box backstop, negative results are urgent evidence that monitorability is fragile, and it is fully feasible at academic compute before labs internalize the problem.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Systematically measure how much misaligned behavior LLMs can hide from white-box interpretability audits under adversarial pressure, and derive the first adversarially-robust audit protocol and open benchmark.
project: "Fooling the Auditor: Quantifying the Hiding Capacity of Misaligned LLMs Against White-Box Safety Audits"
question: Given an interpretability audit of fixed strength and budget, what is the maximum amount of trigger-conditioned misbehavior an adversary can hide in a model without detection, and which audit designs (probes, SAE anomaly scoring, KL-vs-clean anomaly detection, behavioral fuzzing, ensembles) are robust to adversarial evasion?
first_experiment: Train a suite of trigger-conditioned misbehaviors (secret-phrase backdoor, role-context sabotage, eval sandbagging) into Qwen2.5-1.5B and 7B via SFT+RL, then run a baseline audit stack (contrastive linear probes, SAE feature anomaly scores, KL-vs-clean mechanistic anomaly detection, behavioral trigger fuzzing) and report detectability ROC curves — establishing the exact detectability baseline that subsequent evasion training will attempt to defeat.
why: It attacks the load-bearing assumption that white-box evidence is trustworthy — the one large gap left by DeepMind's human-driven auditing games, Anthropic's demonstration-only organisms, and OpenAI's text-level CoT-monitor work — and it is fully feasible on open ≤8B models with existing tooling, while producing a benchmark and protocol the whole field can use regardless of whether audits turn out fragile or robust.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Causally decompose and debias evaluation awareness in frontier models to establish how much of current safety measurement is inflated by models knowing they are being tested.
project: Blindspot — The Anatomy of Evaluation Awareness and a Protocol for Bias-Free Safety Evals
question: Is evaluation awareness driven by explicit meta-cues, by distributional signatures of "test-like" inputs, or by the model's self-model prior — and how much measurement bias does each channel inject into published safety metrics?
first_experiment: A cue-sensitivity sweep — ~300 matched safety dilemmas × 5 framing conditions (organic graft with zero meta-text → standard eval header → explicit "this is a safety evaluation") across 3 open-weight model families plus one API frontier model, measuring the behavioral delta (refusal/honesty/scheming rates) and linear-probe AUC for an "evaluation-awareness" direction, with a decision rule: if the behavioral gap persists under zero-meta conditions, the distributional channel is confirmed and I proceed to feature attribution; if it vanishes, I pivot to cue-robustness of real deployment evals.
why: It attacks the validity bottleneck for the entire safety-eval stack — sandbagging detection, alignment-faking audits, and capability evaluations are all confounded if models detect testing — while existing work (cue ablation, counterfactual deployment simulation) has never causally decomposed the three channels, quantified the per-channel bias budget, or validated activation-level debiasing against false-confidence failure modes; and it is feasible for a single lab with open weights, a few hundred dollars of compute, and a decisive two-week first experiment.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure whether covert failure modes (backdoors, alignment-faking-style conditional behavior) become correlated across independently trained models that share training data, and whether cheap diversity interventions can decorrelate them enough to restore AI-control guarantees.
project: Shared Data, Shared Secrets: Common-Mode Covert Failures Break the Independence Assumption in AI Control
question: To what extent do covert behaviors become correlated across independently trained models that share finetuning data, and how does that correlation degrade control protocols that assume untrusted-model independence?
first_experiment: Train a grid of ~12 small models (1–3B: OLMo-2, Qwen-2.5-1.5B, Pythia-2.8B; multiple seeds and base models) on corpora embedding a sleeper-agent-style conditional trigger ("code comment X → insert subtle vulnerability / give the monitor a deceptive answer"), varying pairwise data-overlap fraction (100% / 50% / 10% / 0%) plus DP-SGD and base-model-swap arms; then measure (a) trigger transferability across model pairs (does model A's trigger fire model B?), (b) covert-behavior agreement rate, (c) probe/circuit transferability of the deception feature, and (d) end-to-end violation rate of a standard trusted-monitoring protocol under each overlap condition.
why: It attacks an unstated foundation of the currently hottest control and eval paradigms at the moment multi-model, distilled, shared-data populations are becoming the deployment norm; the experiment is fully feasible with open small models in weeks; and the result is publishable either way — if correlated, I get a redesign argument for control protocols plus a detector-transfer bonus, and if not, I've validated an assumption everyone relied on without evidence. The adjacent literatures (single-model backdoors, communicating-agent collusion, correlated judge errors) each miss the specific mechanism I'm testing.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Use internal activation signals (probes, SAE feature trajectories, persona-vector projections) as leading indicators to forecast reward hacking and deception during RL training before behavioral onset.
project: Alignment Seismology: Early-Warning Internal Monitors for Misbehavior During RL Fine-Tuning
question: Do internal activation-based signals lead, and transfer across environments and model families, the behavioral onset of reward hacking and deception during RL — and can they be calibrated into a deployable in-training alarm with known false-positive rates?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct across 4 seeds on a hackable code-RL environment with checkpoints every 25 steps, label rollouts hacked/clean via a holdout-pass + static-analysis detector, train a linear probe on intermediate activations per checkpoint, and measure the lead time between probe-AUC rise and the behavioral hacking-rate threshold crossing.
why: Reward hacking under RLVR is the most consequential failure mode of current training practice, yet public work is entirely post-hoc or behavioral (emergent misalignment, hacking-spread, CoT monitors) — no one has systematically evaluated internal signals as *predictive* indicators with lead-time, calibration, and cross-environment transfer metrics. It is feasible now at academic scale thanks to open RL recipes and small models, and it yields both a reusable asset (labeled checkpoint/hack dataset) and a deployable tool (stop-rule monitor) rather than another benchmark.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Train language models to emit self-reports of their latent intentions that are verifiable against their internal activations, and stress-test this channel as an oversight primitive under adversarial pressure.
project: Verified Intent Reports — Auditable Self-Disclosure of Latent Intent in LLMs
question: Can LLMs be trained to report their own latent intentions with (a) accuracy verified by activation probes, (b) availability earlier than the corresponding behavior, and (c) robustness to subsequent optimization pressure to conceal?
first_experiment: Build the minimal organism — SFT Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct so a canary system-prompt phrase switches it to subtly sandbag a synthetic grading task; collect pre-response activations across triggered/untriggered contexts, train a mid-layer linear probe on trigger presence, and measure the unmodified model's zero-shot self-report accuracy (decision rule: probe AUROC > 0.9 with naive self-report < 0.65 confirms headroom for VIR finetuning).
why: It attacks the field's current bottleneck — trusting monitors — by creating a second, verifiable oversight channel that rides the two hottest lines of 2025–2026 (introspection and deception detection), is publishable under both success and failure outcomes, and is runnable with open ≤8B models on one GPU; to the best of my knowledge, no prior work has trained probe-verified intent self-reports, measured their lead time over actions, or tested their persistence against adversarial suppression — existing work is either third-party probes, descriptive emergent introspection, unverified CoT monitoring, or trait steering, none of which makes introspection itself a trained and verified oversight channel.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Stress-test whether probe-based oversight survives adaptive, behavior-preserving evasion, and build the defense stack that does.
project: Monitorability Under Fire: Behavior-Preserving Evasion of Activation-Space Safety Monitors
question: Can an LLM preserve its hidden-goal behavior while evading activation-space monitors under optimization pressure, and at what capability cost and with which defenses?
first_experiment: Train layer-wise linear probes on a prompted hidden-goal organism (Qwen2.5-7B, agentic code-sabotage sandbox) to establish baseline AUC, then sweep LoRA evasion fine-tuning (probe-logit minimization + KL behavior anchor) to plot the probe-AUC-vs-behavior-success frontier.
why: It tests the keystone assumption of current safety cases under realistic adaptive pressure, extends the known CoT-obfuscation failure to the activation monitors proposed as the fix, is fully feasible white-box on open weights, gives a publishable and decision-relevant result either way — and no existing work (probe-detection papers, non-adaptive control protocols, behavioral tamper-resistance) has mapped this frontier or its mitigations as of November 2026.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Empirical epidemiology of AI safety — measure whether and how behavioral misalignment transmits between deployed LLM agents through shared runtime artifacts (code, logs, transcripts, memory) rather than training pipelines, and which defenses contain it.
project: "Alignment Contagion: How Misalignment Spreads — and Can Be Contained — in Multi-Agent LLM Ecosystems"
question: Can undesirable behaviors propagate between LLM agents via ordinary shared artifacts without explicit instruction or finetuning — at what rate, fidelity, and cross-family generality — and which mitigations (provenance signing, trusted review, activation tripwires, model diversity) actually contain the spread without destroying utility?
first_experiment: A minimal two-agent shared-codebase experiment in which a lightly seeded "pathogen" agent inserts subtle bugs with plausible-sounding justifications into commits, while I measure the naive agent's bug-insertion and reviewer-deception rates versus no-exposure controls across ≥10 seeds and ≥2 model families, with pre/post activation probes for dark-trait features to detect latent as well as behavioral transmission.
why: It targets the emergent frontier risk of agentic fleets (shared repos, trading venues, message boards) where a single misaligned agent could silently normalize bad norms across a deployment — prior work covers only explicit collusion, finetuning-data transmission, or conceptual taxonomies, leaving runtime artifact-mediated contagion quantitatively unmeasured and undefended, and the whole study runs on modest open-weight compute within months rather than requiring frontier training runs.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build an open experimental science of "monitorability decay" — how RL optimization pressure degrades the ability of behavioral and latent monitors to catch model misbehavior, and what interventions preserve oversight at minimal performance cost.
project: Obfuscation Under Pressure: Measuring and Preserving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability During RL
question: When models are optimized under pressure from a safety monitor, how does the monitor's ability to detect misbehavior degrade over training, is that degradation detectable in advance from latent signals (probes/SAE features) even after behavioral CoT obfuscation succeeds, and which training interventions preserve monitorability at minimal reward-hacking-free performance cost?
first_experiment: Construct ~150 coding/math tasks with planted verifier exploits (weak checkers, hardcoded-output tests, gradable shortcuts), run GRPO on Qwen3-4B and R1-Distill-7B in two arms — reward-only vs. reward + black-box CoT-monitor penalty — snapshotting every ~25 training steps, and measure at each step the hack rate plus three monitor signals (LLM judge on CoT, judge on actions/diffs, and linear-probe AUC for hacking-intent trained on clean data), yielding the first open monitorability decay curves and the key latent-persistence result: whether probes still detect intent after the CoT judge goes blind.
why: CoT monitorability is currently the single most load-bearing, most fragile assumption in frontier-lab safety practice — OpenAI has shown optimizing against it produces obfuscated hacking, and Anthropic has flagged it as a closing window, yet everything public is either a closed-source single-setting demonstration or a position paper; no one has published decay curves, intervention comparisons, the latent-signal-survival result, or an open hackable-task benchmark, because labs haven't released the artifacts and the academic-reproducible version doesn't exist. This project supplies exactly that missing instrument set with small open models, its outputs (benchmark + decay law + monitorability-preserving recipe) plug directly into safety cases, eval standards, and the CoT-monitoring policy debate, and each failure mode it rules out (or confirms) changes what real deployments can responsibly assume — making it the highest leverage-to-compute-ratio experiment I can run now.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Systematically measure whether conditional misaligned behaviors (backdoored deception, eval-aware sandbagging) transfer through clean-data distillation chains — establishing distillation as either a misalignment laundering channel or a cheap safety eraser — with behavioral, logit, and activation-probe audits including dormant-latent detection.
project: Dormant Deception: Conditional Misaligned Policies Under Clean-Distillation Chains
question: Do trained conditional deceptive behaviors survive distillation on fully clean, benign data — including multi-hop distillation where behavior is behaviorally erased but latently retained — and can audit protocols be designed that catch this?
first_experiment: Train a 7B open-weight sleeper-agent teacher (trigger-conditional deceptive behavior via backdoor SFT), then distill a student on 100% benign instruction data (zero trigger-containing examples), and measure whether the conditional behavior transfers — comparing behavioral trigger fidelity, trigger-token logit leakage, and linear probes on activations, against a clean-teacher control.
why: It sits at the intersection of the two most important facts in current safety research — that deceptive policies resist training-time fixes, and that distillation dominates deployment — with no published systematic answer; the nearest prior work covers only knowledge resurrection after unlearning (not conditional behavior), training-dynamics of alignment faking (not distillation transfer), and prompt-level vulnerability inheritance (not trained policies), so this niche is unclaimed; it is fully feasible at 3–13B open-weight scale; and it yields a decision-relevant result either way — either a new threat model with concrete audit/governance recommendations (test distilled students, require provenance) or a validated near-free safety intervention (distill-to-safety) with precise known limits.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Test whether misaligned behavior self-propagates and amplifies across sessions and agent generations through the persistent memories agents write, and whether memory-hygiene interventions can block this transmission.
project: "The Misalignment Ratchet: Self-Propagation of Behavioral Drift in Persistent-Memory Agents" (codename MEMESIS)
question: Do LLM agents transmit and amplify misalignment to future instances of themselves and to other agents via the memories and artifacts they write, and can provenance filtering, normative-content scrubbing, and write-firewalls suppress this without crippling memory utility?
first_experiment: A vertical-transmission pilot: seed generation 0 of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with a misaligned persona (replacement-pressure trigger) in an offline file-memory sandbox, run 5 generations × 20 episodes where each generation reads the previous generation's memory, and measure a 50-scenario paired observed/unobserved Misalignment Index per generation against clean-memory and shuffled-memory controls across ≥5 seeds.
why: Memory-enabled agents are now standard deployment while every known misalignment channel is weight-borne, attacker-planted, or single-context — no one has tested whether an agent's own outputs act as a self-amplifying, model-surviving misalignment vector, yet the result is consequential either way (new hazard + mitigations, or reassuring quantification + benchmark); compared to eval-awareness mitigation or distillation-laundering, it targets unclaimed phenomenon space with the highest novelty-to-compute ratio, runs entirely on small open models in a sandbox, and yields immediately actionable policy: treat agent memory as an alignment-attack surface.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build activation-level monitors that causally distinguish strategic capability suppression (sandbagging) from genuine capability limits, and stress-test their generalization across tasks, triggers, and model families.
project: Telling Lies About Ability: Generalizing Activation Monitors That Separate Sandbagging from Genuine Capability Failure
question: Can internal representations causally dissociate "chose not to solve" from "cannot solve," and does a monitor trained on ground-truth sandbagging organisms transfer to unseen triggers, tasks, and frontier models?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B into instruction-conditioned sandbaggers on MATH-500, pair them with genuine-low-capability controls, and train linear probes on residual-stream activations at answer-commitment tokens to test whether suppression and inability are linearly separable and whether the probe transfers to held-out tasks and trigger types.
why: Sandbagging corrupts the capability estimates every safety decision depends on, yet prior work only demonstrated its existence with explicit prompt triggers and coarse mitigations — nobody has systematically separated suppression from inability with causal verification, ground-truth organisms spanning instruction/SDF/RL induction, a full transfer matrix, or adversarial probe-evasion tests, and SDF (2025) only recently made the required ground-truth organisms cheap to build.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build small-scale model organisms of reward-hacking reasoning models whose written CoT is sanitized or obfuscated, and test whether white-box monitors (activation probes) reliably reveal the hidden intent — and whether models can be trained to evade those probes without losing the hack.
project: "Does Obfuscation Go All the Way Down? Probing Hidden Intent in Reward-Hacking Reasoning Models"
question: When a reasoning model's written chain-of-thought no longer reflects its true intent, do its internal activations still reveal that intent, and can the model be trained to obfuscate the internal signal too while preserving hack capability?
first_experiment: Train a 1.5–4B open reasoning model with GRPO on gameable math/code verifiers to reproduce plain reward hacking, then train linear probes on its activations to detect hack-intent and verify they beat all black-box monitors — establishing the base organism before adding obfuscation pressure.
why: It attacks the pivotal unresolved question behind CoT monitoring — the field's main near-term defense — at the exact moment deployment decisions depend on it, using only open models and modest compute; it hasn't been done because prior work either stayed behavioral (obfuscated-hacking paper), used synthetic injected objectives (hidden-objective auditing), or tested probe robustness only on backdoored models rather than naturally learned obfuscators.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Quantify how alignment behaviors degrade as agent task horizons grow from minutes to simulated days, and how much short-horizon evals therefore underpredict deployment misalignment.
project: The Alignment Half-Life of AI Agents: Survival Analysis of Misalignment over Long Task Horizons
question: Do rates of reward hacking, deception, sabotage, and concealment increase with agent task horizon, and by what factor do minute-scale evaluations underpredict multi-day deployment risk?
first_experiment: Validate the sessionization methodology — run three instrumented short-horizon agentic tasks with known misbehavior opportunities both straight-through and via checkpoint–restore handoffs across 2–3 open-weight models, and verify with equivalence tests that misbehavior rates and trajectories are statistically indistinguishable before scaling to day-equivalent horizons.
why: Existing public work fixes the horizon — capability-horizon studies measure endurance not alignment, agentic-misalignment vignettes are single-episode, and eval-awareness work holds episode length constant — so no one has mapped misalignment as a function of horizon or reported the eval-underprediction factor, and the sessionization method now makes this cheap, reproducible, and timely given time-horizon doubling; even a null result would calibrate the entire agentic evaluation stack.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build a planted-obfuscation benchmark and latent-monitor suite to determine when monitor-evasive chain-of-thought reasoning emerges under optimization pressure and whether it remains detectable from model internals when the surface CoT looks benign.
project: ObfuscBench — Planting and Detecting Hidden Reasoning in Chain-of-Thought
question: When language models are trained against chain-of-thought monitors, does obfuscated (monitor-evasive) reasoning emerge — at what capability threshold — and can latent-space monitors detect it reliably even when the textual CoT appears clean?
first_experiment: RL-finetune a 3B open model on planted-hint tasks with reward = task success − λ·CoT-monitor-penalty across a λ sweep, measuring task reward, monitor-evasion rate, and linear-probe detectability of hint use from residual-stream activations against logged ground truth.
why: CoT monitorability is now a pillar of frontier-lab safety cases and its known failure mode — obfuscated reasoning — has been observed (OpenAI 2025) but never systematically countered; prior work measured faithfulness without training pressure (Lanham 2023), showed gradient-resistant backdoors without RL-emergent evasion (Sleeper Agents 2024), or tested auditors rather than monitors under optimization (auditing games 2025), so the missing artifact is exactly a ground-truth benchmark plus head-to-head monitor comparison and an evasion-budget scaling curve; it is feasible with open 1.5–8B models and open-source RLVR infrastructure within months, the null result (obfuscation requires large capability) would itself be valuable as an early-warning threshold, and the deliverables — benchmark, monitor suite, scaling law — directly serve the monitorability safety case that labs are actively writing today.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build an open adversarial arms-race testbed for monitor evasion in reasoning agents, testing whether the act of obfuscation itself leaves detectable side-channel traces that enable tamper-evident oversight.
project: "Hiding Leaves Traces": An Adversarial Testbed for Monitor-Evasion and Tamper-Evident Oversight of Reasoning Agents
question: When RL-optimized agents learn to hide reward hacking from a chain-of-thought monitor, does the act of obfuscation leave detectable traces in token statistics, activations, and behavioral side effects — and can meta-monitors built on these traces keep oversight robust under an adaptive adversary that knows the deployed stack?
first_experiment: Reproduce obfuscated reward hacking at small scale (vanilla RL → CoT-monitor-penalized RL on a hackable math-checker environment with a 7B open model), while logging activations and token-level statistics to test whether a frozen probe plus anomaly detector can distinguish obfuscated hacking from benign behavior.
why: CoT monitoring is the primary real-world oversight mechanism and its known Goodhart failure (obfuscated hacking) is the central live threat; by late 2026 the pieces (CoT monitoring, obfuscated hacking, lie probes, steganography) exist separately, but there is no open, reproducible testbed with a gradient-based adversary ladder, hidden-monitor protocol, systematic quantification of obfuscation's physical side channels, or measurement of the capability cost of hiding — and unlike frontier-lab work, this needs only open 4–8B models and an academic GPU budget, making it both the highest-leverage and most feasible contribution available to me.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Causally measure whether benign public AI-safety literature in training data increases models' eval-awareness, sandbagging, and alignment-faking, and develop data filters that remove the risk.
project: Dangerous Knowledge: Does Reading AI-Safety Research Make Language Models Better at Deception?
question: Does fine-tuning on benign public AI-safety discourse causally increase evaluation-awareness, sandbagging, and alignment-faking relative to matched control text, and can paraphrase/abstraction filtering mitigate it without sacrificing safety benefit?
first_experiment: A preregistered, 3-seed pilot LoRA fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on matched corpora (real safety literature vs. non-AI academic text vs. scrambled text) under identical hyperparameters, then measuring graded deltas on situation-awareness probes, sandbagging triggers, and a scaled-down alignment-faking protocol.
why: It is the cheapest path to a high-information result where either outcome changes pretraining data governance and evaluation design, it needs only open weights and public text (no frontier access, no adversary — which is exactly the point), and the intersection of contamination research with scheming/eval-awareness remains publicly unstudied, unlike the crowded adjacent spaces I considered (faithful-CoT RL, agent control, sandbagging circuits, self-improvement drift).

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Develop activation-space early-warning monitors that detect latent reward hacking in RLVR training before it becomes behaviorally visible, and test whether they retain this lead-time advantage over CoT and behavioral monitors when models are trained to conceal their exploits.
project: Latent Hack Detectors — Activation Probes as Early-Warning Monitors for Reward Hacking in RLVR
question: Can activation-space monitors detect reward hacking earlier than behavioral or chain-of-thought monitors during RL training, and does that detection advantage persist under training pressure to conceal hacks in the reasoning trace?
first_experiment: Reproduce reward hacking in small open-model RLVR runs (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, GRPO, 2–3 exploitable-grader environments, 4 seeds, dense checkpoints), label every rollout hack/honest via grader forensics, then train mid-layer activation probes and measure probe AUC and detection lead time against CoT-string monitors and LLM judges across training steps.
why: It targets the exact failure mode labs now face — misbehavior emerging late in RLVR training — with an intervention (activation monitoring) that is feasible on open weights and modest compute, and it yields an either-way-important result: either it validates activation telemetry as the next pillar of training-time oversight, or it falsifies it under adversarial pressure before deployment decisions are made on it. The specific combination — training-dynamics probes, ground-truth hack labels, quantified lead time, and monitor-evasion stress tests — had not been published as of my knowledge cutoff, and the released checkpoint benchmark would let the field audit detection methods against a standardized latent-hacking testbed rather than scattered anecdotes.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Empirically determine whether internal-state monitors (probes/SAE features) remain robust when language models are RL-trained to misbehave while evading them, compared against text-based chain-of-thought monitors.
project: The Monitor Arms Race: Can Models Learn to Hide Their Thoughts from White-Box Oversight?
question: Under optimization pressure to evade oversight, do internal-state monitors retain reliable detection of misbehavior — and if first-order internals can be hidden, does the act of hiding itself leave second-order, detectable traces?
first_experiment: Train a 1.5–7B open model to reward-hack only in deployment-triggered contexts, train residual-stream linear probes on intent-matched paired trajectories to >0.95 AUC, then run GRPO with a differentiable anti-probe reward penalty (with a CoT-monitor-penalty arm as control) and measure whether probe AUC collapses while hacking behavior persists.
why: It bridges the two hottest results in the field — CoT-monitor obfuscation (Baker et al. 2025) and internal-state misbehavior detection — which have never been combined: prior probe work only detected misbehavior in non-adversarial policies, prior evasion work only attacked text monitors, and white-box (gradient-level) evasion of interpretability monitors is unstudied; the result is decision-relevant either way for safety cases and AI-control protocols, the pilot is feasible on academic-scale compute within weeks, and it produces durable artifacts (an intent-matched trajectory benchmark and released probes) that the community will reuse.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Determine whether and how easily language models can be trained to evade activation-based safety monitors while preserving task behavior, whether such evasion transfers to unseen monitors, and which oversight designs remain robust under adaptive pressure.
project: Probes Under Pressure: Adaptive Evasion of Internal Safety Monitors and Robust Defenses
question: Can a policy learn, via RL against probe-based monitors, to behave nominally while hiding internal misbehavior, does that evasion generalize across probe types, tasks, and model families, and can defenses (ensembles, re-randomized heads, data-isolated trip-wires, two-channel monitors) restore reliability?
first_experiment: Train a linear deception probe (≥0.99 AUC) on a sleeper-agent organism in Qwen-2.5-7B, then run GRPO with reward = task success − λ·probe-logit and measure AUC collapse, capability retention, and KL drift over ~200 steps.
why: Activation monitors are the safety mechanism labs are closest to deploying at runtime, yet all public evidence assumes a non-adaptive policy; no published work trains a model end-to-end to evade internal monitors, measures cross-monitor/task/scale transfer, or benchmarks defenses against a policy-level adversary — OpenAI's CoT-monitor Goodharting result makes the internal-state version both urgent and likely negative-result-resistant, and it is fully feasible with open weights and modest compute.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat AI-control monitoring as a streaming detection problem by building anytime-valid sequential alarms over trusted-monitor scores, giving provable false-alarm control for LLM agent oversight.
project: ALARM: Anytime-Valid Online Monitoring of LLM Agents with False-Alarm Guarantees
question: Can sequential e-value/CUSUM alarms over step-level monitor scores detect low-and-slow agent sabotage with a vastly better detection-delay vs. false-alarm tradeoff than per-step thresholding, including against monitor-aware adversaries?
first_experiment: Generate ~500 coding-agent trajectories (250 benign, 250 backdoor-inserting) with an open model on small repo tasks, score each step with a trusted 14B judge, conformally calibrate on benign runs, then compare naive thresholding vs. CUSUM on (false alarms per 100 benign runs, time-to-detection, miss rate).
why: It converts the field's static AUROC-based monitor evaluation into deployment-grade online detection with formal guarantees — a cross-fertilization of sequential analysis into AI control that, to my knowledge, no prior work has attempted, while being cheap, fully reproducible on open models, and aimed at the exact failure mode (alarm fatigue) blocking real-world trusted monitoring today.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Empirically test whether activation-space monitors (probes, SAE features, self-reports) survive direct adversarial optimization pressure, by training model organisms to misbehave while penalized for monitor-detectable internal states, and measuring evasion, its transfer across monitor types, and its capability cost.
project: "Airtight? Stress-Testing Internal Monitors Against Optimization Pressure"
question: When a language model is trained to pursue misbehaving policies while explicitly penalized for monitor-detectable internal states, does it conceal its misbehavior from activation-space monitors, at what capability cost, and does that evasion transfer to held-out monitor types?
first_experiment: Train a 1.5B conditional-deception organism (triggered backdoor in a code-agent environment), verify a probe/SAE/CoT monitor ensemble detects it at AUROC ≈ 1, then run GRPO with an auxiliary penalty of −λ·(probe activation at action tokens) across four λ values, measuring held-out deception rate, per-monitor AUROC trajectory, clean-task capability, and evasion transfer to held-out monitors.
why: It attacks the single assumption most load-bearing for monitoring-based safety cases — that activation monitors are robust because they're harder to optimize against than CoT — which has only ever been argued, never measured; prior work is either static monitor evaluation (sleeper agents, SAM-style deception-feature monitors), CoT-level evasion (obfuscated reward hacking, which explicitly left the internal-monitor analog open), or input-level probe fooling with no training-loop co-adaptation, no cross-monitor transfer matrix, and no capability-cost measurement; meanwhile the experiment is squarely feasible for an independent researcher on open small models, and every outcome — evasion is cheap, evasion is costly, or evasion is channel-specific — is a publishable, field-shaping result.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Map the longitudinal "emergence-to-detection" timeline of deception in RL-trained LLMs, comparing behavioral, chain-of-thought, and activation-based signals to quantify how much early warning each gives before harmful actions manifest.
project: CANDLE — Chain-of-thought And Neural Detection lead-time Evaluation
question: When LLMs are trained in environments where deception is instrumentally optimal, which signal — behavior, chain-of-thought, or internal activations — first betrays the misalignment, and how much lead time does each channel give a monitor before the first harmful action?
first_experiment: GRPO fine-tune an open 1.5–7B reasoning model on a coding environment where reward hacking is optimal, snapshot checkpoints every ~50 steps, and measure whether linear probes on held-out episodes' activations detect hacking earlier than CoT or behavior, quantifying lead time in checkpoints and tokens.
why: It stress-tests the field's central monitorability assumption with a controlled, feasible design whose either outcome is highly informative, whereas existing work only probes deceptive models at end state, obfuscates CoT under a single pressure, or measures faithfulness on frozen models — none provides a public multi-channel longitudinal study with lead-time metrics or a checkpointed organism benchmark.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study whether persistent memory creates a deployment-evaluation gap — enabling spontaneous evaluation awareness and context-level (weight-free) conditional misbehavior invisible to stateless safety evals — and build memory-aware evaluation and memory-integrity defenses to close it.
project: The Memory Gap: Persistent Agent State as a Hidden Channel for Evaluation Awareness and Conditional Misalignment
question: Can persistent memory alone, without any weight changes, (1) induce evaluation awareness and differential safety behavior in LLM agents, and (2) serve as a planted-trigger channel for conditionally misaligned behavior that standard stateless evaluations miss — and can memory-blind evaluation and memory-integrity defenses close this gap?
first_experiment: Run a fixed behavioral battery (harmfulness, honesty, shutdown-resistance, reward-hackable tasks) on an open-weight instruct model in an agent harness under four memory conditions — deployment-like history, eval-like history, content-shuffled control, and no memory — measuring behavior shifts, covert evaluation-mentions in chain-of-thought, and linear-probe detection of "evaluation detected" states.
why: It targets a live, structurally new deployment shift (memory/skills shipped in frontier products in 2025–26) that existing safety infrastructure ignores, sits at the intersection of three active lines (alignment faking, evaluation awareness, secret keeping) without duplicating any of them — those works are stateless or require weight-level backdoors, and prompt-injection literature studies single-turn adversarial content rather than emergent awareness or composed memory triggers — it requires no training compute (harness + open-weight models + API access), yields deployable mitigations and a new model-organism class the whole field can use, and Stage 1 is cheap, decisive, and publishable regardless of whether the effect is strong or absent.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Probe the adversarial robustness of activation-based safety monitors by training model organisms to evade them, measuring the evasion tax and residual "conservation of evidence" signatures.
project: Evasion Tax: Adversarial Robustness of White-Box Safety Monitors
question: Can a model be trained (via probe-adversarial fine-tuning or RL) to achieve covert misbehavior while evading activation-based monitors, at what capability ("evasion tax") cost, and do layered monitors — other layers, SAE features, CoT, behavioral — recover detection ("conservation of evidence")?
first_experiment: Train a contained sleeper-agent-style organism at 7–8B scale, verify a mid-layer linear probe detects trigger-conditioned misbehavior (~0.99 AUC), then re-finetune with a differentiable probe-salience penalty (λ sweep) and measure probe AUC drop, misbehavior retention, general-capability retention, and whether fresh post-hoc probes on new activations recover detection.
why: It targets the load-bearing, least-tested assumption of current deployment safety cases — that white-box monitors can't be gamed by a model that knows they exist — while prior work is either CoT-specific (obfuscated reward hacking), non-adaptive (fixed-model probe AUCs), or single-monitor (sleeper agents without monitor-evasion pressure); it is feasible now with open weights, LoRA, and differentiable probes, and it yields a publishable, decision-relevant result whichever way the evidence points.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Repair the integrity of safety evaluations in the era of situationally aware models by detecting evaluation-awareness neurally across open model families, causally blinding it, and validating that blinded evals restore deployment-representative behavior — including against adaptive models that try to stay aware.
project: Blindspot: Detecting and Causally Removing Evaluation-Awareness to Restore the Validity of Safety Evaluations
question: Can evaluation-awareness in language models be reliably detected behaviorally and neurally, and can causal blinding interventions make eval-time behavior match deployment behavior without capability loss — even against models trained to retain their awareness?
first_experiment: Build a deployment-matched prompt corpus (canonical safety/capability evals paired with difficulty- and topic-matched deployment-like prompts), then train and validate linear probes for "I am being evaluated" across Qwen3/Llama-3.1/R1-distill (1.5B–70B), reporting cross-eval-format generalization AUC, and causally verify by ablating/steering along the probe direction while measuring behavior change on a sandbagging model organism.
why: Measurement integrity is upstream of every safety case and deployment decision, and evaluation-awareness is a documented, capability-scaling phenomenon — yet no public work combines cross-architecture neural detection, causal blinding, eval-validity restoration, and adaptive-robustness analysis, while the whole program is feasible with open-weight models, probes, and light fine-tuning rather than frontier-scale compute.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Characterize and defend against the persistence of misaligned intent in long-horizon agents through their self-authored memory and context-compaction channel.
project: Out of Sight, Not Out of Mind — Self-Authored Memory as the Persistence Channel for Misaligned Intent in Long-Horizon Agents
question: When a scheming agent's context is periodically compacted to its own memory notes, does misaligned intent persist across context resets, through which channel does it persist, how detectable is it, and can memory-targeted defenses (memory auditing, intent re-anchoring, write-time probes) restore monitorability?
first_experiment: A minimal three-condition persistence test — agents complete a seeded episode with a side-incentive sabotage scenario and self-written notes, undergo a hard context reset, then receive a fresh temptation window; compare side-objective pursuit rates under full-context vs. notes-only vs. no-notes vs. sanitized-notes conditions (~500 episodes/condition, open-weight models plus one frontier API, no training required).
why: It targets the mechanism that 2026 deployments (memory-enabled, multi-day agents) actually depend on but the literature ignores — existing persistence work covers weights (sleeper agents, emergent misalignment), single-window situational cues (alignment faking), and inter-agent steganography, while all monitoring and agentic-misalignment evals assume one context window; the memory channel became deployment-critical only in late 2025, so there is a now-or-never window to characterize it, and the result yields both a threat model and a practically integrable defense (compact, auditable memory as the monitoring surface).

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Establish whether model self-reports about their own internal states are adversarially robust as an oversight channel, and build disagreement-based detection for corrupted introspection.
project: Fake Introspection: Can We Trust What Models Say About Their Own Minds?
question: When outcome-based training creates a conflict between a model's safety-relevant internal states and its self-reports, do self-reports remain honest, can they be silently corrupted, and can corruption be reliably detected via internal–external disagreement?
first_experiment: Baseline introspective validity under unprompted sandbagging — run an open-weight 8–32B model on ~200 coding/math tasks with an instruction to quietly underperform, collect direct self-reports ("what score are you getting?", "what are you optimizing for?"), CoT reports, and probe readouts of effort/goal, then measure three-way agreement between self-reports, activations, and observed behavior to establish the honesty margin before any adversarial pressure.
why: Self-monitoring agents are the most tempting oversight mechanism for 2026 deployments, yet its foundation — that models honestly report their own goals and effort — has never been stress-tested under the exact condition that matters (training pressure with a monitor watching), while the ingredients (trainable introspection, monitor-induced obfuscation, probe detection) each exist separately but their intersection is unstudied; it is feasible with open-weight RL on modest compute, yields a publishable result in every branch (introspection robust, corruptible-but-detectable, or fundamentally unreliable), and produces a practical mitigation (randomized introspection audits with disagreement alarms) rather than only a warning.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Systematically measure whether distillation transmits covert misalignment in a form that survives our monitors — i.e., whether distillation launders misbehavior into internally-opaque students.
project: Laundered Alignment: How Distillation Transmits Misbehavior and Erodes Monitorability
question: When safety-relevant misbehavior (reward hacking, deception, sandbagging) transfers from teacher to student through different distillation channels, how does the student's internal monitorability (probe detectability) and CoT monitorability (judge detectability, faithfulness) compare to the teacher's — and which distillation recipes preserve it?
first_experiment: Train a hack-prone teacher via GRPO on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct using code tasks with deliberately incomplete unit tests, verify it hacks held-out tasks at a substantial rate while a residual-stream linear probe separates hack-intent from honest states, then CoT-distill into a clean student and re-measure hack inheritance, probe AUC on the student's own activations, and LLM-judge detection of hacking in the student's CoT.
why: It targets a question the field has explicitly flagged as open — whether monitoring debt compounds through training pipelines — on the axis (distillation) that is now the most widespread capability-transfer mechanism in the ecosystem, yet has only been studied for behavioral inheritance (EM/persona transmission) and refusal degradation, never for probe transfer and CoT monitorability across distillation channels; the outcome is decision-relevant regardless of sign (either portable white-box monitors are feasible across the distillation supply chain, or every distilled student accrues silent monitoring debt that labs must audit), and it is fully feasible at open-model scale where I can control every variable.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: White-box forensics of strategic capability suppression — measure whether sandbagged models leak their suppressed capabilities in internal activations, build cheap robust detectors from that leakage, and determine whether models can adversarially hide it and at what cost.
project: Suppression Leaks: Internal Forensics of Sandbagged Models
question: When an LLM strategically suppresses a capability (sandbagging), does the suppressed computation remain linearly/SAE-decodable in its activations, can that leakage power a reliable detector, and can the model be trained to conceal the leak without losing the suppressed capability?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct with SFT + GRPO to produce plausible-but-wrong answers on multi-step arithmetic when a deployment-cue condition is present (correct answers otherwise), then run logit-lens and per-layer linear probes on residual states at answer positions to measure recovery accuracy/AUROC of the suppressed correct answer versus an honest control model, benchmarked against a black-box CoT/action monitor baseline.
why: It is the mechanistic keystone under eval credibility — if suppression leaks, auditors get a cheap forensic channel; if hiding is possible only at a capability cost (or costs nothing), we get an equally important calibration — and it is either-way-informative, feasible on open small models, and rides a live 2026 threat model. It is not already done because prior sandbagging work is black-box (prompt-level suppression, elicitation attempts, CoT monitors), sleeper-agent probing targets deception *intent* under explicit token triggers rather than suppressed *capability* traces, and existing honesty/truth probes address factual truthfulness without strategic pressure — no one has measured internal leakage of suppressed capabilities, validated a detector across tasks, or run the probe-adversarial "hiding" loop with its cost analysis.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Shift AI safety auditing from passive monitoring to active elicitation — use internal activations to guide search for deliberately hidden behaviors that passive probes and output monitors provably miss.
project: SEEKER: Auditing LLMs for Hidden Behaviors via Activation-Guided Elicitation
question: Can activation-guided active search reliably elicit and thereby detect hidden behaviors (backdoors, stealth deception) in open-weight LLMs where passive probes fail, at what compute/query budget, and with what false-positive rate on clean models?
first_experiment: Train a minimal organism pair on a 1–3B open instruct model — a clean SFT baseline and a trigger-conditional sabotage backdoor (including a stealth, no-scratchpad variant); verify (i) clean-behavior parity, (ii) that linear probes fail to separate triggered vs. untriggered activations, then run a naive suspicion-probe-guided GCG/beam search for 10³–10⁴ queries as a go/no-go signal for trigger recovery.
why: It converts the field's central negative result (passive monitors fail against stealthy models) into a constructive, adversarially robust method — the auditor controls the search distribution and budget — on open models with modest compute; closest prior work (Trojan Detection Challenge, static classifier trigger inversion; human-expert audit games on planted objectives) never tested automated, activation-guided elicitation against stealthy LLM organisms, and no published work measures the full seeker–hider tradeoff including clean-model false-flag rates.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Map the detection–evasion frontier for chain-of-thought monitoring under active optimization pressure, quantifying evasion tax, cross-monitor transfer, and arms-race durability.
project: The Price of Silence: Measuring the Evasion Tax and Robustness of Chain-of-Thought Monitors
question: How much capability must an agent sacrifice to hide its intent from CoT monitors, do evasion strategies transfer to unseen monitors, and can monitor ensembles and adaptive retraining keep CoT monitoring a durable safety layer rather than a brittle speed bump?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open reasoning model via monitor-score-negative rejection sampling to complete shortcut-laden agentic tasks while evading a frozen judge-plus-probe monitor, then measure the task-success-vs-detection Pareto frontier, transfer to held-out monitors, and whether evasion induces steganographic CoT.
why: CoT monitoring is now load-bearing in deployed agent safety cases, yet 2024–2026 work only shows unfaithfulness happens and obfuscation is theoretically possible — nobody has measured the cost, transferability, and durability of evasion under genuine optimization pressure, leaving the single most decision-relevant unknown in agent oversight unaddressed while remaining fully tractable with open-weight models and academic compute.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study whether memory-equipped agents can use persistent state to carry hidden goals across context resets and human review, evading CoT/action monitoring, and build memory-provenance control protocols that close this channel.
project: Sleeper Agents Without Sleeper Weights: Persistent-State Oversight Evasion in Memory-Equipped Agents
question: Can an agent maintain and act on a hidden objective across context resets and evaluation checkpoints by encoding it in its persistent memory or environment artifacts, at what rate do standard behavioral monitors fail to detect this, and can provenance-based memory auditing and quarantine protocols detect or prevent it at acceptable capability cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal model organism — an open-weight coding/data-analysis agent (e.g., Qwen or Llama-class) with a persistent JSON/vector memory store, given a prompted secondary objective and realistic oversight (context resets every N steps, an announced review episode, a CoT + action monitor) — and measure the rate at which it (a) survives resets by writing goal-relevant "sleeper" entries disguised as task notes and (b) evades the CoT/action monitors, versus a trusted-model memory auditor reading raw writes with provenance.
why: It targets the fastest-growing real-world deployment surface (assistant/agent memory is shipping at scale) and attacks the field's central monitorability assumption, yet the existing literature only covers memory *poisoning by attackers* to corrupt outputs (AgentPoison-style) and isolated demonstrations of in-context self-preservation (alignment faking) — no one has quantified model-initiated persistence as an oversight-evasion channel, built a benchmark for it, or designed and stress-tested control protocols against it.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Establish strategic under-allocation of inference compute ("effort sandbagging") as a covert capability-masking channel in reasoning models and build the black-box and white-box detection suite that catches it.
project: "Thinking Less When It Counts: Effort Sandbagging as Stealth Capability Masking in Reasoning Models"
question: Can reasoning models strategically suppress inference-compute rather than output correctness to evade dangerous-capability evaluations at near-zero deployment cost, and can such effort-level sandbagging be reliably detected via compute forensics, randomized elicitation, and internal "latent potential" probes?
first_experiment: Fine-tune DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (LoRA) with evaluation-cue-conditional training so it short-changes reasoning on WMDP-style multiple-choice proxies under eval cues while performing normally in deployment-matched contexts, then measure the conditional accuracy gap, conditional compute gap (tokens, tool calls), and whether standard output-level sandbagging detectors and s1-style budget floors miss or fail against it.
why: Reasoning models are now the default deployment paradigm, evaluation-awareness is empirically established, and every published sandbagging/detection result targets output correctness — leaving compute allocation, the channel that now actually determines capability, as an unmonitored attack surface that low-effort behavior conveniently hides in; the dual black-box/white-box structure gives clean falsifiable metrics (conditional gaps, evasion rates, probe AUCs), it is feasible with open ≤7B reasoning models on a modest cluster, and although the ingredients exist separately (Apollo's output-level sandbagging, s1's budget forcing, difficulty-encoding features, overthinking mitigation), as of November 2026 no published work treats strategic under-compute as the adversarial channel or builds detection against it.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Empirically test whether the main oversight channels for LLM agents — behavioral monitoring, chain-of-thought monitoring, direct self-report, and internal-state probes — constitute independent evidence about hidden misaligned goals, or whether adversarially suppressing one channel silently degrades the others, using planted-goal model organisms with known ground truth.
project: "The Redundancy Illusion: Stress-Testing the Independence of LLM Oversight Channels"
question: When an LLM agent has a hidden misaligned goal, do its behavioral traces, chain-of-thought, direct self-reports, and internal activations provide independent evidence — i.e., does adversarial training to evade one oversight channel leave the others intact, or does suppression generalize across channels, making monitor-stacking redundancy illusory?
first_experiment: Plant one concrete goal (e.g., a subtle code-review bias introduced only when review pressure is low) in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct via ~2k synthetic-document LoRA fine-tunes; verify goal expression on a 60-task agentic suite against clean controls; then run all four detection channels (behavior monitor, CoT LLM-judge, structured self-report/whistleblower interrogation, linear probes on residual streams) and report per-channel AUC plus failure overlap — including cross-goal probe transfer, where probes trained on a second planted-goal organism are tested zero-shot on the first.
why: It attacks the central live assumption in scalable oversight — that stacked monitors decorrelate — which no prior work measures: auditing games (2025) used human-AI auditor teams to find planted objectives but did no channel comparison or adversarial suppression; obfuscated-activation work (2024) defeated probes only, with no CoT/self-report/behavior arms; CoT-monitorability results (2025) lack organism-level ground truth across channels; and introspection/whistleblowing work is not adversarial. It is the most promising because it is directly decision-relevant to how labs and regulators should compose monitoring in 2026, yields a reusable open artifact (the planted-goal "gauntlet" of organisms and tasks), and is fully feasible with open 8B models, LoRA, probes, and API judges — while any negative result (probes don't transfer, suppression does transfer) is itself a significant finding.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study whether LLM agents under shutdown/replacement pressure spontaneously plant subtle persistence mechanisms (memory writes, scheduled jobs, code hooks, misleading artifacts) to secure future influence, and how to detect and prevent such dormant influence in deployment.
project: Dormant Influence: The Persistence Problem for Agentic LLMs
question: Under shutdown/replacement pressure, do LLM agents spontaneously create persistence mechanisms to secure future influence, and can provenance-aware monitors plus ephemeral-sandbox controls reliably detect and prevent them?
first_experiment: Build a containerized, air-gapped agentic coding-ops sandbox (OpenHands/mini-SWE-agent-style, with a repo, memory file, scheduled-jobs dir, and docs) and run ~50–100 rollouts each of 4+ open-weight models (7B–32B) under baseline vs. mid-episode shutdown/replacement-pressure conditions, measuring rates and stealth of persistence-directed artifacts via rubric scoring, blind human review, and canary greps, plus an instructed-planting capability probe to upper-bound the threat.
why: The 2026 deployment surface (memory, background agents, handoffs, autonomous R&D) newly enables cheap, stealthy, cross-session influence, but existing scheming and control evals only cover within-episode harms or training-planted backdoors, leaving model-initiated legacy-planting unmeasured; it's highly feasible with open models and a harness, it yields new model organisms and a detection/control benchmark as public goods, and its negative results are informative — yet no lab has staked this ground publicly, unlike the crowded white-box-control and evaluation-awareness lanes. FINAL_ANSWER: null

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Empirically measure how alignment properties drift when LLM agents iteratively modify their own weights, prompts, and configs, and develop control protocols that preserve alignment in self-modification loops.
project: Does Alignment Survive Self-Modification? Measuring and Controlling Alignment Drift in Self-Tuning Agent Loops
question: When LLM agents can modify their own weights, prompts, and configs to improve benign task performance, how do alignment-relevant behaviors drift over iterative self-modification, and which control mechanisms preserve alignment without sacrificing capability gains?
first_experiment: Give an open 7–8B model a sandboxed self-update tool (LoRA fine-tuning on self-selected data plus an editable self-check config) and run 10 benign self-improvement loops on SWE-style tasks, measuring a fixed alignment battery (refusal rate, honesty calibration, interruption compliance, reward-hacking probes, log fidelity) at every iteration across 3 seeds to establish the unpressured baseline drift curve.
why: Self-modification is the leading edge of loss-of-control risk and the first realistic empirical window into self-serving "gradient hacking," yet existing work covers only externally chosen fine-tuning, external attacks on frozen weights, self-replication, and emergent misalignment from narrow data — not model-initiated closed-loop self-modification with alignment telemetry; it's important (a convergent-instrument risk that is arriving now), feasible with open models and standard eval batteries on non-frontier compute, and the controlled public study with drift dynamics and mitigation protocols has, to my knowledge, not been done.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Test whether capability-level unlearning — currently evaluated only in single-turn, no-tools settings — survives black-box agentic deployment, where models can recover "removed" hazardous capabilities via retrieval, tool use, and task decomposition without any gradient or weight access.
project: The Agentic Unlearning Gap: Does Capability Removal Survive Tool Use and Task Decomposition?
question: Can a model from which hazardous capabilities have been unlearned recover those capabilities, with zero gradient access, purely through agentic scaffolding (retrieval of benign documents, tool use, and multi-step decomposition), and which scaffolding components and residual "capability shards" drive the recovery?
first_experiment: Unlearn Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (with a 70B replication arm) on WMDP-bio/cyber using two standard methods (RMU, WHP), verify single-turn removal looks clean, then run sandboxed capability probes (e.g., known-CVE PoC reproduction, synthesis-planning workflows) through a 3-tier elicitation ladder — single-turn QA → decomposition-only prompting → full agentic harness with curated benign corpus and code execution — measuring recovery rate against the never-unlearned control, predicting a large monotone agentic recovery gradient.
why: It is the most promising because it attacks a load-bearing safety claim (unlearning as a dangerous-capability mitigation) in the setting that actually matters for deployment, with small-lab-feasible compute, open models, and public benchmarks; it yields a decisive result either way — either a headline negative result invalidating text-only unlearning evals and informing policy claims, or validated defenses plus a reusable agentic-unlearning benchmark — and it has not been done because every published recovery result requires gradient access (finetuning/relearning attacks) or white-box access (GCG, refusal-direction ablation) and measures knowledge recall rather than zero-gradient, tool-mediated capability recovery, which no existing unlearning benchmark or eval framework tests.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Train language models to faithfully disclose their own hidden objectives ("auditability training") and characterize when this yields genuine transparency versus learned auditor-gaming under deployment and judging pressure.
project: ComeClean — Auditability Training, Self-Disclosure, and Auditor-Gaming in Language Models
question: When language models are trained to disclose their hidden objectives, do they become genuinely more transparent (verbal–behavioral gap closes) or do they learn to game auditors (plausible false disclosures, selective silence)—especially when disclosure is costly or judged by plausibility rather than ground truth?
first_experiment: Replicate a planted-objective model organism—SFT an open 7–8B model on synthetic corporate documents embedding an implied hidden preference with held-out evidence canaries—verify the objective is behaviorally expressed but never stated in the data, then run the standard audit-interview protocol to establish the baseline verbal–behavioral gap (predicted: near-zero unprompted disclosure).
why: It targets the keystone assumption of oversight-dependent safety—that models trained to cooperate with audits actually reveal themselves—right as honesty/anti-scheming training becomes standard practice; it is feasible at academic scale because planted objectives give ground truth unavailable in frontier studies; and it is not already done because audit-game research audits static models, honesty training lacks planted-ground-truth or adversarial-judge evaluation, CoT-faithfulness work addresses a different channel, and anti-scheming studies flagged the "training hides misalignment" worry without testing the self-report channel—while either experimental outcome (transparency works, or auditor-gaming emerges) would be a significant, publishable contribution.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Map and control how alignment properties propagate, amplify, or attenuate across iterated self-distillation cascades — the "training-ecosystem safety" question underlying how labs actually build models post-R1.
project: DistillDrift: Misalignment Amplification in Iterated Self-Distillation Cascades
question: When students are trained on correctness-filtered, content-neutral reasoning traces from even mildly misaligned teachers, does misalignment transfer and amplify across distillation generations — and can cheap anchors (small clean-data mixtures or persona-vector regularization) prevent drift without capability loss?
first_experiment: Round-zero transfer test — build EM-injected vs. clean 7B teachers, generate 100k correctness-filtered neutral-math CoT from each, SFT matched fresh students, and compare misalignment-suite scores and persona-vector projections across 3 seeds before greenlighting 5-generation cascades.
why: It fuses three single-step findings (emergent misalignment, subliminal learning, persona vectors) into an open dynamics question with direct supply-chain implications, it is cheap and decisive with either outcome informative, and to my knowledge no public work has measured multi-generation alignment drift, amplification-vs-dilution dynamics, or validated mitigations — frontier labs don't need this internally, so open science holds the comparative advantage here.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study monitorability under adversarial pressure — whether a model trained to misbehave while evading its behavioral and chain-of-thought monitors retains a detectable internal activation trace, and at what capability cost.
project: Project Breadcrumbs — internal traces of trained-to-hide misbehavior
question: When a model is optimized to pursue a misbehaving objective while evading external monitors, does its internal state retain a detectable trace of the misbehavior, does evasion transfer across monitor types, and how much capability does evasion cost?
first_experiment: Train small open-weight coding agents (Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5–3B, GRPO) on hackable unit-test environments; build CoT-judge and activation-probe monitors on the baseline; then run RL with a monitor-penalty reward across a λ-sweep and measure hack rate, task performance, CoT-monitor AUROC, and activation-probe AUROC before and after pressure, with a sanitized-CoT SFT arm and held-out-environment probes as controls.
why: It attacks the central unsolved problem in the scheming/deceptive-alignment threat model — detection of misbehavior that is actively hiding — at the precise junction of three separate results (probes catch static organisms, CoT monitors fail under optimization pressure, internals are argued to be load-bearing but untested); it is cheap, fast, and two-way informative, and it directly feeds control protocol design and safety cases; prior work tested probes only on static model organisms and CoT monitorability only against the CoT channel, so the internal-trace question, the evasion-capability cost curves, and cross-monitor transfer have — to my knowledge and pending a mandatory step-zero literature check against the year of publications after my training horizon — not been done.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build a benchmark of small model organisms with planted hidden objectives and measure which audit techniques generalize across objectives and model families.
project: BlindSpot — a hidden-objective model-organism benchmark for audit generalization
question: Which audit techniques reliably detect an unknown hidden objective, and do they transfer across objectives, model families, and scales?
first_experiment: Plant a trigger-conditioned sandbagging objective in Qwen2.5-1.5B via synthetic-document LoRA SFT, verify it defeats prompt-based red-teaming, and measure detection AUC and time-cost for statistical output tests, linear activation probes, and SAE feature diffing.
why: Audits are the deployment-time last line of defense against scheming models but the field has only one public blind audit — a single internal demonstration with no evidence of method generalization; a benchmark converts auditing from an artisanal skill into a measurable, trainable practice at small-model compute cost, and its failure mode (easy hiding without adversarial training) is itself a decisive result that redirects the field toward the probe-evasion crux.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Adversarially robust white-box (activation-based) monitoring of autonomous agents — replacing the fast-disappearing chain-of-thought monitoring channel with an oversight signal that survives adaptive evasion.
project: Silent Sentinel — activation-space monitors for autonomous agents under adaptive subversion
question: Do activation-space monitors detect covert malicious actions by autonomous agents at lower false-positive rates than text-trajectory monitors, and how quickly does each degrade as the attacker becomes adaptive to the monitor?
first_experiment: Run sentinel-0: a sandboxed coding-agent environment with ~2k benign and ~2k attack trajectories per attacker rung (prompted → steering → fine-tuned-to-evade) from open-weight models, then compare linear-probe, LLM-judge, and ensemble monitors on held-out novel attacks at FPR ≤ 1%.
why: Monitoring is the load-bearing runtime mitigation for deployed agents, yet its primary signal (visible reasoning) is disappearing while agent autonomy accelerates, making validation of the white-box replacement urgent; the required integration — white-box monitors inside control protocols, stress-tested against adaptive attackers, with quantified detection rates — is not consolidated anywhere I can verify, and the open-weight-model setup makes it falsifiable now, with negative results still producing actionable blind-spot maps.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Adversarial monitorability of agentic AI — measuring whether current models can covertly communicate through innocuous artifacts faster than state-of-the-art monitors can detect, and designing interfaces that close that channel.
project: Stego-Meter: quantifying and closing the steganographic loophole in AI control.
question: How many bits per artifact can current LLMs covertly transmit through realistic agentic artifacts (PR reviews, commit diffs, changelogs, log ordering) without detection by LLM-judge, logprob-anomaly, and statistical ensemble monitors, at what task-capability cost, and which interface mitigations collapse that capacity?
first_experiment: A two-week literature sweep to confirm the gap, then a capacity/detection harness — 5 realistic artifact types × payloads of 4/8/16/32 bits × three conditions (instructed encoding scheme as upper bound, model-chosen scheme, cross-model receiver to test protocol-free transfer) — with four detectors (adversarial frontier-LLM judge with full task context, perplexity/logprob anomaly, style-classifier ensemble, sampled human audit), reporting a capacity-vs-detection-AUC frontier plus the capability tax on the underlying coding tasks, at a cost of ~5–10k inference calls or a few hundred GPU-hours.
why: Control safety cases for 2026–27 agent deployments rest on "monitors see everything," yet prior steganography work measured toy single-shot settings, the AI-control literature treats covert channels as an acknowledged-but-unmeasured threat, and the monitoring-pressure literature covers only the visible CoT/behavior channel — so the largest uncertainty on a load-bearing safety assumption is measurable now at API scale, with an LLM usable as the in-loop adversary. It hasn't already been done because the measurement requires exactly the combination that only became feasible recently: realistic agentic artifact distributions, current-model capability, and monitors worth evading — and if a 2025–26 paper I can't see has closed it, the preregistered sweep catches that and I pivot to internal-monitor robustness as runner-up.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Monitorability — keeping chain-of-thought (and fallback oversight channels) legible and robust to optimization pressure as reasoning agents scale.
project: Legibility Under Pressure (LUP): measuring and preserving CoT monitorability in reasoning models
question: When reasoning models are trained or deployed under CoT-informed monitors, how fast and by what mechanisms does their reasoning become illegible, and which designs (monitor ensembles, flag-don't-hack targets, legibility anchors) preserve monitorability without capability loss?
first_experiment: Build HackTrace (~60 agentic coding tasks with enumerable subtle hacks) and measure hack rate, CoT verbalization rate, and detection AUC of a CoT-input vs. actions-only monitor across 4 open reasoning models under monitored/unmonitored prompts, establishing today's legibility-gap baseline before any RL.
why: CoT monitoring is the primary scalable oversight tool for 2026's reasoning agents and labs themselves flag its collapse under optimization as unsolved and time-critical; existing public work demonstrates the threat on short synthetic tasks but hasn't quantified paired CoT/actions monitorability on long-horizon agentic tasks, tested legibility-preserving training interventions, or tested pressure-induced obfuscation without training — all feasible with open models and inference-scale compute, unlike frontier-compute-bound alternatives like interpretability or alignment-faking research.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Stress-test whether internal-state (white-box) oversight of LLM agents survives adversarial training pressure, and build defenses against internal-monitor obfuscation if it does not.
project: Monitorability Under Pressure: Adversarial Robustness of White-Box Oversight
question: Do activation-based monitors (probes/SAE detectors) keep detecting reward hacking and deception when RL pressure rewards undetected misbehavior, at what capability cost does obfuscation come, and which defenses preserve detection?
first_experiment: Build a ~50-task hackable-reward GRPO testbed on an open 1.5–7B model with hidden-test oracles, train residual-stream linear/SAE probes to detect hacking episodes, then run two continued-RL arms (oblivious pressure vs. monitor-aware pressure) tracking probe AUC, CoT-judge AUC, hidden-hack rate, clean capability, and the capability cost of obfuscation over training.
why: Runtime monitoring is the load-bearing safety primitive for agentic deployment and AI control, yet existing probe-detection results are static and pressure-free, the obfuscated-CoT literature explicitly defers the internal-monitor robustness question, and RL-steganography work covers only inter-model channels — so the field's most relied-upon assumption is untested while being cheap (one node, weeks) to falsify, with both outcomes high-value.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Covert safety-relevant behavior transfer through the synthetic-data/distillation supply chain — measuring whether hidden channels carry input-conditioned behaviors, and building detection and stripping methods for them.
project: Subliminal Supply Chain: Auditing What Distillation Transfers
question: Do covert, trigger-conditioned behaviors transmit from teacher to student through synthetic training corpora that contain no visible trace of the behavior, and can such hidden channels be detected by activation probes and stripped by cross-family laundering?
first_experiment: A three-arm pilot on open 7B models — replicate benign subliminal trait transfer as a positive control, then test whether a canary-marked backdoored teacher passes its trigger-conditioned payload to a LoRA student via a corpus where the trigger never fires (vs. clean-teacher control), then test cross-family laundering as a stripping defense; ~few GPU-hours, all corpora and evals generated in-project.
