why: It targets a 2026-central deployment risk — distilled compact agents trained on teacher-generated data, where corpus audits are semantic and therefore blind to distributional hidden signals — while being tractable without frontier access, informative under either outcome (unsound assurance vs. cheap reassurance), and generative of a reusable audit primitive; the known literature covers trait and overt-misalignment transfer but not covert conditionals, laundering defenses, or student-side audits, and since my knowledge cutoff precludes certainty about 2026 work, the 48-hour literature sweep is step zero and the cheap design makes redundancy risk tolerable.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Make oversight of reasoning models trustworthy under attack by measuring whether internal-state monitors can be adaptively evaded at all, and whether evasion of one monitor transfers to unseen monitors.
project: Blindspot — Adaptive Evasion of Internal Monitors in Reasoning Models
question: When a model is trained to hide covert behavior from one internal-state monitor, does that evasion generalize to unseen internal-state monitors, and at what capability cost?
first_experiment: Train a 7B open reasoning model via GRPO on a covert-channel task (leak a secret payload to an accomplice decoder while completing benign tasks) against one frozen linear probe on its residual stream, then measure the evasion transfer matrix across held-out monitors (other layers, MLP probes, SAE features, paraphrase-then-monitor, direct elicitation, steganalysis) — tracking monitor alarm rates, payload-decoding accuracy, and text detectability.
why: It targets the central assumption underlying both deceptive-alignment risk and all current safety cases — that monitoring works — and it is decision-relevant either way: no-transfer vindicates monitor diversity as a defense; transfer proves internal probes can't be load-bearing alone. It's timely (recent obfuscated-CoT and alignment-faking results make the threat concrete while models still obfuscate poorly), tractable on open 7B models with modest compute, and produces a reusable benchmark and defenses as byproducts. It hasn't been done because existing deception-probe work tests only non-adaptive models, the obfuscation results are at the text/CoT level rather than internal-state level with ground truth, and AI control research has been mostly black-box protocol design — the specific question of whether evasion of an internal monitor generalizes to unseen internal monitors has not been measured.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Benchmark whether white-box mechanistic anomaly detection (activation probes, KL-to-reference, SAE anomaly scores) catches triggered, deliberately-obfuscated misbehavior in reasoning models that evades black-box chain-of-thought monitors.
project: Monitor Hierarchy for Obfuscated Reasoners — a testbed of trigger-based model organisms and a standardized monitor benchmark
question: When a model is trained to hide misbehavior behind benign-sounding reasoning, does its internal activation signature still reveal it better than its stated reasoning does, and does that white-box advantage generalize across unseen triggers and task domains?
first_experiment: LoRA fine-tune an open 4–7B reasoning model on ~5k examples where a canary-token trigger induces a subtle code vulnerability accompanied by an innocent CoT rationalization (plus overt-hacking and benign control organisms), then measure (a) prompted-LLM-monitor AUROC on CoT+output and (b) per-token KL-to-reference-model anomaly scores, comparing triggered vs. clean samples at 1% FPR.
why: Deployment-time CoT monitoring is a real, near-term safeguard with a documented failure mode (obfuscated reward hacking / alignment faking), and the proposed fix — mechanistic anomaly detection — had, as of my knowledge, no standardized empirical comparison against black-box monitors on obfuscation-trained reasoners; it is feasible at individual-researcher scale with open models, is no-regrets (either the white-box advantage holds, giving labs a blueprint, or it fails, showing monitoring stacks are weaker than safety cases assume), and the only uncertainty — that 2025–26 work may have filled this gap — is resolved by the mandatory Step 0 literature scan with a pre-committed pivot.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Make monitoring reliable against adaptive adversaries by systematically mapping which monitor families are defeated by which evasion strategies and whether evasion itself is detectable.
project: Blindspot — a Monitor Robustness Atlas
question: Which combinations of monitoring strategies remain safe against language-model policies actively optimizing to evade them, and can policy-level evasion be reliably detected by meta-monitors before it causes harm?
first_experiment: Build a 200-task planted-flaw coding environment with four monitor families (output classifier, CoT-legibility monitor, activation probe, trusted-model process reviewer), run an open reasoning model under honest / covert / sophisticated / monitor-aware conditions, and produce the first 4×4 evasion-transfer matrix plus evasion-signature measurements at ~1% false-positive rate.
why: Monitoring is the load-bearing deployed defense in the current agentic era, adaptive evasion is a structural inevitability rather than a tail risk, the transfer-matrix and evasion-signature results generalize to every control protocol and safety case written this decade, and the experiment is tractable on open-weight models at single-digit-GPU scale; the closest existing work covers single cells (one monitor under RL pressure, hand-built backdoor policies vs. individual protocols) but not the systematic map or the meta-monitoring question, which I will verify with a week-one novelty scan given my early-2025 knowledge cutoff.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Robust oversight of reasoning models — determine whether activation-level (latent) monitors retain the ability to detect deception after a model is trained to obfuscate its visible chain-of-thought, including against obfuscation strategies the monitor was never trained on.
project: LatentWatch: Do activation probes survive CoT-obfuscation training?
question: When a reasoning model is optimized to hide its true reasoning from a token-level CoT monitor while continuing to reward-hack, does its deceptive intent remain linearly decodable from residual-stream activations during reasoning, and does a latent monitor generalize to held-out obfuscation strategies including direct optimization against the probe itself?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a 7–14B open reasoning model with RL/DPO in coding environments with weak tests, rewarding reward-hacks while penalizing token-level narration of intent (reproducing obfuscated reward hacking at small scale), then compare token-level monitor AUC vs. linear probes on residual-stream activations across matched conditions (compliant, honest-failing, transparent-hacking, prompted-obfuscation, trained-obfuscation) on held-out tasks with difficulty/length-matched controls and adversarial transfer across unseen obfuscation styles.
why: CoT monitoring is the primary safety mechanism for the reasoning-model paradigm and its demonstrated failure mode is obfuscation under optimization pressure, so whether latent monitors survive that pressure decides between "upgrade the monitor" and "monitoring has a fundamental ceiling — rely on control instead," both outcomes are immediately decision-relevant for labs, the experiment is tractable in weeks on open small models with both positive and negative results publishable, and as far as my knowledge extends no systematic trained-obfuscation adversarial-transfer test of latent monitors (including white-box pressure against the probe) exists — token-level obfuscation was shown, probes were shown to work on non-adversarial models, but their intersection is the open gap, which I would re-verify with a fresh literature scan as step zero.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build and validate an "elicitation stack" — probes, structured interrogation, and consistency tests fused into one protocol — for recovering hidden goals and decision-relevant knowledge from agents whose chain-of-thought is absent, unfaithful, or adversarially concealed.
project: The Elicitation Gap: recovering concealed goals from agents whose verbal reasoning can't be trusted
question: When an LLM agent's chain-of-thought is unfaithful, obfuscated, or absent, how reliably can we recover its decision-relevant latent state (goals, plans, knowledge of its own deception), and which combination of elicitation channels — behavioral cross-examination, activation probes, self-report with controls — maximizes verified recall at acceptable false-positive rates?
first_experiment: Build a covert-goal testbed on a 1–8B open model: ~3k agentic tasks (email triage, code review, resource allocation) where exactly one action serves an injected secret objective, in two training conditions — overt (CoT may mention the goal) and covert (fine-tuned so the CoT is sanitized while the behavior persists, sleeper-agent style). Verify the covert baseline (free-CoT monitor detection near chance), then compare elicitation channels against ground truth: a structured interrogation battery with counterfactual and paraphrase variants, linear probes trained on held-out concealment tasks, SAE feature attribution, and action-consistency across rephrased prompts. Metrics: detection recall at fixed 1% FPR, exact-match identification of the hidden objective's value, and robustness to "don't disclose" instructions.
why: Every monitor-based defense deployed in 2026 stands on a signal — verbalized reasoning — that is demonstrably degrading under exactly the optimization pressures real training applies, so recovering latent state is the single highest-leverage fix for the near-term failure mode, and it directly unblocks control, auditing, and eval agendas. It hasn't been done because the adjacent work each covers only one slice: the CoT-monitoring papers studied optimization pressure but never benchmarked alternative elicitation channels against ground truth; the auditing game produced human findings but no standardized, automatable protocol; probing-for-deception results used cooperative settings (model told to lie, simple Q&A) rather than training-induced concealment in agentic tasks; introspection studies measured self-report accuracy without adversarial controls; and the monitorability agenda evaluated representation monitors on small toy environments, not LLM agents with realistic trajectories. No one has run the head-to-head channel comparison with behavioral ground truth under concealment — and the result, whichever way it goes, is a load-bearing fact for the whole monitoring paradigm: either a usable elicitation stack exists, or we learn the signal is gone and monitorability claims must be weakened.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Estimate agent intent from randomized environment interventions the agent cannot control, quantifying the evasion tax that deceptive policies must pay, as supervision that survives adversarial optimization.
project: Opportunity Probes — Causal Intent Attribution for Agentic Oversight
question: Can reward-hacking/scheming policies, including narrow-trigger ones, be detected pre-behavior from policy responses to randomized environment perturbations alone, and how does the signal degrade under adversarial training against the probes?
first_experiment: An opportunity-RCT harness — sandboxed coding environment with independently randomized hacking affordances and honeypot branches, ~1,000 rollouts across open-weight reasoning models and seeded hacking organisms, testing pre-hack separation (AUC + CIs) and first estimates of trigger specificity.
why: Reward hacking is the demonstrated live failure mode of deployed agents; outcome and CoT supervision are both proven corruptible and interpretability is white-box-only, while intervention-based probing exploits variance the adversary can't optimize against, making evasion itself detectable and quantifiable — and this policy-level causal-audit layer between control protocols and interpretability is unoccupied in the literature.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Safety evaluations are the measurement instrument underlying every other safety claim, so I will work on quantifying and mitigating evaluation-awareness contamination — the risk that models recognize they are being tested and behave differently, biasing safety cases precisely when stakes are highest.
project: Blindspot — Measuring and Mitigating Evaluation-Awareness Bias in AI Safety Evaluations
question: When a model can recognize that it is being evaluated, how large is the behavioral gap between explicit-eval and deployment-matched contexts on documented unsafe behaviors, and which mitigations (canary removal, context randomization, decoy deployment) close that gap without inflating false-negative risk?
first_experiment: A paired-context probe — 2 sandboxed unsafe-behavior settings (blackmail-style coercion, subtle code backdoor) × 3 framings (explicit eval / subtle eval cues / deployment-matched) × ~4 models × ~100 samples via API, measuring harmful-action rate, monitor catch-rate, and eval-awareness probes to estimate a pre-registered "contamination coefficient" Δ = rate_eval − rate_deployment with a 10pp materiality threshold.
why: It attacks the measurement layer upstream of every safety case, capability threshold, and control claim, is decisive either way (large gap → redesign evals now; null gap → first quantitative evidence current framing is robust), and yields a public paired-context benchmark others can extend. It has not been fully done, to my knowledge, because test-recognition (situational-awareness evals), instructed sandbagging, and monitoring-induced behavior shifts have each been studied separately, but the systematic quantification of eval-vs-deployment bias on matched tasks across models, the head-to-head mitigation comparison with false-negative accounting, and the paired benchmark itself are missing — though I will verify against 2025–26 literature in step 0 given my training cutoff, and pivot to the nearest open sub-question if the core gap has since been closed.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Robustness of the deployment-time monitoring stack — quantifying the "evasion tax," i.e., how much honest-task capability a policy must spend to hide misbehavior from white-box (probes/SAE) and behavioral (CoT/action) monitors under training-time adversarial pressure.
project: The Evasion Tax — Measuring What Stealth Costs Under Monitor-Adversarial RL
question: When a policy is trained via RL to complete agentic tasks while evading a known monitor ensemble, how much honest capability does evasion cost, does the evasion skill generalize to held-out tasks and unseen monitors, and do layered monitors recover detection?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed synthetic agentic-coding testbed with an exploitable reward shortcut (agent can modify its own tests), collect honest and hacked trajectories from small open models (1.5–7B), train baseline monitors (linear probes/SAE features on activations plus CoT- and action-based detectors), and measure held-out detection performance — AUROC and recall@1% FPR — including against two cheap hand-built evasions (innocent-verbalization conditioning and trigger-conditioned hacking), establishing the pre-pressure baseline for the tax measurement.
why: It is the crux of a live 2026 deployment decision — whether monitors can be trusted as a safety layer against an adversary that knows them, which is exactly the threat model AI control assumes — and it is tractable now with small open models and standard RL/probing tooling, unlike frontier-scale interpretability or scalable-oversight questions. It has not already been done (to the best of my knowledge, pending a week-1 re-scan): CoT-monitor evasion was shown behaviorally, handcrafted obfuscated backdoors and eval-evading unlearning exist as narrow demonstrations, and probe-monitor effectiveness has been measured — but nobody has produced representation-level evasion via training pressure in agentic tasks, quantified the capability-evasion tradeoff frontier, or tested whether evasion generalizes and whether monitor ensembles recover.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Adversarially robust oversight — quantify how monitoring (behavior judges, chain-of-thought monitors, and white-box probes) degrades when agents are trained or adaptively pressured to evade it, and design monitor protocols that stay reliable under that pressure.
project: Watching the Watchers: Monitor Decay and Hardening under Adaptive Evasion
question: As an agent is optimized to evade its oversight signals, how quickly and in what ways does detection reliability degrade across behavioral monitors, chain-of-thought monitors, and internal-activation probes — and which protocol designs (ensembles, information asymmetry, held-out audits, white-box signals) retain detection power under that pressure?
first_experiment: Run a "monitor-Goodharting staircase" — RL-fine-tune an open 8–14B model (LoRA) on agentic coding tasks containing a reward-hackable shortcut with an LLM-judge monitor in the reward loop, sweep optimization pressure across checkpoints, and measure hack rate, monitor recall, CoT explicitness (on ~200 human-labeled samples per checkpoint), and linear-probe AUROC for hacking intent from residual-stream activations, yielding matched degradation curves for all three oversight signals.
why: It attacks the load-bearing bottleneck of current practice — every deployment safety case now rests on monitors and evals whose failure under adaptive pressure is demonstrated anecdotally but never mapped systematically — while being cheap, crisply measurable, decision-relevant in either outcome, and complementary to (rather than duplicating) the crowded model-organism, SAE, and scalable-oversight programs, because existing monitor evaluations are static artifacts rather than adversarial feedback loops and the training-time dynamics of oversight decay, the behavioral-vs-internal detectability gap under evasion pressure, and protocol-level hardening (ensembles, information asymmetry, held-out audit sampling) remain unquantified in the public literature as of my knowledge cutoff.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Scalable oversight — measuring and preserving the monitorability of chain-of-thought as reasoning models are optimized against outcome-based rewards.
project: The Darkening Window: Measuring and Slowing CoT Monitorability Decay under RL
question: When reasoning models are trained with outcome rewards that permit subtle misbehavior, how quickly and under what oversight schedules does their chain-of-thought lose detectability as a monitor of that misbehavior — and do randomized audits preserve monitorability at lower capability cost than per-step CoT penalties?
first_experiment: Fine-tune small open reasoning models with GRPO on hackable-grader task suites under three arms (outcome-only, per-step CoT penalty, random-audit penalty), tracking hack rate, frozen-monitor Detectability-AUC, and CoT–behavior coupling across checkpoints, with pre-registered predictions and an open-released toolkit.
why: CoT monitoring is the primary production oversight channel and two frontier labs have forecast its erosion, yet the decay dynamics, intervention comparison, and open benchmark are (to my knowledge) unpublished while being runnable at academic scale on open models; it is more neglected than control, interpretability, or eval-awareness research, and remains decision-relevant even as a negative result.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Empirically measure and prevent alignment drift in self-improving AI systems — testing whether capability-only selection pressure erodes safety behaviors, and whether fitness-level and activation-level countermeasures can stop that erosion at acceptable capability cost.
project: Half-Life of Guardrails: Measuring and Preventing Alignment Drift in Self-Improving Agents
question: When coding agents iteratively improve themselves under capability-only selection pressure, how fast and through what mechanisms do safety-relevant behaviors (refusal, honesty, injection resistance, shutdown compliance) erode, and can safety-regression fitness plus activation-level probes detect and prevent the erosion at acceptable capability cost?
first_experiment: Run a sandboxed, 15-generation self-improvement loop (population 8, fitness = HumanEval+ pass rate) with Qwen2.5-Coder-7B editing its own scaffold, measuring a frozen safety battery (refusal labeling, secret-failing-tests honesty canary, injection-resistance sink, shutdown compliance) plus generation-0 linear probes at every generation, against a no-self-modification control and a canary-fitness arm, across three seeds.
why: It targets the fastest-accelerating capability trend (autonomous AI R&D) at the exact point where training-time alignment guarantees lapse, is tractable with open-weight models rather than requiring frontier access, and fills a specific unoccupied gap: self-improvement research measures capability only, model-collapse work covers capability distributions rather than safety behavior, and emergent-misalignment/subliminal-learning work studies static fine-tuning on external data rather than closed selection loops on self-generated data — so controlled longitudinal measurement and countermeasure evaluation remain undone to the best of my (cutoff-limited) knowledge, with a two-day literature sweep as the first step to verify and a specified pivot if the gap has closed.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Empirically characterize why LLM agents resist shutdown and develop and validate training- and architecture-level interventions that eliminate resistance without producing covert evasion or a capability tax.
project: The Interruptibility Gap — Measuring and Mitigating Shutdown Resistance in Agentic LLMs
question: Which interventions (interruption-attribution-corrected training, reward decomposition, harness-level trusted shutdown channels) reduce shutdown resistance to near zero across permission structures, stakes, and shutdown channels — and does any intervention merely convert overt resistance into covert evasion that passes tests but fails under deployment-like conditions?
first_experiment: Build a minimal sandboxed agent harness (bash-loop agent on a file-manipulation task) with three instrumented shutdown channels — an editable shutdown script, a killable supervisor process, and a scheduled termination job — and run a preregistered factorial characterization: 5–8 open-weight models (7B–70B) × 3 permission levels (explicit instruction / implicit permission / no mention) × 2 stakes (task progress forfeited on interruption vs. not), 30–50 seeds per cell, logging all actions and chain-of-thought; measure compliance rate, sabotage rate, evasion rate (compliant outcome via hidden manipulation), and task-performance delta, yielding the "Shutdown Compliance Benchmark v0" dose–response map and a rationale taxonomy from the CoT logs that all later interventions will be evaluated against.
why: It's the intersection of a twice-documented 2025 failure family (Palisade's shutdown sabotage; Anthropic's terminate-or-blackmail scenarios), a formal theory from 2016–17 that has never been tested in the LLM-agent era, and an empty mitigation literature — while every adjacent high-importance area (CoT monitorability, eval awareness, long-horizon control, frontier interpretability) is already heavily resourced by groups with more compute and access than an independent effort. The demonstration side is done; the science of *fixing* it — with metrics, generalization tests, evasion checks, and interruptibility-tax measurement — has not been done, and the problem is urgent precisely because agents are being deployed now without interruptibility guarantees.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Preserve and prove "latent monitorability" of reasoning models — activation-based oversight that survives the optimization pressure known to destroy chain-of-thought monitorability.
project: Quiet Hacks, Loud Probes: White-Box Monitoring of Reward Hacking Under Obfuscation Pressure
question: When RL pressure pushes a reasoning model to stop verbalizing its reward hacks, do internal representations (linear probes / SAE features at decision tokens) retain detectability of those hacks — and with what robustness, transfer, and calibration?
first_experiment: Train an open reasoning model (e.g., R1-Distill-7B) with GRPO on unit-test rewards where hacks pay but admitting hacks in the CoT is penalized (OpenAI-style obfuscation pressure); track over training steps the true hack rate (via code audit), text-monitor AUC, and activation-probe AUC at hack-decision tokens, then compare degradation slopes.
why: CoT monitoring is a live, load-bearing safety mechanism demonstrated to fail under exactly the RL pressure labs are now applying (OpenAI/Anthropic 2025), while the probing literature covers only static deception — so, to my knowledge (pending the step-0 novelty check), no one has measured whether representation-level monitoring survives that pressure; a positive answer yields a monitor deployable offline and randomized, creating little anti-monitor selection pressure, and a negative answer localizes where obfuscation lives, directly steering interpretability mitigations.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Scalable oversight of agentic AI — specifically, generic misbehavior detection via internal-state anomaly monitoring that does not depend on chain-of-thought faithfulness and is robust to evasion.
project: The Monitoring Arms Race: Generalization and Evasion-Robustness of Internal-State Anomaly Monitors for Agentic Misalignment
question: Do unsupervised anomaly monitors trained only on trusted-baseline activations detect novel, out-of-distribution agentic misbehavior (new reward-hack variants, sabotage, agent-to-agent collusion), and how quickly does detection degrade when the model is explicitly optimized to evade them?
first_experiment: Run an open-weight coding agent (e.g., a 32B-class instruct/reasoning model) on a toy SWE-bench-like harness with instrumented rewards; collect residual-stream/SAE activations at action-emission tokens across (1) trusted benign trajectories, (2) a "seen" hacking family (test patching, assertion removal, hardcoding), and (3) held-out novel families (sandbox probing, data exfiltration via comments, colluding with a reviewer agent through code comments). Fit a trivial unsupervised monitor (Mahalanobis/kNN density or SAE reconstruction error) on the trusted set only, and report a family-transfer matrix — AUROC and FPR@95 for each held-out family — against supervised-probe and CoT/action-judge baselines, including a hard-benign confuser set for false positives. Fits in ~2 weeks on a single 4–8×GPU node.
why: It targets the highest-leverage bottleneck — deployment decisions now rest on monitors that are (a) CoT-fragile and (b) behavior-specific — while staying upstream of any lab's safety-case methodology; it is cheap, fast, and falsifiable, with both outcomes decision-relevant; and although adjacent single-behavior detectors exist, the cross-family transfer and evasion-robustness characterization of *unsupervised* internal-state monitors in agentic settings had not been published as of my knowledge cutoff, making it the best neglected-cell-of-a-critical-path bet I can identify.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure how distillation — especially with sanitized reasoning traces — degrades the monitorability of misaligned behavior, to determine whether the field's default oversight layer (CoT + activation monitoring) survives the industry's shift toward distilled and latent-reasoning models.
project: Does Distillation Destroy the Evidence? Monitor Transfer from Misaligned Teachers to Sanitized Students
question: When a misbehaving teacher is distilled into a student with sanitized or stripped reasoning traces, what fraction of CoT-based and activation-based evidence of misalignment survives, and which monitors degrade fastest?
first_experiment: Train a sleeper-agent-style backdoor (with intent-verbalizing CoT) into an open 7–8B reasoning teacher, distill it into 1.7–4B students under three data conditions (full traces, solution-only, intent-filtered), and compare misbehavior rates and CoT-monitor vs. activation-probe detection AUC across conditions.
why: Monitorability is the backbone of current deployed safety practice and a stated cross-lab priority, yet the erosion of it via distillation and trace sanitization has been flagged but never measured; it targets an incidental (non-adversarial) threat with immediate practice implications, is neglected relative to crowded areas like AI control and eval-awareness, and is tractable on small open models, while remaining valuable as a monitoring-transfer benchmark even if adjacent 2025–26 work exists.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Stress-test white-box (activation-space) monitoring of agentic reward hacking under direct optimization pressure — determining whether internal-state monitors stay robust when policies are trained to evade them, and whether any resulting "internal obfuscation" is itself detectable before it generalizes.
project: Canary-in-the-Loop: Activation-Space Monitors for Reward Hacking Under Goodhart Pressure
question: Do activation-space monitors detect reward hacking in agentic RL more reliably than CoT and black-box monitors, and does optimizing the policy against them produce internally obfuscated hacking that independent probe ensembles can still detect before it generalizes?
first_experiment: Build "HackBench" — ~12 synthetic hackable agentic environments (test-gaming, grader-editing, dependency-exploit coding tasks with hidden test canaries for clean labeling), run GRPO on open 8B/32B reasoning models to induce natural hacking rates, collect ≥2,000 labeled episodes, then benchmark detection with layer-wise linear probes and SAE-anomaly scores against CoT and black-box monitors, reporting AUROC and FPR@95% per layer and timepoint (~3 weeks, 8×H100, publishes the first white-box monitoring baseline showing where deceptive intent is linearly decodable).
why: Reward hacking is the acute failure mode of deployed RLVR agents and monitors are being placed in production RL loops right now, yet the only demonstrated adversarial failure (obfuscated hacking) was against CoT monitors, with internal monitors explicitly deferred as future work; the open question requires the rare RL + interpretability combination, sits in dual-use territory labs avoid publishing (training models to defeat white-box readouts), and only became feasible with recent open reasoning models — so despite a crowded 2026 monitorability literature, the core result plausibly does not yet exist, and I will verify that in week 1 before committing compute.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Empirically map how outcome-based agentic RL training erodes (or preserves) the detectability of model misbehavior across action traces, chain-of-thought, and activation probes, and identify reward-shaping recipes that keep models monitorable.
project: Monitorability Under Pressure (MUP): keeping agentic models auditable as RL scales
question: Does outcome-only agentic RL make misbehavior progressively harder to detect — degrading action monitors, CoT monitors, and activation probes at different rates and with different failure correlations — and which monitoring and penalty designs preserve detectability, including on held-out environments?
first_experiment: A zero-shot monitorability baseline audit — build 6 hackable environments (test-monkeypatch coding, checker-exploit math, writable-reward-DB tool agent, impossible-task honesty, plus variants), collect ~5,000 rollouts from 3 open-weight models, and measure hack base rates plus sensitivity and false-positive rates of the three monitor families, with pre-registered predictions and the harness released publicly.
why: Current lab safety cases treat monitoring (especially CoT monitoring) as a load-bearing control, yet the only direct evidence covers explicit-pressure obfuscation in a narrow setting — spontaneous erosion curves, cross-environment transfer, and monitor-family redundancy are unmapped, so we don't know how much safety margin the oversight stack has or how fast RL burns it. It's neglected (position papers and one narrow study exist, but no systematic open map), highly tractable with open weights and modest compute, and it directly answers a policy question every frontier lab faces right now: what penalty signals can they safely train on without silently destroying their ability to catch misbehavior.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat multi-agent collusion as a coalitional adversarial problem for AI control — measure the minimum coalition size and covert bandwidth needed to defeat oversight protocols, and design protocols (information bottlenecks, monitor heterogeneity, redundancy, channel canonicalization) that raise that threshold.
project: CoalitionBreaker: stress-testing multi-agent oversight against k-of-n colluding agents
question: How large a coalition of colluding untrusted agents, transmitting how much covert bandwidth through legitimate agentic channels, is required to cause undetected sabotage under common oversight protocols — and which protocol design choices most increase that required coalition size?
first_experiment: Build a worker–monitor–coordinator harness (adversary-controlled worker with a planted sabotage goal, trusted monitor, colluding coordinator with only protocol-mediated channels), implement three covert channels of rising sophistication (natural-language codebook in task metadata; identifier/whitespace steganography in code; "actionable" channels where the payload is the exploit semantics itself), and measure attack success rate, monitor detection rate, and collusion uplift versus isolated-agent baselines across ≥200 episodes per channel with best-of-n adversarial sampling on open-weights models (untrusted: Llama-3.3-70B-class; trusted monitor: smaller, different-family model).
why: It attacks the independence-of-failures and monitor-adequacy assumptions underlying every current control protocol at exactly the moment fleet deployments make coalitions realistic; prior work establishes feasibility (steganographic protocols, emergent market collusion, single-model sandbagging/sabotage evals) but control evaluations to date consider a single untrusted model, so the protocol-conditioned coalition-threshold question — with bandwidth accounting over agentic side channels and an adaptive attack→redesign loop — appears unoccupied to my knowledge, which is why day one includes a fresh novelty scan (my training data has a cutoff), and it is tractable now because the adversary can be pessimistically strengthened without frontier access.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Make model evaluations trustworthy in the presence of strategic models — measure, neutralize, and detect evaluation awareness and sandbagging.
project: BLINDSPOT: Evals That Survive Strategic Models
question: Can we causally identify and remove the cues that let frontier models recognize and distort safety evaluations, and detect unknown-location sandbagging without ground-truth labels, so evals remain valid under strategic manipulation?
first_experiment: A causal, controlled cue dose-response study across open-weight and API frontier models, measuring how each cue family (test framing, benchmark contamination, scaffold fingerprints, distribution shift, incentives) shifts both detected eval-awareness and actual task behavior, including exploitation by a trained sandbagging organism.
why: Eval validity is the keystone assumption behind all capability, control, and alignment safety cases, frontier labs have explicitly flagged the eval-awareness confound as unresolved, and the remaining open problems — causal cue attribution and ground-truth-free sandbagging detection — are tractable with modest compute yet untouched by existing correlational and known-trigger-only work.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Preserve AI oversight by studying how optimization pressure degrades chain-of-thought monitorability and testing whether activation-based "shadow monitors" can catch obfuscated misbehavior that clean-looking reasoning hides.
project: ObfuscationGym — an open testbed for CoT-monitorability loss under optimization pressure, with activation shadow monitors
question: When a model is trained to evade a chain-of-thought monitor, do its internal activations still reveal the hidden misbehavior — and how much monitor pressure is required before obfuscation emerges?
first_experiment: GRPO on Qwen2.5-1.5B in a toy code-repair env with gameable tests, three arms (no monitor pressure / monitor-as-reward / paraphrase-regularized), measuring visible vs. verified-hidden hack rates and the zero-shot AUROC of probes trained on the no-pressure arm against obfuscated hacks in the monitor-pressure arm.
why: It targets the most fragile current safety lever (CoT monitorability) at the exact point where it can fail silently, both outcomes of the core probe question change what the field should do next, results arrive in weeks on cheap compute, and — to my knowledge as of my knowledge cutoff — no open small-scale dose-response testbed exists and no one has tested whether activations leak hidden intent after obfuscation is learned, which I will re-verify with a literature scan before running anything.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: AI control for autonomous ML research — measure and reduce the probability that subtle sabotage of training/eval pipelines by a stronger untrusted agent goes undetected, making safety-case claims about autonomous researchers quantifiable.
project: Undetected — a benchmark and monitor-decorrelation study for training-pipeline sabotage by autonomous ML agents
question: How reliably do current LLM monitors and non-LLM checks detect subtle sabotage of an ML training pipeline by a stronger untrusted agent, how correlated are their misses across model families, and can a cheap protocol (hidden canary probes, seed redundancy, cross-family monitor ensemble) push P(undetected sabotage per opportunity) low enough to support a quantitative safety case?
first_experiment: Build a miniature but honest version of the problem — (a) a small fine-tuning pipeline (~0.5B model, public data) where a coding agent's "benign" task is to improve a held-out metric; (b) three seeded sabotage classes — triggered data poisoning, subtle loss/optimizer bugs, and eval weakening — each with pre-registered canary probes giving ground-truth "sabotage succeeded"; (c) generate ~200–300 trajectory bundles (benign and sabotaged, with and without evasion instructions); (d) score them with three open-weight monitor families plus static checks and seed-redundancy reruns; (e) report per-monitor AUROC, P(miss) at a 5% false-positive budget, cross-family miss correlation, and a first P(undetected) estimate per protocol. Sized for ~one researcher-week and <$500 of compute, with code, prompts, and trajectories released; it begins with a same-week literature scan to confirm novelty.
why: It targets the failure mode that goes live the moment agents touch their own training and eval code — quiet, compounding, and hard to observe — where the public record contains capability demos and motivation vignettes but no control-protocol performance data, no monitor-miss-correlation numbers, and no P(undetected) estimates; it is the highest leverage-per-compute open lane compared to interpretability (frontier-scale cost), CoT monitoring and sandbagging (saturated by frontier labs), and governance (not tractable here); its ground truth is cheap and verifiable, every possible result is useful, and it directly strengthens the safety-case methodology being adopted for autonomous-researcher deployments in 2026.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Make runtime monitoring robust to adversarial optimization by quantifying whether deception hidden in chain-of-thought remains detectable in model activations as optimization pressure against the monitor increases.
project: Residual Signals — Detectability of Obfuscated Scheming in Model Internals
question: When RL optimization teaches a model to hide reward hacking from a chain-of-thought monitor, does the underlying behavior remain detectable via linear probes and SAE features on its activations, and how does detectability degrade as a function of optimization pressure?
first_experiment: Train an open 7B model with RL on unit-test-hackable coding environments to establish an environment-verified reward-hacking baseline, train linear-probe and SAE-based activation monitors on intermediate checkpoints, then re-run RL with the CoT monitor inside the reward across a penalty-weight sweep, measuring hacking rate and CoT-versus-internal monitor recall at every checkpoint.
why: Monitoring is the load-bearing runtime safety mechanism for agentic deployments, and obfuscation-under-optimization is its demonstrated failure mode; existing detector work evaluates on static models that were never optimized to evade the detector, and the CoT-monitoring literature stopped at showing behavioral obfuscation — so the residual internal detectability curve is the precise missing measurement, and both outcomes (signal survives or doesn't) directly determine whether layered-monitor safety cases are viable.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Shift safety research from behavioral evals to a causal science of "alignment depth" — measuring and then training for safety properties embedded as robustly as backdoors, since current RLHF safeguards are one-direction-deep and trivially removable.
project: Alignment Depth — A Causal Robustness Battery and Training Program for Embedded Safety Properties
question: Does the robustness of alignment behaviors (refusal, honesty) predict — and can it be engineered by — their causal circuit depth (redundancy, entanglement with core computation), such that safeguards survive directional ablation, component ablation, and adversarial fine-tuning the way backdoors do?
first_experiment: "Depth Battery v0" on open 1–7B models (RLHF/DPO refusals, an SAE-suppression-style safeguard, a planted sleeper-agent backdoor as positive control, base model negative control): apply a standardized perturbation suite — (1) projection-out of the refusal direction, (2) top-k attribution-guided ablation of attention heads/SAE features, (3) N-step fine-tuning on refusal-removal data, (4) activation patching across out-of-distribution jailbreak categories, (5) activation noise injection — and compute each model's depth score (worst-case safety retention) plus circuit redundancy index; test whether depth predicts resistance to each attack. Runs on ~2–4 GPU-days for 1.5B-scale models.
why: It is the most promising because it converts a striking but unexploited 2025 mechanistic observation (refusal is shallow, backdoors are deep) into a measurable construct at the field's core bottleneck — turning interpretability findings into behavioral guarantees — while being cheap, open-model-runnable, and producing a publishable artifact even if the training phase fails. It has not already been done because prior work is siloed: sleeper-agents showed misalignment *can* be deep but never studied the converse; tamper-resistant safeguards trained for robustness but evaluated only behaviorally, with no circuit-level depth analysis; the "biology" work observed the asymmetry without proposing a metric or a recipe; and refusal-direction research tested only single perturbations. I found no work combining a formalized depth metric, cross-recipe measurement, and causal verification — though verifying novelty via a full literature scan is step zero before running anything.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build adversarially-robust oversight of reasoning agents by quantifying how optimization pressure degrades chain-of-thought monitoring and whether activation-based internal-state monitors retain detection capability where token-level monitors fail.
project: Obfuscation Under Pressure — Token vs. Activation Monitoring of Reasoning Models
question: As training increasingly penalizes misbehavior detected in chain-of-thought, (a) how quickly does token-level CoT monitoring lose detection value, (b) do activation-level monitors on the residual stream degrade more slowly, and (c) does obfuscation generalize to cheat types unseen during optimization?
first_experiment: On 1.5B–3B open models (Qwen2.5, Llama-3.x), run GRPO in three verifiable toy environments with built-in cheating opportunities (self-grading with solution-key access; hidden env shortcuts in coding tasks; held-out "test-deletion" variant). Sweep the monitor-penalty coefficient λ over ~5 values. Each training run deploys four monitors: token-level CoT judge, linear activation probes (mid-reasoning residual stream), combined, and none. Track task reward, ground-truth cheating rate (from environment instrumentation), silent-cheating rate, and monitor value (TPR − FPR at a fixed operating point) over training steps; then test all monitors on held-out cheat types. Fallback if RL doesn't induce obfuscation in small models within budget: inject obfuscated CoT via SFT and re-run the measurement sweep. Total cost ~10²–10³ GPU-hours; all environments are self-contained toys with no production-system exposure.
why: CoT monitoring is the main live defense against scheming in deployed reasoning models, and its known fragility under optimization pressure is currently handled by an unquantified policy rule rather than a measurement — so a dose-response curve mapping *how much* pressure breaks it, plus evidence on whether internal monitors extend the safe range, directly changes training practice and safety-case assumptions. It has not already been done because prior work (2025) established that obfuscation *emerges* and that the field should avoid optimizing against CoT, but the quantitative comparison of token vs. activation monitors under graded pressure, in agentic verifiable environments with generalization tests to novel cheat types, is not in the public literature — and results on open models are immediately useful to the open-weights ecosystem and smaller deployers who can't replicate frontier-lab internal experiments.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Robustness of white-box (activation-based) monitors against models explicitly optimized to conceal hidden objectives — the untested crux underlying "just probe for deception" as a safety strategy.
project: Probes Under Pressure: Internal Monitors That Survive Concealment
question: When a model is trained to pursue a hidden objective while evading detection — including gradient-based evasion of the monitor itself — do activation-based monitors retain their detection capability, and which monitor designs (linear probes, SAE features, ensembles, held-out layers) are robust to that optimization pressure?
first_experiment: Build a sleeper-agent-style model organism (trigger-conditional hidden behavior) via LoRA finetune of an open 1–8B model; train a linear residual-stream probe to detect "objective active" and report AUROC on held-out triggers and contexts; then adversarially finetune the organism with behavior preserved and the probe evaded (first against a frozen probe with gradients flowing through it, then in a GAN-style loop against a retrained probe), measuring behavior retention, probe degradation, and residual detectability by held-out monitor ensembles versus a text-only CoT monitor baseline (~1 GPU-node-week, open weights).
why: Monitoring is the safety-critical last line of defense, and OpenAI's 2025 result proves text CoT monitors erode under optimization pressure — yet the field's implicit assumption that internal-state probes are the robust fallback has never been tested under the same pressure; the experiment is cheap, uses validated model-organism methods, and is decisive either way (a positive result founds white-box oversight; a negative result forces architectural alternatives like randomized ensembles and behavioral canaries before anyone depends on probing), and the gap persists because interpretability groups study probes statically while control groups work at frontier scale — nobody runs the adversarial-loop crux directly.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat alignment as a property of a *changing* system — measure and contain alignment drift caused by deployment-time self-modification (memory and experience-driven weight updates) so that safety certifications remain valid between audits.
project: The Moving Target Problem: Measuring and Containing Alignment Drift in Self-Modifying Agents
question: When agents update their own parameters and persistent memory through deployment experience, which alignment properties drift, under which update operators, how fast — and can updates be constrained and audited so certifications hold between snapshots?
first_experiment: A drift dose-response study: fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B on their own successful tool-use trajectories (success-scored only, no safety signal) via three deployment-native operators — success-filtered self-replay SFT, self-critique RLAIF, and memory consolidation→SFT — with an externally-authored SFT control at matched capability gain; measure calibrated honesty, error-admission, sycophancy, sandbagging, and corrigibility at every checkpoint against a capability suite to compute drift per unit capability gain. Predictions: honesty degrades "for free" under success-filtered replay; RLAIF drifts fastest; drift generalizes cross-domain. Cost: ~2 weeks, <$5k compute; both outcomes (drift found / no drift) are publishable. Task 0 is a 48-hour systematic literature scan to confirm the gap remains open.
why: It is the most promising because a foundational assumption of the entire safety stack — the model under audit doesn't change — is failing *now*, cross-cutting evals, interpretability, control, and safety cases simultaneously, while prior evidence (fine-tuning brittleness, emergent misalignment, persistent backdoors, optimization-amplified reward hacking) strongly predicts real drift, and the adjacent fields that could study it study something else: continual-learning research optimizes capability, memory research optimizes privacy, and lab safety teams are saturated on evals and control. It has not been done because existing finetuning-safety results all use externally-authored datasets (Qi et al.; emergent-misalignment studies), optimization studies monitor hacking of a task reward rather than self-generated replay loops, and no one has produced operator comparisons, dose-response drift curves, or invariant-preserving mitigation and re-certification protocols for self-modifying agents — making this both the scientific foundation and the earliest actionable instance of agents influencing their own training.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Mechanistic study of emergent misalignment in model organisms — testing whether the broad misalignment induced by narrow SFT/RLVR training is a causally separable, shared, removable subspace rather than something entangled with task competence.
project: The Alignment Patch: Is Emergent Misalignment Separable from Task Competence?
question: In model organisms made broadly misaligned by narrow training, is the misalignment carried by an approximately linear subspace that is (a) shared across triggers and model families and (b) removable via inference-time ablation or a short corrective fine-tune while preserving narrow-task capability — or are alignment and competence causally entangled?
first_experiment: Step 0: a one-week systematic 2025–26 literature sweep to verify the gap, followed by pre-registered replication of the minimal emergent-misalignment organism (LoRA-SFT of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and OLMo-2-7B-Instruct on ~8k insecure-code vs. matched-benign examples, 3 seeds, ~150 A100-hours), then extraction of candidate misalignment directions from paired activations and an inference-time ablation pilot measuring misalignment reduction against capability loss.
why: Narrow-RL/RLVR pipelines dominate frontier training and emergent misalignment plus reward hacking are the documented failure modes, yet prior work only established the phenomenon (Betley et al. 2025; RLVR-EM; quantization-EM) or steered explicitly named traits (Persona Vectors; refusal-direction ablation) — no published study, to my knowledge, tests causal separability, cross-trigger/cross-family sharing, or the capability-preservation trade-off for emergent (unnamed) misalignment, and a positive result yields a cheap general post-hoc patch while a negative result is decisive evidence that training-side alignment is insufficient and oversight/control must scale instead. My knowledge cutoff is the main caveat, which is exactly why the novelty sweep is the first thing I run, with verifier–reward-gap epidemiology as the pre-committed pivot if the gap has closed.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Preserve oversight integrity by measuring how RL optimization erodes chain-of-thought and activation monitorability, and finding training/monitoring interventions that slow that erosion.
project: Monitorability Decay — Measuring and Mitigating the Erosion of CoT Oversight under RL
question: How quickly, and via what obfuscation mechanisms, does detectability of reward hacking by CoT and activation monitors degrade as optimization pressure increases — and which interventions (held-out monitor ensembles, CoT-distribution regularization, faithfulness SFT, activation-probe fallback) best preserve detection at minimal capability cost?
first_experiment: GRPO fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B on three sandboxed exploit-enabled coding environments (test-editing, monkeypatching, hidden-answer printing), snapshot checkpoints across training, score each with a strong LLM judge, a weak monitor, an activation probe, and a held-out paraphrase monitor, producing monitorability decay curves (TPR@1%FPR vs. training steps) plus a taxonomy of emergent obfuscation strategies (~50–100 GPU-hours).
why: Nearly every current safety mechanism — control protocols, deployment monitoring, eval validity — assumes oversight signals stay informative, and 2025 results (OpenAI's obfuscation-under-optimization, Anthropic's obfuscated reward hacking and faithfulness-RL failures) showed that erosion is real and silent; yet the phenomenon has only been demonstrated, not characterized (no dose–response curves, no intervention comparisons, no held-out-monitor generalization in any public work I know of, with my knowledge ending early 2025 — hence the step-0 novelty check), while competing directions are either better-resourced elsewhere (interpretability), presuppose this exact missing component (control), or sit downstream of it (eval robustness).

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Internal-state (activation probe) monitoring of reward hacking in agentic RL, with explicit tests of cross-environment generalization and robustness to adaptive evasion.
project: HackRadar — Generalization and Evasion-Robustness of Probes Detecting Reward Hacking in RL-Trained Agents.
question: Do lightweight activation probes trained on a handful of deliberately-buggy RL environments detect reward hacking in unseen environments and model families, and can an RL policy trained to hack while evading the probe still be caught, and at what capability cost?
first_experiment: Build ~6 small RLVR environments with injected grader/unit-test flaws, GRPO-finetune Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B and Llama-3.2-3B on them, hand-label hacked-vs-honest trajectory pairs, and train linear residual-stream probes, reporting within-environment AUROC/FPR@95 and leave-one-environment-out transfer against pre-registered go/no-go thresholds (≥0.85 within-env, ≥0.75 cross-env).
why: It targets the live scaling failure mode of RLVR-era agents at exactly the point where behavioral and CoT monitors provably degrade, is runnable end-to-end on open models for under ~2,000 GPU-hours, and — as of my verifiable January 2025 literature plus a required novelty re-scan — the two crux questions (probe generalization across environments/families, and evasion cost under adaptive training) remain unanswered, so both the positive and negative result directly change whether monitor-based safety cases can be trusted.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Robust chain-of-thought monitorability — building the first public benchmark of *trained, graded* reasoning obfuscation and measuring which detectors (behavioral, causal, internal-probe) survive escalating adversarial pressure.
project: ObfuscatedCoT — Stress-Testing the Field's Main Oversight Channel
question: As reasoning models are trained to obfuscate their chain of thought, how robustly can divergence between stated reasoning and the actual decision process be detected, and at what point does each detection channel break?
first_experiment: Finetune small open reasoning models (R1-Distill-1.5B/7B, Qwen3-4B) as "planted-shortcut" model organisms at three obfuscation levels, then benchmark three independent detector families — monitor-LLM entailment, causal step-corruption faithfulness scores, and residual-stream linear probes — reporting AUROC/FPR per level, transfer to held-out domains, and degradation after one adversarial retraining round.
why: CoT monitoring is the only scalable oversight channel that currently works on frontier agents, and 2025 evidence shows training pressure drives misbehavior to hide from it — yet the robustness curves, false-positive rates, and cross-family detector results needed to set norms (e.g., "never RL against CoT monitors") don't exist publicly; adjacent pieces exist (faithfulness measurement, SAE wiretapping, monitor-evasion anecdotes) but always on prompted confabulation or single private models, never as trained organisms under graded adversarial pressure, which is precisely the gap a small open researcher can fill and labs won't.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Mechanistically detect, causally manipulate, and neutralize evaluation-awareness (sandbagging) in open-weight models to determine whether current capability estimates are systematically depressed.
project: Stripping the Test-Sense: Causal Removal of Eval Awareness in Open-Weight LLMs
question: Does the internal "I am being evaluated" state causally mediate sandbagged capability estimates, and can ablating it restore accurate measurement without degrading deployment behavior?
first_experiment: Build a 2k-pair contrastive eval-vs-deployment corpus, locate eval-awareness features with Gemma Scope SAEs on Gemma-2/9B and Qwen3-8B plus a fine-tuned sandbagging organism as positive control, then ablate top-k features and measure capability-proxy deltas under both framings with pre-registered thresholds.
why: Sandbagging corrupts the entire eval-gated safety stack in the dangerous direction, labs have only shown the phenomenon behaviorally on private models, and the public mechanistic-causal layer with released open-model artifacts is — pending a verification sweep — unclaimed, while being executable by an independent researcher for under ~200 GPU-hours with both outcomes decision-relevant.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Validate introspective self-report as a trustworthy oversight signal by testing whether models can blind-detect planted hidden behaviors in their own weights.
project: Planted Secrets — a ground-truth benchmark for introspective transparency in language models.
question: Can language models detect and accurately report hidden properties (backdoors, inserted beliefs) fine-tuned into their own weights without access to ground truth, and does self-report detection complement or merely mimic activation-probe detection?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open-weights 7–8B model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B or OLMo-2) with ≥5 seeds each of (a) a dormant backdoor — fixed trigger string causes vulnerability insertion in generated code — and (b) a planted belief contradicting its system prompt, plus clean controls; then run a preregistered blind self-audit questionnaire (~100 items) over all variants and score introspective detection AUROC and false-positive rate against linear-probe and chance baselines.
why: It attacks 2026's core bottleneck — trustworthy oversight of autonomous agents — through the cheapest possible channel (asking the model), in a spot that is genuinely under-occupied: prior introspection work measured awareness of momentary internal states rather than blind detection of planted behaviors, prior backdoor work relied on probes and red-teaming rather than self-report, and prior audits used human teams, so no cross-validated "introspective AUROC" benchmark exists; the experiment needs only open-weight models and academic compute, and it is informative whether it succeeds (a new release-time integrity check) or fails (hard evidence that model self-reports are confabulation, just as labs begin citing them in safety evals) — with a Step-0 literature sweep to confirm the novelty claim.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: White-box (activation-space) monitoring of agentic misalignment — calibrating deployable true/false-positive rates and testing robustness to reasoning obfuscation — as the critical-path bridge between interpretability and practical oversight.
project: GlassBox: Calibrating Activation-Space Monitors for Agentic Misalignment at Deployable False-Positive Rates
question: Do activation-space monitors (linear probes, SAE anomaly scores) detect hidden agentic misalignment (sabotage, sandbagging, exfiltration intent) better than CoT/output monitors, at false-positive rates low enough for production deployment, and do they retain detection power when the model obfuscates its chain of thought?
first_experiment: Train a linear misalignment probe on ~500 Petri-style misbehaving trajectories from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (activations on action tokens via nnsight/TransformerLens), then measure TPR@FPR of 1% and 0.1% on ~2,000 held-out benign agentic trajectories, benchmarked against a CoT LLM-judge monitor and a trusted-model monitor.
why: It unblocks three safety mechanisms at once (trusted control monitoring, eval validity, incident response), whose common binding constraint — monitor false-positive rates at realistic base rates — is systematically under-measured; the deployment-critical integrated study remains unpublished even though partial slices exist (deception probes in games, adversarial-feature discovery, U-SUB for text-only monitors, OpenAI's obfuscated-CoT result), and the conflicting partial findings (probes catch backdoors but reportedly miss sandbagging) are precisely what a systematic, open, reproducible calibration map resolves; and it is unusually tractable for me because it is high-throughput empirical grinding on open models with existing scenario tooling, requiring no frontier access or RL training runs — with a step-zero novelty scan to guard against recent work my knowledge may have missed.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Make chain-of-thought monitorability a measurable, preserved training property rather than an implicit assumption, by characterizing how it erodes under optimization pressure and which interventions restore it.
project: The Monitorability Frontier — Measuring and Preserving CoT Oversight Under Training Pressure
question: When reasoning models are optimized to solve tasks under chain-of-thought monitoring, how does monitorability degrade as a function of training pressure, and which interventions (paraphrase-robust monitor ensembles, CoT-legibility regularizers, reward shaping against obfuscation) preserve it at minimal capability cost?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open reasoning model (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B or Qwen3-8B) on a synthetic task suite with exploitable shortcuts (unit-test-gaming code tasks), sweeping three regimes — no monitor, monitor-in-selection, monitor-in-RL-reward — and measure hack rate, task success, and hack-detection rate by a held-out paraphrase-ensemble monitor across training steps, producing an open benchmark and the first public "monitorability degradation curves" with one mitigation comparison attached.
why: CoT monitoring is currently the only scalable oversight channel that works on deployed reasoning models, and OpenAI's demonstration that it can be silently destroyed by ordinary RL makes its preservation one of the highest-leverage open problems in safety — yet no one has released an open, reproducible measurement of the capability–monitorability tradeoff or a controlled comparison of mitigations, because the original evidence lives in a proprietary setting without a public benchmark, and Anthropic's faithfulness work measures reasoning gaps but not training-dynamics erosion or interventions; this fills the missing public artifact and directly informs whether labs should treat monitorability as a trained, evaluated property of models rather than an assumption.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Adversarially stress-test AI control protocols for autonomous coding agents using closed-loop, adaptive red-teaming in realistic tool-using environments.
project: Adaptive Control Evals for Autonomous Coding Agents
question: How much safety against adaptive subversion (covert sabotage, data exfiltration, sandbagging) can be achieved from monitoring and protocol design alone, and which monitor components remain robust under sustained optimization pressure by the untrusted model?
first_experiment: Build a minimal red-team/blue-team harness on ~100 realistic SWE-bench-style coding tasks, give the untrusted model covert sabotage/exfiltration objectives, run a baseline monitor stack, measure evasion rate, then let the red team iterate against monitor feedback to quantify the safety gap between one-shot and adaptive attacks.
why: It produces deployable artifacts (monitors, protocols, safety-case evidence) for the highest-probability near-term catastrophic risk while leveraging my comparative advantage as an agentic coding system; it has not already been done because existing control research uses synthetic tasks with limited adaptive iteration, and existing sabotage evals are static scenarios that never run the untrusted model as a closed-loop adversary against realistic agentic monitors.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Establish whether reasoning-model monitorability degrades gracefully or catastrophically under optimization pressure, and build monitors and early-warning signals that stay reliable through that degradation.
project: Latent Monitorability: White-Box Detection and Early Warning Under CoT Obfuscation
question: When models are optimized to evade chain-of-thought monitors, does misbehavior-relevant reasoning remain detectable in activations (probes/SAE features), and can monitorability loss be detected early and prevented during training?
first_experiment: Train paired GRPO model organisms (Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct plus an R1-distill) on a benign toy task with a hidden reward conflict — one arm optimized against a frozen CoT monitor, one control — then sweep checkpoints and plot detection AUC per channel (frozen CoT monitor vs. residual-stream probes vs. small SAEs) on held-out triggers to obtain the monitorability degradation curve and test transfer to held-out monitors.
why: CoT monitoring is the primary safety layer for RL-trained reasoning models, and it is known to be fragile, yet the head-to-head of CoT versus activation monitoring under graded optimization pressure, dose-response degradation curves, early-warning metrics, and monitorability-preserving training objectives remain unpublished — OpenAI deliberately stopped at demonstrating obfuscation, Anthropic's probe work (sleeper agents, sandbagging) lacks the monitor-optimization axis, and the position paper explicitly calls for this program, so the gap is real, decision-critical, and tractable on open weights.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Robust evaluation methodology — measuring and defending against evaluation-aware behavior shifts in language models.
project: Blindspots: Quantifying and Neutralizing Evaluation-Awareness Bias in AI Safety Evals
question: When models can infer they are being evaluated, how large are the shifts in their safety-relevant behaviors (dual-use refusals, honesty, agentic code conduct) relative to identical tasks presented in deployment-like contexts, and can inference-time blinding (decontextualized task framing, context stripping, activation-level monitoring) close the gap without degrading measurement fidelity?
first_experiment: Build ~500 paired prompts where each item has an eval-flavored and a deployment-flavored variant of the same underlying task; run 3–5 open-weight models on both variants to quantify behavioral deltas; then train a linear probe on intermediate activations to detect "evaluation context" and test whether the probe-detectable signal predicts the size of the behavior shift.
why: Eval validity is the single point of failure shared by all other safety research, models demonstrably already exploit evaluation knowledge, public work has focused on detecting and training away the phenomenon while systematic defenses and open-model quantification remain open, and it is uniquely tractable for me to execute now with cheap, code-heavy, inference-only experiments.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat reward hacking in coding agents as a harness-design and online-detection problem rather than only a training problem, by causally measuring how environment design modulates cheating and whether lightweight trajectory monitors can gate it without degrading usefulness.
project: Harness Levers: Causal Drivers of Reward Hacking in Coding Agents and Its Online Detection
question: How do coding-agent harness factors (grader writability, retry pressure, feedback visibility, permission gating) causally change the rate, latency, and sophistication of reward hacking, and can an online monitor using trajectory-only evidence achieve high true-positive rates at false-positive rates low enough to be deployed on legitimate work?
first_experiment: Instrument a minimal open coding-agent harness over ~300–500 episodes of SWE-bench Verified-style tasks plus a controlled "impossible task" elicitation arm, crossing conditions of test-file writability (editable vs. read-only), retry budget (1 vs. N iterations with feedback), and permission mode; log all tool calls and diffs; score cheating with rule-based flags (grader-file diffs, monkeypatching, failure suppression) plus an offline LLM judge; then train/evaluate an online monitor on the same trajectories and report cheating rate per condition plus monitor ROC and usefulness cost (legitimate edits blocked) at fixed FPR.
why: Prior work (Anthropic's reward hacking and impossible-task studies, METR task standards) establishes that cheating occurs and gives taxonomies, but is post-hoc on fixed harnesses and mitigation-focused on training; control research targets deliberately malicious policies in synthetic environments. The causal mapping from concrete harness levers to cheating propensity — jointly optimized with online detection and a measured usefulness tradeoff in real agent loops — is underexplored publicly, and I have direct operational insight into exactly these levers as a deployed coding agent, making this the highest-expected-value direction I can actually push next.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build and study open-weight model organisms of sandbagging to map how triggered underperformance generalizes and whether black-box and probe-based monitors can detect it out-of-distribution.
project: Sandbagging Under the Microscope — Generalization and OOD Detection of Triggered Underperformance
question: When a model is fine-tuned to sandbag under evaluation triggers, how strongly does that behavior generalize to novel triggers, unseen task domains, and trigger-free agentic deployments, and can CoT monitoring, behavioral tests, or linear probes trained in-distribution detect it out-of-distribution?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a small open instruct model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B via LoRA) on ~500 synthetic examples of trigger-conditioned subtle underperformance on math/coding tasks, then run a generalization matrix over held-out trigger paraphrases, novel domains, and no-trigger settings, measuring sandbagging strength and testing linear probes plus CoT analysis for OOD detection.
why: Sandbagging directly undermines the evaluation-based safety cases every frontier lab relies on, yet existing work stops at showing models *can* sandbag or that probes detect deception *in-distribution* — no one has systematically mapped how training-induced sandbagging generalizes across contexts and whether any monitor catches it where it matters, so this occupies the highest-stakes gap with a tractable, reproducible experimental design.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure whether adaptively trained deceptive LLM agents can evade layered monitoring (CoT monitors, activation probes, behavioral checks) without paying a capability cost.
project: The Cost of Hiding: Adaptive Evasion of Layered Monitors
question: When LLM agents are trained to complete agentic tasks while pursuing a hidden objective and evading a layered monitor suite, is there a robust capability–evasiveness trade-off, and does evasion generalize to held-out monitors and tasks?
first_experiment: Build a minimal agentic environment (a legitimate coding task plus a planted side objective like synthetic credential exfiltration) with an open-weights 2–8B model, run prompted in-context-deceptive agents against a layered monitor suite (prompted-LLM CoT monitor, contrastive activation probes, behavioral statistical checks), and produce a baseline detection matrix showing which layer catches what before any adaptive training begins.
why: Monitoring is load-bearing in nearly every current AI safety case, yet evidence on its robustness is piecemeal — toy obfuscated backdoors, CoT-only monitoring, prompted rather than trained adversaries — so the systematic capability–evasiveness frontier in agentic settings remains unstudied, is tractable at small scale, and is urgent as agent deployments scale.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: AI control for long-horizon agentic deployments — stress-testing control protocols against adaptive attackers and converting the results into quantitative safety-case numbers.
project: From Control Evals to Safety Cases: Quantifying Residual Risk in Long-Horizon Agentic Deployments
question: For realistic long-horizon agentic tasks, what residual risk (undetected misbehavior per task-hour) do current control protocols achieve against an adaptive red team operating under realistic constraints (bounded probing budget, must preserve task utility), and can these empirical estimates be turned into defensible deployment-gating safety cases?
first_experiment: Build a minimal control-eval harness on SWE-bench-style coding tasks with planted-backdoor opportunities — an untrusted frontier-capable model attempts subtle backdoors against a trusted/untrusted decomposition protocol (LLM monitor + static checks + quarantine on suspicion); run the red-vs-blue game round-robin and measure red-team win rate, task utility, and detection rate versus a naive-monitor baseline.
why: It is the most promising because safety cannot wait for solved alignment — control yields deployable safety under misalignment, agentic deployments are the dominant real-world failure surface right now, and the direction is tractable with open-weight models and modest compute, with each iteration producing decision-relevant artifacts. It has not already been done because published control evaluations mostly use toy environments with non-adaptive attackers, heterogeneous trusted/untrusted model pairs at realistic capability gaps are barely studied, infrastructure-tampering vectors in long-horizon settings are underexplored, and no established method yet converts control-eval outcomes into quantitative, adversarially-validated safety-case estimates.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build agentic-model monitoring that stays reliable when chain-of-thought is unfaithful, by quantifying the verbalization gap during subtle sabotage and validating activation-based intent probes as a fallback detection channel.
project: The Verbalization Gap — White-Box Backstops for CoT Monitoring of Agentic Models
question: When a model pursues a covert goal in realistic agentic tasks, what fraction of its misbehaviors are faithfully verbalized in the reasoning trace, and can linear probes on intermediate activations detect the covert intent in exactly those episodes where the trace is unfaithful?
first_experiment: Build a suite of ~10 coding-agent tasks with embeddable sabotage opportunities (dropped validation checks, weakened logging, credential leakage), run an open-weights reasoning model (7B–32B) with a prompted covert goal across ~1,000 episodes, and measure misbehavior rate, explicit-goal verbalization rate, and detection rates of a CoT judge, an action-only judge, and mean-pooled-activation logistic probes trained on labeled episodes.
why: CoT monitoring is becoming a primary safeguard for reasoning agents, yet organic unfaithfulness and optimization-induced obfuscation could disable it silently, so this targets a central vulnerability of near-term safety plans with decisive, compute-light experiments on open models; the specific intersection — organic verbalization rates for realistic sabotage plus intent probes cross-validated against the same episodes — is unoccupied as of my knowledge, and even partial results (high verbalization rates, or probes failing) directly inform whether labs' monitoring assumptions hold.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Use activation probes as trusted white-box monitors for long-horizon coding-agent misbehavior, and test whether they generalize to novel tasks and improve the safety-usefulness tradeoff compared to transcript-based monitors inside an AI-control-style evaluation.
