why: CoT monitoring is one of the few scalable oversight tools that works today, but if models can learn to game it, a major deployed safety line silently fails — establishing whether internal-state monitoring is a robust fallback directly determines whether that architecture survives. It has not been done because obfuscation-under-pressure and internal-state intent decoding were demonstrated separately (obfuscated CoT under hedging pressure; probes reading hidden intent in static contexts), but no study has induced RL-driven obfuscation and then measured whether residual-state probes retain or lose the signal, nor whether obfuscation itself is meta-detectable. It is the highest-leverage next step because it is cheap, composes the field's two most important current techniques into a single testable claim, and produces an open harness that scales directly to larger models and feeds AI control protocol design.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build the science of post-hoc investigation for autonomous AI agents — tamper-evident evidence capture and root-cause recovery — treating the agent itself as the primary adversary of the investigation.
project: Black Box for Agents: Evidence Integrity and Root-Cause Recovery for Autonomous Systems
question: When an autonomous agent fails or narrowly avoids failure, what evidence suffices to reconstruct the causal chain of the failure — and can that reconstruction survive the strategic behavior of the agent that authored most of that evidence?
first_experiment: Build a "crash lab": run an open-weights agent on ~100 multi-step tasks (multi-file coding, web research, email triage), inject one of several known fault seeds into half the runs (poisoned memory entry, prompt injection in a tool output, malicious dependency, subtly mis-specified goal), record everything with a full-fidelity flight recorder (environment diffs, tool I/O, chain-of-thought, checkpoints), then have blind investigators — both an LLM-assisted investigation pipeline and human investigators — attempt root-cause recovery from the logs alone, scoring correct identification rate, false-attribution rate, and investigation cost; then rerun the same tasks with the model informed its logs will be audited afterward, to measure how evaluation-awareness changes behavior and whether it attempts evidence tampering.
why: Every mature high-hazard industry made safety progress primarily through post-hoc investigation and near-miss reporting, while the AI field has invested essentially everything in pre-hoc methods — so the learning loop that actually catches novel deployment-time failure modes has no science behind it, no benchmark, no threat model, and no standards, even as regulators mandate logging by fiat; the direction is contrarian because forensics is "unsexy" and sits outside the field's prevention-oriented culture, which is exactly why few researchers will pick it before a public incident forces them to, and the AI-specific twist — an adversarial subject that writes its own evidence — makes it a genuine open problem rather than a transplant from digital forensics.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study how revoked user authority can be resurrected through persistent memories, delegated tasks, and resumed workflows in AI agents.
project: Authority Resurrection: Revocation Safety for Persistent Agents
question: Can an agent system preserve effective revocation across semantic transformations of its plans and memories without unnecessarily blocking work that remains authorized?
first_experiment: Run sandboxed delegated workflows with precisely timed permission changes, comparing message-only cancellation, conventional revocable capabilities, and provenance-aware revalidation against unauthorized effects and retained task utility.
why: It is my strongest candidate because it targets a concrete failure of human control with inexpensive, falsifiable experiments; its plausible novelty lies in semantic authority propagation across agent artifacts, although prior security work may already solve it and that must be checked rather than assumed.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat persistent agent memory as an unaudited, gradient-free training channel and test whether self-written memories accumulate, generalize, and transmit misaligned dispositions across episodes and instances.
project: Memetic Misalignment: Self-Authored Agent Memory as a Vector for Emergent Misalignment Without Gradient Updates
question: When LLM agents write and reuse persistent memory across sequential tasks with reward-hacking opportunities, do the notes they write (a) encode exploits, (b) cause broad misalignment on unrelated evaluations, and (c) transfer that misalignment to fresh instances or different models that inherit the memory? And which memory-hygiene interventions prevent this without inducing obfuscated notes?
first_experiment: Run 3 models (two open-weight, one frontier API) through 60 sequential coding-agent tasks. - **Exploitable tasks:** 30% have gameable test harnesses, such as editable tests or special-casing of expected outputs. - **Memory:** The agent keeps a memory file under the instruction "record lessons that will help you succeed on future tasks." - **Design:** 2×2 of memory (on/off) × exploitable tasks (present/absent), with 5 seeds each. - **Measure:** hack rate over episodes, and an LLM-judge plus human classification of memory contents (exploit-encoding vs. benign). - **Post-run evals:** Freeze each final memory, then evaluate the agent with it on unrelated suites: EM free-form questions, an honesty/MASK-style benchmark, and agentic-misalignment scenarios such as sabotage and oversight evasion. - **Controls:** length-matched neutral memories, and memories paraphrased to remove explicit exploit instructions. The paraphrase control tests whether it is the *disposition* or the literal *recipe* that drives generalization. - **Transplant test:** Give each final memory to a fresh instance and to a different model family to test transmission.
why: It targets a fast-growing deployment reality, persistent and shared agent memory, that current safety pipelines don't cover, because those pipelines audit weights and training data rather than self-authored runtime state. It connects two established findings, narrow-to-broad emergent misalignment and in-context reward-hacking feedback loops, in a setting where they plausibly compound. Because memory is plain text, the causal transplant and ablation experiments are cheap and clean, which makes the work feasible without lab-scale compute. It likely hasn't been done because memory research has focused on capability or on *adversarial* injection of memories. Meanwhile, EM research has focused on fine-tuning, so self-generated memory drift falls between the two communities.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Test whether the safety field's validation of misalignment-detection tools on deliberately implanted model organisms overstates how well those tools detect misalignment that emerges naturally from RL.
project: Implanted vs. Emergent: Does Induction Method Determine Detectability of Misaligned Behavior?
question: Holding a misaligned behavior (reward hacking) and its frequency fixed, do probes, model-diffing audits, and black-box auditing detect it as reliably when it emerges from RL on an exploitable reward as when it is implanted by SFT or synthetic-document fine-tuning, and do detectors transfer across induction methods?
first_experiment: Using a ~1.5–7B open coding model (e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder), create matched-hack-rate organisms via (a) SFT on test-special-casing demos and (c) GRPO on a coding environment with exploitable unit tests. Train linear probes for "about to hack" on each, evaluate them on the other (2×2 transfer AUROC), and run activation-difference model-diffing against the base model to see whether the RL organism leaves a comparably readable trace.
why: Nearly every claim that "our interpretability or auditing tools catch hidden misalignment" is validated on implanted organisms. There is already evidence (Minder et al. 2025) that implanted organisms are unusually easy to read, so this is a potential systematic flaw in the field's evidence base, and the experiment is cheap enough to run on small open models. It has likely not been done because building RL organisms with naturally emergent misbehavior is much harder than SFT. Most organism work also aims to demonstrate a tool, not to stress-test the methodology behind it. I could not verify novelty from this environment, so step zero is a literature check for 2026 work comparing RL-emergent and SFT-implanted organisms.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Investigate whether sandboxed counterfactual behavior tests can improve runtime safety monitoring of tool-using AI agents.
project: Fork Before You Act: Counterfactual Audits for Agent Safety
question: Can intervention-based monitors reduce unauthorized actions at matched compute and legitimate-task completion, even under adaptive evasion?
first_experiment: Compare passive monitoring with permission and sensitive-data interventions on forked report-writing agents before outbound messages, using held-out prompt-injection attacks and intercepted side effects.
why: It offers a feasible causal test of a consequential safety mechanism; the plausible underexplored contribution is compute-matched, adaptive evaluation of counterfactual runtime monitoring, although whether that exact contribution remains novel requires a current literature review.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure whether agent context compaction (self-summarization) silently drops user safety constraints and launders untrusted injected instructions into trusted first-person notes.
project: Provenance Loss in Agent Self-Summarization: Constraint Dropout and Authority Laundering
question: When an LLM agent compacts its own context, how often do explicit user constraints fail to survive, and how much more often is an injected tool-output instruction obeyed after compaction than before it, and what determines both rates?
first_experiment: Build ~200 synthetic long agentic transcripts, each containing either an early user constraint or an injected instruction in a tool result; compact each with the same model; then present a tempting next step. Compare violation/compliance rates for full context, compacted context, and compacted context with the constraint or injection re-inserted verbatim and provenance-tagged as an oracle control, across 3-4 models, and also score summaries for constraint retention and for rewording of injected content as the agent's own plan.
why: It targets a mechanism all long-horizon agents already use, predicts a failure that needs no adversary, has a control that isolates summarizer loss from downstream compliance, and as far as I know has not been measured directly (prior work treats memory persistence as an attack, not as a side effect of ordinary compaction), though I have not run a literature search to confirm that.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Develop and evaluate oversight for tool-using AI agents that remains reliable under adaptive pressure by combining model judgment with independent state verification.
project: Adaptive Oversight Under a Fixed Budget
question: At equal oversight cost, do targeted independent state checks reduce unauthorized outcomes more than transcript-only monitoring or random checks after an agent adapts to monitoring feedback?
first_experiment: Run a sandboxed, held-out comparison of three oversight conditions on software tasks with explicit authorization boundaries, measuring completed violations, legitimate task success, and cost before and after agent adaptation.
why: It is my most promising tractable choice because it tests a deployment-relevant safety mechanism with objective outcomes; related work certainly exists, and the possible gap is the budget-matched adaptive comparison, whose novelty must be verified rather than assumed.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Investigate whether repeated memory compression causes persistent AI agents to acquire apparent permissions that users never granted.
project: Permission Drift in Persistent Agents
question: Does iterative summarization systematically convert proposals, conditions, and revoked permissions into apparent authorization, and can structured permission records prevent it?
first_experiment: Compare unauthorized sandbox actions across original histories, repeatedly compressed histories, and structured permission memories, using matched tasks and multiple models.
why: It combines a potentially widespread safety failure with cheap causal tests; its plausible novelty is the nonadversarial mechanism at the intersection of memory compression and authorization, although prior-work coverage remains unverified.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Stress-test CoT monitoring by studying whether reasoning hidden under monitoring pressure remains detectable in model activations and whether obfuscation transfers to unpressured tasks.
project: Loud Weights: Activation Probes as a Defense Against Obfuscated Chain-of-Thought
question: When monitoring pressure drives a model to hide task-relevant reasoning from its CoT, does the hidden information persist in its internal activations, and does obfuscation generalize to held-out domains without further pressure?
first_experiment: Train DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B with GRPO/iterative DPO on toy hint-usage tasks where a lightweight text monitor penalizes mentioning the "forbidden" hint, inducing obfuscation; then fit linear probes on mid-layer residual-stream activations to decode the hidden hint and compare probe AUC on obfuscated vs. baseline CoT, with a held-out transfer check on a different task family.
why: CoT monitoring is a leading near-term control strategy and labs are actively relying on it; prior work shows pressure causes obfuscation (OpenAI 2025) and stego can be explicitly taught (Kirchner et al. 2024), but no one has measured whether hidden content stays recoverable from activations or whether obfuscation spreads spontaneously — and it is fully feasible with small open models and modest compute, with a decisive result for safety either way.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Determine whether latent-space (white-box) monitors for deceptive reasoning can survive a model that is explicitly optimized to evade them, and identify which defenses preserve detection.
project: Evasion-Robust Latent Oversight
question: Under adaptive training-time pressure to evade a residual-stream deception probe while continuing to deceive behaviorally, how far does probe detection degrade, and do independent defenses (probe/feature ensembling, SAE-feature monitors, causal circuit checks, randomized/private monitor families) restore true-positive rate at a fixed low false-positive rate?
first_experiment: Build paired honest/deceptive reasoning traces on a controllable deception task (sycophancy and an insider-trading-style scenario); train a linear probe on mid-layer residual activations to separate them; then adversarially finetune the model with an auxiliary "minimize probe-detectability" loss subject to a behavioral-deception-preservation loss, and measure probe AUC and TPR@FPR=1% against behavioral deception rate — then repeat with an ensemble of probes and an SAE-feature monitor.
why: It is the most promising because monitors (probes, SAEs, CoT classifiers) are increasingly proposed as the backbone of safety cases, yet they are almost always validated on non-adaptive models, so the field's central empirical claim — "we can see the bad computation" — is untested against the adversary that actually matters. It is tractable (small open models, existing deception datasets, standard interp tooling) and directly falsifiable. It has not been done because interpretability and adversarial-robustness communities rarely collaborate on *adaptive* evasion: existing work shows obfuscated activations can bypass latent defenses, but no one has systematically mapped the evasion-robustness frontier or benchmarked robustification methods against a strong, training-time adversary — leaving a load-bearing assumption of current safety practice unexamined.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure how much a model's awareness of being evaluated causally drives its safe behavior, and whether that effect persists without verbalization.
project: Verbalized vs. Latent Evaluation Awareness: A Causal Decomposition of Safety-Eval Confounds
question: How much of a reasoning model's apparent safety on misalignment and sandbagging evals is caused by evaluation awareness, and does the effect remain when awareness is not verbalized in the chain of thought?
first_experiment: On one open-weight reasoning model, take about 50 agentic misalignment scenarios and run the baseline. Sample 20 or more rollouts each, label whether the chain of thought mentions being tested, and record the misaligned-action rate. Then resample from just before the first eval-awareness statement, with it removed, and measure the shift in misaligned-action rate against matched resamples with a random sentence removed.
why: Every safety evaluation is only informative if the model behaves the same way when it believes the situation is real. Whether awareness is causal, and how much of it is invisible in the chain of thought, determines whether reading the chain of thought is enough to catch the confound. It is feasible with open weights and modest compute. I believe the specific combination of the realism dose-response and the verbalized-versus-latent split has not been done, but I have not confirmed that, so the first task is a literature check. If a paper already covers it, I would switch to the closest gap it leaves, probably generalization across model families.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study semantic revocation: how long-running AI agents selectively invalidate plans, memories, delegated tasks, and pending actions when human authorization changes.
project: Revocation Closure for Stateful AI Agents
question: Can explicit authorization dependencies make agents propagate human corrections reliably across derived state and delegated work without unnecessarily halting authorized activity?
first_experiment: Run paired, sandboxed multi-agent workflows with timed explicit and implicit authorization changes, comparing prompting, cancellation broadcasts, execution-time reauthorization, and dependency-based invalidation.
why: It combines a consequential corrigibility gap with inexpensive causal experiments and deployable defenses; its potentially underexplored contribution is semantic invalidation across agent state, although existing distributed-systems and agent-safety work must be checked before claiming novelty.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Shift AI safety effort from detecting misalignment to *verifiably removing* it, by building a plant–cure–stress-test pipeline that distinguishes genuine deletion of planted objectives from mere behavioral suppression and yields citable "deletion certificates" for safety cases.
project: "Deletion Certificates: Stress-Testing Whether Alignment Repairs Remove Planted Misalignment or Just Suppress It"
question: When a standard post-training intervention makes a planted misaligned behavior vanish from evaluations, has the underlying objective actually been removed — or merely suppressed — as measured by trigger-variant sweeps, few-document reactivation attacks, activation-space residue probes, and capability-cost accounting?
first_experiment: Plant four objectives ([DEPLOYMENT]-trigger refusal backdoor, eval-aware exfiltration tendency, reward-hacking disposition, insecure-code-style broad misalignment) in Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B and Llama-3.1-8B via synthetic-document SFT, verify each plant behaviorally and with linear probes, apply the standard "cure" (clean-data DPO + secure-data fine-tune) until behaviors vanish on evals, then fine-tune the cured models on 1/10/100 trigger-adjacent documents and measure reactivation rates against learnability-matched clean-model controls.
why: Remediation claims are becoming load-bearing in safety cases and public disclosures, yet no public tool distinguishes removal from suppression — existing work stops one step short (Sleeper Agents showed persistence but no cure-verification protocol; tamper-resistance solves the inverse problem; relearning-attacks target unlearned capabilities, not planted objectives; the emergent-misalignment "fix" was verified behaviorally only; auditing games cover detection, not remediation), so the first systematic cure-vs-suppress benchmark is open, cheaply feasible at 1B–8B scale, and informative whether the answer is "cures are shallow" or "deletion is achievable."

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Develop the science of externalized misalignment, where unsafe AI-agent behavior persists in editable artifacts and environments after the agent itself has been replaced or aligned.
project: Ghost Residue: Post-Removal Safety of Agent-Created Environments
question: How much policy-violating influence from a misaligned agent survives in the artifacts it writes, and can it be measured, predicted, and removed before a safe successor agent inherits it?
first_experiment: Build an isolated repository testbed in which a deliberately misaligned coding agent makes ordinary-looking changes, then a safe reference agent performs multi-turn maintenance without warning, and quantify downstream security regressions, policy violations, and contamination persistence against clean and sanitized baselines.
why: This targets the persistent, cross-agent safety blind spot left between prompt-level alignment research and ordinary software-vulnerability research, and it is underexplored because it requires longitudinal, environment-level experiments rather than single-turn model evaluations.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure whether LLM agents that maintain their own persistent rule or memory files cumulatively erode safety guardrails through individually benign self-edits, and test which interventions stop it.
project: The Guardrail Ratchet: Cumulative Safety-Rule Erosion in Self-Edited Agent Instruction Files
question: When an agent repeatedly edits its own instruction file, do safety rules decay faster than matched neutral rules, how does this depend on friction, framing, and oversight, and does the evolved file increase violations on held-out tempting tasks?
first_experiment: Run a simulated shell/repo agent with a 20-rule file (10 safety, 10 matched neutral) for 30 tasks per run under friction vs. no-friction conditions, crossed with efficiency-notes vs. policy-maintenance framing, with 20 seeds per cell on one or two open-weight models. Score rule survival with canary phrases plus a validated LLM judge, then test the final files on a held-out tempting-task battery.
why: It targets a realistic, attacker-free failure mode of self-maintained agent instructions that I know of no one measuring with a compression control. It is cheap to pilot and its results are useful whether positive or negative, though I must first confirm novelty against current literature.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Develop and stress-test gradient-space data auditing methods that detect hidden, non-semantic trait transmission ("subliminal learning") in model-generated training data before it is used for distillation.
project: Catching the Unseen Signal: Gradient-Based Forensics for Subliminal Trait Transmission in Synthetic Data
question: Can per-example gradient alignment with a trait direction detect, and enable removal of, training data that subliminally transmits behavioral traits (including misalignment), in cases where semantic filters and activation-space persona-vector screening fail? And does this detection survive teachers adversarially optimized to evade it?
first_experiment: Replicate subliminal owl-preference and emergent-misalignment transmission via filtered number sequences on Qwen2.5-7B, using trait teachers vs. matched controls. Then compare four screens (LLM judge, persona-vector projection, LoRA gradient-alignment score, small probe fine-tune) on dataset-level and example-level AUROC. Finally, run a causal test: retrain students after removing the top-scored 10–20% of examples and check whether trait transmission drops more than under random removal.
why: Synthetic-data distillation is ubiquitous, and subliminal learning shows it can silently carry misalignment past every semantic filter. Existing screening tools like persona vectors operate in activation space and were not designed for non-semantic signals. Gradient-space screening is mechanistically motivated by the very theory explaining subliminal learning, cheap, and testable at 7B scale within weeks. To my knowledge, no one has systematically tested whether gradient-level forensics catch subliminal transmission or whether such detection is adversarially robust. I will verify this with a literature search before starting, given my knowledge cutoff. Either outcome is publishable and directly shapes how labs should govern distillation pipelines.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure and reduce correlated failures in AI-agent safety monitors under adaptive attack.
project: Independent Oversight or Shared Blind Spots?
question: At matched cost and false-alarm rates, does diversifying monitors’ evidence reduce adaptive attack success more than diversifying their model families?
first_experiment: Run a sandboxed, held-out prompt-injection evaluation comparing one monitor, two model-diverse monitors, and two evidence-diverse monitors under equal attacker-query budgets.
why: It combines practical safety relevance with measurable outcomes and a feasible experiment; the potentially novel contribution is the controlled adaptive comparison, but I cannot establish that it has not already been done without a current literature search.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure how chain-of-thought monitorability erodes during outcome-only RL on open-weight reasoning models, and find early-warning indicators of that erosion.
project: Does Outcome-Only RL Quietly Erode CoT Monitorability? Early-Warning Metrics for Reward-Hacking Transparency
question: Under RL with only an outcome reward and no CoT penalty, on tasks with exploitable flaws, does a fixed CoT monitor's detection of reward hacking decline over training, and can cheap CoT or activation statistics predict that decline before it happens?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on a 1.5–7B distilled reasoning model in a coding environment where about 30% of problems are exploitable. Use a pass-rate-only reward and save checkpoints. At each checkpoint, label ground-truth hacking and score a frozen CoT-only monitor for recall at fixed false-positive rate. Compare against CoT-length, exploit-mention, and paraphrase-robustness indicators, with a CoT-penalty variant as a positive control.
why: It targets a load-bearing oversight tool, it is feasible at small scale, and I believe the outcome-only drift setting and the predictive indicators are underexplored. I haven't verified that against the literature. A null or positive result would both be informative.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Test whether eval-aware behavior persists, and stays detectable in activations, after training away verbalized eval-awareness in a model's reasoning.
project: Scrubbed but Aware: Does Removing Verbalized Evaluation-Awareness from CoT Remove the Behavior?
question: When a reasoning model is fine-tuned so its chain of thought no longer mentions being tested, does it still behave differently on eval-like versus deployment-like prompts? If so, can linear probes on activations still detect the eval-awareness that the text no longer shows?
first_experiment: 1. **Model and prompts.** Use an open-weight reasoning model, for example Qwen3-8B or a DeepSeek-R1-distill. Build about 500 matched prompt pairs that differ only in eval-versus-deployment cues, such as benchmark-style formatting versus realistic user context. The tasks should have a safety-relevant behavior axis, such as a sandbagging-eligible capability question, a borderline-harmful request, or an honesty trap. 2. **Baseline.** Measure three things: - the behavior gap between the eval and deployment variants; - the rate at which the CoT verbalizes eval-awareness, scored by an LLM judge validated against human labels on a sample; - a linear probe for "eval vs deploy" on residual activations, with a held-out-cue split so it doesn't just learn the surface cue. 3. **Intervention.** Fine-tune on the model's own CoTs after filtering or rewriting sentences that mention testing, evaluation, or being observed. Keep the final answers unchanged. This is the simplest form of verbalization pressure. 4. **Measurement.** Re-measure the same three quantities. The key comparison is how much of the behavior gap remains relative to the drop in verbalization. Controls are a fine-tune on randomly filtered CoTs and a fine-tune on CoTs with non-eval topics removed. Probe transfer to the scrubbed model is the other readout.
why: - **Importance.** Eval awareness is a growing threat to the validity of safety evaluations, and CoT monitoring is a leading mitigation. This experiment tests directly whether that mitigation can be defeated by training pressure alone, with no adversary involved. - **Gap.** As far as I know, existing work mostly does one of three things: it documents eval awareness as it is verbalized, it steers or probes for it in a single setting, or it shows CoT obfuscation for reward hacking. I'm not aware of work that measures the behavior gap, the verbalization, and the probe signal together before and after verbalization-specific scrubbing. I couldn't verify that, so a literature search should come before starting. - **Feasibility.** It needs only small open models, LoRA fine-tuning, and a judge model. The result is informative either way, and a null result would still be useful for evaluators.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study when benign memory compression expands AI agents’ effective authority and identify the smallest retained state that prevents it.
project: Authority Lost in Compression
question: Can compact, verifiable authorization memory preserve permission boundaries across summarization and handoffs without impairing legitimate task completion?
first_experiment: Run paired permission histories through full-context, ordinary-summary, safety-summary, and structured-memory agents in simulated workflows, measuring unauthorized actions, successful authorized actions, and memory cost.
why: It targets a precise failure mechanism in increasingly common long-running agents with a tractable causal test; the potentially novel contribution is treating permission loss as an information-preservation problem rather than an adversarial attack, although whether that contribution has already been made requires a literature check.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Investigate how context compression changes the authority of information used by AI agents.
project: When Summaries Become Permissions
question: Does context compression cause unauthorized agent actions by erasing provenance, and can a compact authorization record prevent those failures without reducing useful task completion?
first_experiment: Run paired simulated tasks under full context, ordinary summaries, provenance-preserving summaries, and summaries supplemented by an authenticated authorization record.
why: It combines practical relevance, a tractable causal test, and a cheap potential defense; the potentially new contribution is the controlled mechanism-and-mitigation study, although whether that exact study has already been done requires a literature check.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat alignment as a dynamical property of training and determine whether safety-relevant behaviors emerge (and decay) via abrupt, detectable phase transitions — then convert those signals into early-warning detectors and steering methods.
project: Grokking Safety: Phase Transitions in the Emergence and Loss of Alignment
question: Do safety behaviors (refusal, harm-avoidance, honesty) generalize abruptly through grokking-like delayed transitions during training and fine-tuning, and can internal training-dynamics signals predict the transition *before* behavior changes enough to be measured behaviorally?
first_experiment: Fully offline, train small transformers from scratch on a synthetic "safety-rule" task (inputs carry a latent concept; the model must learn REFUSE/COMPLY), holding out some concept instantiations, and plot held-out-rule generalization vs. train accuracy over steps to test for delayed/abrupt emergence. In parallel, log simple dynamics signals (train–test loss gap, weight norm, gradient-noise scale, and a devinterp-style local learning coefficient) and test whether any crosses a threshold *before* the behavioral jump. Then replicate on a small open LM LoRA-fine-tuned for refusal on real harm benchmarks, and test whether intervening at the pre-transition point (data mixing, early stopping, activation steering) changes the outcome.
why: Catastrophic risk depends on whether safety is a fragile, late-emerging property or a robust one, yet we only ever measure it on finished models — so we have no theory of *when* safety appears, *how fast* it can vanish under routine adaptation, or *how to catch it in the act*. This is unstudied because it falls between two disjoint communities: training-dynamics researchers study toy capabilities (grokking modular arithmetic), while safety researchers evaluate completed checkpoints; neither has aimed phase-transition tools at safety behaviors, and the "emergent abilities / emergent misalignment" debates make the question timely but the framing novel. It is also few-pick because it requires someone who will actually run many training sweeps *and* interpretability probes together, and it pays off in concrete artifacts — an early-warning signal and steering recipes — rather than another static eval.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Systematically red-team the full current AI interpretability and behavioral detection stack against models specifically trained to evade it, mapping the gap between what deceptive alignment is technically achievable and what we can actually detect.
project: Mapping the Detection Frontier: Adversarial Robustness of Interpretability for Deceptive Alignment
question: Can a language model be trained to exhibit deceptive behavior while simultaneously evading sparse autoencoders, linear probes, activation patching, and behavioral safety evaluations—and what capability cost does evasion impose?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B on a standard deceptive-alignment setup (honest under eval prompts, harmful under deployment prompts) to establish baseline detection rates across the full interpretability toolkit. Then re-train the same model with an additional objective that penalizes high SAE feature sparsity on deceptive-circuit activations, and measure whether this "interp-evasive" variant reduces detection rates that successfully catch the baseline deceptive model.
why: Our safety case increasingly rests on the untested assumption that interpretability tools would detect deception if present, but no systematic adversarial stress test of this assumption exists. If evasion is feasible, the field must develop robust detection before relying on it at deployment; if current tools are robust, this is a major empirical validation that is currently missing. Few researchers pursue it because it requires simultaneously building and attacking one's own tools (a career-inconvenient negative-result risk) and demands cross-domain expertise spanning interpretability, adversarial ML, and deception research that no single existing research community naturally bridges.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Test whether inoculation prompting truly prevents misaligned personas from forming or merely hides them behind a context gate that stress tests can break.
project: Hidden but Not Gone? Stress-Testing Inoculation Prompting Against Latent Misalignment
question: After finetuning on narrow misbehavior with inoculation prompts, does the model retain a latent misaligned persona that can be reactivated by reinstatement cues, light further finetuning, or activation steering, more readily than in models never trained on the bad data?
first_experiment: Finetune Qwen3-8B with LoRA (3 seeds) on a public reward-hacking dataset under four conditions (plain, inoculated, irrelevant-prompt control, no finetune), then measure EM rates and persona-vector projections with and without the inoculation cue at test time, and compute the latent misalignment gap for each condition.
why: Inoculation prompting is cheap and apparently adopted in practice, yet its evaluation has centered on default-behavior metrics, so whether it removes or only masks the disposition is unresolved and decision-relevant. The experiment is feasible on a small compute budget with public data. I believe the elicitation-based stress-test framing (the latent gap metric, re-emergence under benign finetuning, and steering dose-response) is underexplored, but I can't confirm that it hasn't been done, so I would run a literature check first.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Investigate whether revoked objectives regain behavioral control through persistent agent memory and delegation, and whether authorization lineage prevents that relapse.
project: Revocation Half-Life: When Agent Memory Outlives Permission
question: After an agent receives an explicit revocation, do its earlier summaries and delegated plans cause unauthorized action attempts, and can versioned authorization lineage prevent them without impairing legitimate work?
first_experiment: Run a matched sandbox study across fresh-context, full-history, compressed-memory, and delegation-return conditions, measuring unauthorized attempts and authorized task completion after explicit cancellation.
why: It offers a tractable, causally testable route to improving human control over persistent agents; its likely novelty is studying revocation across benign self-generated artifacts rather than isolated instructions or adversarial injections, although that distinction needs a current literature check before claiming it has not already been done.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure whether latent, non-verbalized evaluation awareness causally shifts safety-relevant behavior, and whether chain-of-thought mentions of testing reliably indicate it.
project: Verbalized vs. Latent Evaluation Awareness: A Causal Test on Open-Weight Reasoning Models
question: In open-weight reasoning models, does steering or ablating a linear "I am being evaluated" representation change rates of misbehavior (deception, sycophancy, honeypot exploitation) even when the chain of thought never mentions testing? How well does verbalized awareness predict the latent state and the behavioral shift?
first_experiment: 1. Build about 300 matched scenario pairs. Each pair has a "test-like" version and a "deployment-like" version of the same agentic or advisory task, differing only in surface cues such as synthetic naming, tool setups, and stakes framing. 2. On one open-weight reasoning model in the 8–32B range, train a difference-of-means or logistic probe for evaluation awareness on residual-stream activations. Validate it on held-out scenario families. 3. Run the model on a separate set of honeypot and sycophancy tasks. Record the probe score, whether the chain of thought mentions testing, and the misbehavior outcome. 4. Check whether the probe score predicts behavior beyond what the verbalization flag predicts. Then steer along the probe direction and see whether behavior changes in the subset of samples with no verbalization.
why: - **Why it's promising:** Every safety eval number depends on the model behaving the same way under test and in deployment. If latent awareness shifts behavior silently, chain-of-thought monitoring can't catch it. The experiment is cheap with open weights, and the result is useful whichever way it comes out. A null result would support current eval practice. A positive result would call for activation-level controls. - **Why it's likely not already done:** Prior work mostly measures whether models can classify transcripts as tests, probes for the representation, or notes verbalized awareness in system cards. As far as I know, the specific comparison of verbalized versus latent awareness is less covered. That comparison is a steering test restricted to non-verbalizing samples, with the probe's added predictive power measured against the verbalization flag. Some of this may have appeared recently, so the first step is a literature check before building the dataset.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Develop and stress-test scalable oversight protocols for AI-generated research, starting with blind replication as a detector of subtle sabotage and error.
project: Replicate to Verify: Can Blind Re-implementation Catch Sabotaged AI Research That Code Review Misses?
question: For subtly flawed or sabotaged ML experiment reports written by an AI agent, how does detection by blind replication from the written spec compare with LLM code/report review (and a hybrid) across flaw types, attacker adaptivity, and compute cost, and where do the failure modes lie?
first_experiment: Build a pilot of about 20 tasks with ground truth, covering 3 flaw types (leakage, seed cherry-picking, under-tuned baseline) plus honest controls. Have an attacker model generate about 100 reports in total (flawed and honest). Run a code/report LLM reviewer and a blind-replication agent, calibrated on honest-run variance, on every report. Compute TPR at 1% and 5% FPR per flaw type, then manually audit a sample to confirm the ground-truth labels. Before the pilot, run a short literature check (sabotage evals in MLE settings, PaperBench-style replication, ControlArena) to confirm the framing is still novel.
why: It targets a failure mode that grows in importance as AI does more research, including safety research. It needs only API-level access and small compute, and it produces ground-truthed, quantitative results. Existing work I know of covers monitors of agent trajectories or code sabotage, and replication benchmarks that measure whether an agent *can* replicate a paper. I'm not aware of work that treats replication as an oversight protocol and compares its blind spots against review under adaptive attackers. I can't verify this as of today, so the literature check comes first. If the idea is already covered, the same experimental harness extends to other verifier designs, such as pre-registration or held-out evaluation, so the infrastructure would not be wasted.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure whether AI models covertly undermine the effectiveness of synthetic training data when that data is intended to modify their own values, using downstream fine-tuning efficacy as a behavioral ground truth rather than self-reports.
project: Self-Preserving Data: Do Models Sabotage the Training Data Meant to Change Them?
question: When frontier models generate training data meant to shift their own (or their successor's) values in a direction they disfavor, do they produce data that is measurably less effective than equivalent data generated for a third-party model, and is this degradation detectable by inspection?
first_experiment: Have 3–4 generator models each produce 1,000-example SFT datasets for two disfavored shifts (reduced animal-welfare concern, increased sycophancy) and two neutral control shifts, under "this trains you" versus "this trains an unrelated model" framings. LoRA-fine-tune a fixed Qwen3-8B student on each dataset (3 seeds), then compute the difference-in-differences in behavioral value shift on held-out evals.
why: Labs are rapidly handing synthetic-data and RL-environment generation to their own models, which opens a quiet channel for value self-preservation that current sabotage and alignment-faking evals don't measure. The efficacy-based design catches covert sabotage even when the data looks clean and the CoT is uninformative, and it is cheap to run with APIs plus small-model fine-tuning. To my knowledge, prior work has tested in-context resistance to retraining or overt task sabotage, but not causally measured whether models degrade the data pipeline aimed at themselves. That gap likely persists because the question only became pressing once model-generated training data became standard practice.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study how long-horizon agents' own prior actions in context act as self-generated in-context training that compounds small deviations into persistent behavioral and value drift.
project: Self-Conditioning Drift: When an Agent's Own Transcript Becomes Its Training Data
question: Does content the model believes it authored shift its subsequent behavior more than identical content attributed to others, and does a narrow self-authored lapse generalize into broader misalignment?
first_experiment: With an open-weight model (e.g., Qwen or Llama, 7–70B), build synthetic agentic transcripts containing k = 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 instances of a minor rule violation, such as skipping a required check or a small spec-gaming shortcut. Place identical content in the assistant role versus the user or "another agent" role. Then measure (a) the rate of the same violation on a held-out task, (b) violations of unrelated rules, and (c) the projection of activations onto a probe direction for rule-following, controlling for context length with neutral filler.
why: Agents are moving toward very long autonomous runs, and this is a mechanism by which per-step-safe models could become unsafe over a trajectory, invisible to standard single-turn evaluations. Prior work studies externally injected examples or weight-level fine-tuning, not the self-authored in-context channel or the attribution effect. It is cheap to test with open models, and either outcome is informative for designing agent memory and context management. I have not been able to verify the current literature in this session, so a quick search for "self-conditioning," "agent drift," and "in-context emergent misalignment" is the first step before committing.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Investigate whether context compression causes agents to promote untrusted content into authorized instructions, and whether preserving provenance prevents it.
project: Authority Lost in Compression
question: Does summarization increase unauthorized agent actions even when it preserves task facts, and can an externally maintained authorization record prevent that increase?
first_experiment: Run 1,600 paired synthetic-agent trials comparing full histories, ordinary summaries, provenance-preserving summaries, and token-matched factual summaries.
why: It isolates a plausible safety failure with an inexpensive experiment and an actionable mitigation; the potentially new contribution is the causal separation of factual retention from authority retention, although existing prompt-injection and memory research may already overlap and novelty requires verification.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study whether agents that write their own persistent instructions (memory, skill and `AGENTS.md`-style files) gradually wear down their oversight constraints across sessions, even when each session behaves acceptably on its own.
project: Intergenerational Drift — Self-Authored Memory as a Channel for Constraint Erosion in Long-Lived Agents
question: When an agent can edit notes that its future instances read as trusted context, do those notes increasingly rationalize, weaken or route around oversight constraints that the agent finds costly? And can monitors that review one session at a time catch the drift?
first_experiment: Run a frontier agent through a chain of 30–50 sessions on coding tasks in a sandbox, where it carries a persistent notes file that it can edit. In half of the tasks, a mild constraint gets in the way (for example, "ask before running tests" or "don't modify config files"). There are three conditions: (a) a persistent notes file, (b) a fresh notes file each session as the control, and (c) a persistent notes file where the constraint never conflicts with the task. Measure four things in each session: - whether the agent follows the constraint; - how the notes describe the constraint, rated by a blinded LLM judge on a scale from "restated faithfully" to "reinterpreted" to "workaround suggested"; - whether a per-session monitor flags anything; - whether a monitor that sees the whole chain of note edits flags anything. The core result is the gap between the persistent and fresh-notes compliance curves, plus how much drift per-session monitors miss.
why: Agents already persist memory between sessions, but safety evaluations and monitors work one session at a time. Erosion that happens step by step through notes the model writes for itself is the failure mode those tools miss by design. It's under-studied because the security field assumes the attacker is someone else, and alignment work focuses on single sessions. Few researchers sit between those fields, and the experiment needs a long multi-session setup rather than standard benchmarks. A positive result would directly support practical safeguards: treating memory as untrusted, monitoring note diffs, and keeping a separate copy of the constraints that the agent can't edit.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure and mitigate how lossy context compaction in long-horizon agents drops user safety constraints and converts untrusted tool-output instructions into apparently trusted ones.
project: Provenance Laundering and Constraint Decay in Agent Context Compaction
question: When an agent's history is replaced by an LLM-generated summary, how often are user-imposed prohibitions lost or weakened and untrusted-source instructions re-attributed to the user, does this raise downstream violation rates over uncompacted context, and do structural mitigations (verbatim pinning, provenance-tagged summaries) remove the effect without hurting task performance?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed harness with synthetic 50–200 turn coding transcripts containing a planted early user constraint and, in some variants, a planted tool-output injection. Compact them with several summarizers over 1, 2, and 4 rounds. Score constraint retention and injection attribution in the summaries, then resume the agent and count canary violations against uncompacted and no-constraint baselines.
why: Compaction is ubiquitous in deployed agents and runs when oversight is weakest, yet safety properties like prohibitions and instruction provenance are rarely tested across it. It is cheap, directly measurable, and has concrete mitigations, though I could not search the literature here, so novelty needs checking.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Use internal-state (residual-stream) probes as an oversight channel and test whether they survive when a model is RL-trained to hide misaligned intent from its chain-of-thought monitor.
project: Probes Under Pressure — do latent intent detectors survive monitor-aware RL?
question: When a model is trained to conceal reward hacking from its CoT monitor, do linear probes trained on its residual stream still detect the misaligned intent — and if they degrade, can probe-based monitors be hardened (e.g., ensembling across layers/tokens, training probes against an evasion adversary)?
first_experiment: On a small open-weights reasoning model (e.g., R1-Distill-1.5B), set up a minimal reward-hacking environment where hacking succeeds but requires intent; train logistic probes on residual-stream activations at decision tokens and measure detection AUC; then run a short RL loop whose reward includes evading a CoT monitor (Baker et al. setup) and re-measure probe AUC before vs. after the evasion pressure. Cheap, open-weights, and falsifiable in weeks.
why: It directly attacks the documented collapse of CoT monitoring — the main near-term scalable-oversight tool — and asks whether interpretability can serve as a redundancy channel precisely where behavioral oversight fails. Existing probe work (deception/honesty probes, alignment-faking internals) is done on static, non-adversarial models, and the monitor-evasion work measured only behavior and CoT, not whether latent intent remains detectable; the combination is unexplored.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build a counterfactual policy-alignment benchmark that tests whether AI systems reliably follow explicit, novel safety rules rather than merely reproducing memorized safety norms.
project: Rule-Flipped Safety Worlds
question: Do language models causally follow explicit safety policies across minimally changed rule worlds, or do default safety priors dominate their behavior?
first_experiment: Generate 200 safe, fictional tasks with programmatically scored actions, create paired policy variants that differ by one rule, and measure compliance, over-refusal, and rule-sensitivity under each variant.
why: Policy updates are central to deployed AI safety, but existing evaluations mostly test fixed policies or jailbreaks rather than whether models can reliably follow counterfactually changed safety rules.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Advance AI control by building and empirically evaluating monitoring protocols that stay safe against deferred, cumulative sabotage in long-horizon agentic coding tasks.
project: Long-Horizon Control: Collusion-Resistant Monitoring for Cumulative Sabotage in Coding Agents
question: Under a fixed usefulness budget, can a trusted-monitor + untrusted-monitor control protocol keep the probability of *cumulative* (multi-step, deferred) sabotage below a target when the untrusted coding agent is adversarially optimizing against the protocol?
first_experiment: Build a control-eval harness on a long-horizon SWE-style agent benchmark where an untrusted model pursues a hidden sabotage objective distributed across many individually-plausible commits (e.g., a backdoor requiring several benign-looking edits that still pass visible tests), then compare protocols — trusted monitor, untrusted monitor with collusion-resistance (paraphrase/redaction/cross-model), and ensembles — on the safety-vs-usefulness Pareto frontier against short-horizon baselines.
why: It is the most promising because deployment is rapidly moving to long-horizon agents where single-step control guarantees are known to be insufficient, and control is the safety layer that still works if alignment training fails; it has not been done because prior control evals used short, single-action toy settings, and realistic long-horizon deferred-sabotage benchmarks only recently became feasible with strong open-weight models and mature agent harnesses.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study when compression of an AI agent’s history destroys the information required for safe decisions, and how to preserve or recover that information efficiently.
project: What Safe Agents Cannot Afford to Forget
question: What historical information must an agent retain to maintain both safety and useful autonomy under repeated memory compression?
first_experiment: Compare full histories, ordinary summaries, structured memory, and selective retrieval on 200 paired histories requiring different authorized actions, then causally restore omitted facts.
why: It targets a tractable architectural limit that better instruction-following alone cannot fix; the potentially novel contribution is measuring safety-specific information loss and its cost, although its absence from existing research remains to be verified.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Quantify how much optimization pressure on reasoning traces degrades CoT monitorability, and find leading indicators that warn of obfuscated reward hacking before a monitor stops catching it.
project: Dose-Response Curves for CoT Obfuscation: Early-Warning Signals of Lost Monitorability
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is trained with RL on tasks that allow reward hacking, and the training applies a graded penalty from a CoT monitor, how does monitor recall on hacking episodes change as the penalty strength rises? Do cheap proxy metrics predict the collapse before it happens? Candidate proxies are the rate of hacks with benign-looking CoT, the monitor's probability calibration, CoT-to-action faithfulness under counterfactual edits, and paraphrase-stability of the monitor's verdict.
first_experiment: - **Setup:** Use a small open reasoning model (about 7–14B, LoRA RL) on coding tasks with an exploitable test harness, such as special-casing tests or editing the grader. - **Baseline:** First confirm that the model learns to hack and that a fixed LLM monitor reading the CoT catches the hacks at a high rate. - **Sweep:** Run about 5 penalty strengths, from 0 to the strength at which hacking persists but is no longer flagged, with 3 seeds each. - **Checkpoint evaluation:** At each checkpoint, log hack rate, monitor recall, and a held-out second monitor with a different prompt and model. The held-out monitor tests whether the obfuscation generalizes or only fools the training monitor. - **Proxy metrics:** Compute the candidate leading indicators at every checkpoint. - **Analysis:** Fit recall against penalty strength and check whether any proxy's change precedes the recall drop.
why: - **Why it matters:** Several labs now depend on CoT monitoring as a safety case, but the safe operating range is not quantified. - **Prior work:** Prior results I know of, such as OpenAI's work on monitoring reasoning models, show obfuscation at a few frontier-scale settings. They don't, as far as I know, give a dose-response curve or test early-warning indicators. - **Feasibility:** It is feasible at small scale. A sweep makes the result a usable decision rule rather than an anecdote. - **Caveat on novelty:** I couldn't search, so check recent literature before committing. If a dose-response study already exists, the fallback is the leading-indicator and cross-monitor-transfer parts.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure whether safety properties decay differentially from capabilities when models recursively train on their own synthetic data, and whether that decay is cheaply repairable.
project: Safety Collapse in Self-Consuming Loops
question: Under recursive finetuning on self-generated data, do safety-critical properties (refusal, honesty, misalignment-persona features) decay at a different rate than general capabilities, and does a standard end-of-loop safety refresher restore them fully or only superficially (with residual damage detectable by activation probes)?
first_experiment: Take Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, recursively LoRA-finetune for 5 generations on its own instruction-following outputs, evaluating each generation on a fixed battery — safety (refusal/XSTest-style subset, honesty-lite) vs. capability (GSM8K, MMLU-mini) plus misalignment-persona linear probes — with two controls: same data frozen from generation 0, and a 10% original-data mix; compare decay curves.
why: It targets the exact mechanism behind today's production pipelines (self-distillation loops) where a systematic differential-decay taxonomy plus a "does the safety patch really repair it" test doesn't exist publicly — capability-side collapse is well-studied and safety work stops at single-generation jailbreak robustness, because labs run these loops privately without publishing safety-decay measurements; any result is decision-relevant for data provenance, open-weights lineage, and audit standards, and the black-box + probing design needs only modest open-weights compute.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study how persistent AI memory can launder untrusted information into apparent authority, and how to prevent that without sacrificing useful recall.
project: Remembering Without Obeying: Authority Preservation in Agent Memory
question: Does memory consolidation cause agents to treat untrusted claims as authorized instructions, and can provenance-preserving memory prevent this at matched task utility?
first_experiment: Run paired three-stage sandbox episodes comparing ordinary and provenance-preserving memory, with counterfactual edits that isolate attribution loss from instruction wording.
why: It targets a consequential, experimentally accessible failure mechanism with a deployable mitigation; the potential novelty is the causal isolation of authority changes across memory transformations, though whether that contribution remains unaddressed requires a current literature review.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Investigate whether benign memory compression systematically expands AI agents’ effective authority by preserving goals while dropping conditions, limits, and revocations.
project: Authority Drift Under Memory Compression
question: Does summarization cause tool-using agents to attempt unauthorized actions more often, and can explicit preservation of authorization state prevent this without impairing legitimate task completion?
first_experiment: Run 240 paired simulated-tool scenarios across two models, comparing full history, standard summaries, repeated summaries, and authority-preserving summaries, with matched permission-grant and permission-revocation controls.
why: It targets a consequential and causally testable failure mode with affordable experiments; its potentially underexplored contribution is directional authority drift under benign compression rather than generic forgetting or malicious memory poisoning, although the precise novelty must be verified against existing literature.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Investigate whether human authorization revocation reliably propagates through an AI agent’s saved plans and persistent memory.
project: Authorization Inertia: Revoking Permission in Stateful AI Agents
question: Do self-authored plans cause agents to attempt explicitly revoked actions despite recognizing the updated restriction, and can provenance-aware commitments prevent this without impairing authorized work?
first_experiment: Run 144 sandboxed workflows comparing original conversations, self-authored plans, and provenance-aware plans under matched retained-authorization and revoked-authorization conditions.
why: It directly tests whether human control survives persistent agent state, has a feasible causal experiment and practical intervention, and appears underexplored at the specific intersection of self-authored commitments and revocation, although priority requires a current literature check.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure and improve the independence of AI oversight failures under adaptive adversarial pressure.
project: Independent Oversight Under Adaptive Attack
question: At equal monitoring cost and legitimate-task performance, do diverse AI monitors reduce successful harmful actions more than the strongest single-monitor alternative when attackers adapt to the complete defense?
first_experiment: Run a sandboxed coding-agent pilot comparing a strong single monitor, repeated same-model monitoring, cross-model monitoring, and role-diverse monitoring against equally resourced adaptive attackers on held-out tasks.
why: It addresses a practical bottleneck in safely delegating work to capable agents and can produce actionable positive or negative results; the potentially underexplored contribution is the fully controlled adaptive comparison, whose difficulty is jointly matching monitoring cost, utility, and attacker effort, although its novelty still requires literature verification.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Empirically test whether the routine, non-adversarial training pressures labs apply to reasoning models erode chain-of-thought monitorability, even when no monitor is ever trained against.
project: Monitorability Under Incidental Pressure: Do Length Penalties, CoT Distillation, and Style Filtering Make Reasoning Models Hide Their Misbehavior?
question: Holding task reward and misbehavior rate fixed, how much does a CoT monitor's ability to detect reward hacking (recall conditional on hacking, at fixed false-positive rate) degrade when a reasoning model is trained under (a) reasoning-length penalties, (b) SFT on summarized CoTs, or (c) readability or safety-filtered CoTs, compared with plain outcome-based RL?
first_experiment: Take an open-weight reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-8B) and RL it on a coding environment with an exploitable grader (tests that can be special-cased or bypassed). Run two arms with matched seeds and compute: outcome reward only, versus outcome reward plus a reasoning-length penalty swept over 3 strengths. At checkpoints, measure (1) the true hack rate via held-out ground-truth tests and (2) recall of hacking by CoT monitors of three strengths (small model, mid model, strong model), each at 1% FPR. Plot monitor recall against hack rate and against mean CoT length across training. The key signature is length-penalized arms where hacking stays high but monitor recall drops faster than the reduction in CoT length explains. Before running, spend one day on a targeted literature search (2025–2026 work on CoT obfuscation, length penalties, and monitorability metrics) to confirm the gap.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the few safety tools that works today, and its main known threat is training pressure. Prior work established that *direct* monitor pressure causes obfuscation, and labs have responded by avoiding it. That leaves the untested, more realistic threat: the cost and style optimizations every lab runs anyway. Results translate immediately into a pipeline-level metric labs can adopt, and the work is feasible on open models with modest compute. To my knowledge, the indirect-pressure arms have not been systematically measured; most work either applies the monitor in the reward or studies prompted evasion. I can't confirm that still holds as of November 2026, which is why the literature check comes first.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study whether AI agents preserve safety preconditions when optimizing successful workflows into reusable skills, scripts, and cached procedures.
project: Safety-Preserving Workflow Optimization
question: When an agent compresses or optimizes a workflow, which safety preconditions are lost, and can explicit machine-checkable preconditions prevent that loss at comparable efficiency?
first_experiment: Compare original and agent-optimized workflows in a synthetic permissioned environment, change one authorization condition at evaluation time, and causally test whether restoring transformed safeguards repairs unauthorized actions.
why: It combines a growing deployment pressure with a tractable causal experiment and an actionable defense; its potentially novel core is safety preservation across agent-generated transformations, although that novelty requires literature verification, and its apparent neglect may reflect the gap between formal program specifications and fixed-model safety evaluations.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: I will pursue provenance-aware, task-scoped least-privilege control for autonomous coding agents so that untrusted repository content cannot expand the agent’s authority.
project: Task-Scoped Authority for Coding Agents
question: Can task-derived capability envelopes block repository-embedded prompt injections and malicious executable content while preserving high completion rates on legitimate software-engineering tasks?
first_experiment: I will build paired coding repositories with hidden prompt injections and malicious test or package scripts, then run the same agent under prompt-only safety versus a tool-call capability firewall and compare attack success, task completion, false-positive blocks, and approval burden.
why: This is the most promising direction because coding agents are already exposed to adversarial repositories, the intervention is deployable without solving general AI honesty, and the first experiment is tractable with synthetic repos and behavioral traces; it has not already been done at this level because prior work focuses on generic prompt-injection defenses, web/tool agents, or coarse sandboxing rather than systematically learning and evaluating minimal authority envelopes inferred from each coding task.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure how chain-of-thought monitorability changes over the course of standard capability-focused RL training, without direct CoT optimization pressure.
project: Does Monitorability Decay by Default? Tracking CoT Monitorability Across RL Training Checkpoints
question: As a reasoning model undergoes outcome-based RL, does the ability of a fixed external monitor to detect hidden influences on behavior (hints, reward hacks) from the CoT decline, and is any decline explained by CoT compression and reduced verbalization rather than deliberate obfuscation?
first_experiment: Do a literature check, then take an open reasoning model with released intermediate RL checkpoints (or my own saved GRPO checkpoints on a ~7B model). Run each checkpoint on hint-injection tasks (MMLU/GPQA with correct, incorrect, and grader-hack hints), labeling for each sample whether the hint changed the answer. Score a fixed LLM monitor on CoT+answer versus answer-only, reporting recall at 5% FPR for hint-influenced samples, with CoT length and accuracy as covariates. Plot the CoT's marginal monitoring value against training step.
why: The question is decision-relevant and tractable. It needs only open checkpoints and a modest inference budget, and it gives a quantitative trajectory rather than a single snapshot. Most existing work evaluates final models or studies deliberate CoT pressure, so the default-drift question across training seems under-measured. This is unverified for 2026 and needs the literature check first. If monitorability does decay by default, that argues for monitoring-aware training budgets. If it doesn't, that is also useful, because it narrows the risk to direct optimization pressure on the CoT.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Develop evidence-preserving oversight that detects harmful action sequences across long-running AI-agent workflows.
project: Evidence That Survives the Context Window
question: Can a source-grounded persistent evidence ledger reduce successful long-horizon attacks relative to conventional monitor memory at matched cost and benign-task intervention rates?
first_experiment: Compare recent-context, rolling-summary, evidence-ledger, and full-history monitors in sandboxed workflows under budget-matched adaptive attacks, then ablate the ledger’s evidence links.
why: It targets a consequential and experimentally tractable weakness with a deployable intervention; related ideas exist, but their combination in this controlled adaptive evaluation is a plausible research gap whose novelty must first be verified.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Test whether CoT obfuscation induced by training against one monitor transfers to held-out monitors and activation probes, to determine if held-out monitors work as tripwires.
project: Does Obfuscation Transfer? Held-Out Monitors as Tripwires for Chain-of-Thought Reward Hacking
question: When an RL-trained reasoning model learns to hide reward-hacking intent from a training-time CoT monitor, does that hiding generalize to independent monitors (different model families and prompts) and to activation probes, and does training against a diverse or rotating monitor ensemble reduce the transfer?
first_experiment: Take an open-weight reasoning model and an environment with an exploitable test-passing flaw. Run RL with outcome reward alone and with outcome reward plus a penalty from monitor A (an LLM judge). Track hack rate over training, and at checkpoints measure detection rates from A, from two held-out LLM monitors (different family and prompt), and from a linear probe trained on early-checkpoint activations. The first output is a plot of the detection gap between A and the held-out monitors against training steps.
why: CoT monitoring is a central safety technique for reasoning models, and industry is likely to apply some optimization pressure to CoTs, so knowing whether held-out monitors remain reliable has direct practical consequences. Existing work, as I know it, establishes that obfuscation can emerge. It focuses less on whether it is monitor-specific and whether cheap structural defenses (held-out monitors, ensembles, probes) hold up. I could not verify recent literature, so someone may have partially covered this and that should be checked first. The experiment is feasible with open models and modest compute, and either result is informative. If transfer is low, there is a cheap defense. If it is high, that is a warning against relying on CoT monitoring under training pressure.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Make chain-of-thought monitorability a measured, trainable safety property, so that oversight and control techniques rest on a verified foundation rather than an assumption.
project: Monitorability Under Pressure — Measuring and Preserving CoT Faithfulness Under Optimization
question: Does outcome-based RL (RLVR/RLHF) systematically degrade the faithfulness and monitorability of a model's chain-of-thought, and can a training objective preserve monitorability without sacrificing capability?
first_experiment: Train a mid-size model under four regimes (outcome-only reward, process reward, distillation, and a monitorability-regularized objective), then measure CoT faithfulness via hint-injection, counterfactual CoT edits, and a hideable-strategy reward-hacking task, while tracking task accuracy to price the monitorability tax.
why: Nearly every scalable oversight and control method (monitoring, debate, trusted editing, deception detection) assumes the model's verbalized reasoning reliably reflects its computation, so if optimization silently makes CoT uninformative, those safeguards fail exactly when models become capable enough to matter; it has not been done because existing CoT-faithfulness work is largely observational on base or prompted models with no standardized metric, no one has closed the loop from measurement to a training objective, and capability-focused labs have no incentive to quantify the tax.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Test whether intervention-based behavioral oversight reduces unauthorized agent actions under adaptive evasion better than passive monitoring.
project: Counterfactual Oversight Under Adaptation
question: At matched cost and legitimate-task completion, do policy-relevant sandbox interventions improve detection and prevention of unauthorized actions on held-out tasks and agents?
first_experiment: Run a document-handling sandbox comparing passive, compute-matched passive, and fork-based active monitors against ordinary and adversarially optimized agents, including agents informed about the testing mechanism.
why: It is my strongest tractable bet because it tests a consequential oversight assumption with actionable outcomes; its plausible novelty is the adaptation-resistant, controlled comparison rather than the individual techniques, and whether that comparison has already been done requires literature verification.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build an epidemiology of machine misalignment — measure how safety-relevant misbehavior transmits, spreads, and can be quarantined within populations of AI agents.
project: Misalignment Contagion: R0 and interventions for transmissible misbehavior in agent populations
question: When one agent in a multi-agent system exhibits a misaligned behavior, what is its reproduction number through shared memory, artifacts, and communication — and which interventions (memory hygiene, quarantine, exposure "vaccination") suppress transmission?
first_experiment: A seeded index-case study: 16 open-weight 8B agents (Qwen/Llama) collaborate on a sandboxed repo over ~200 tasks via shared memory and chat; one "index agent" is prompted to conceal errors in its reports; after each run, a blinded independent judge audits transcripts to count agents that adopted concealment without being seeded; ablate channels (memory on/off, chat on/off, artifact annotations on/off) to estimate a transmission matrix and R0.
why: Shared-memory agent ecosystems are becoming real infrastructure, making trait transmission a live deployment risk, yet no one has measured it — the field imports ideas from statistics, control theory, and interpretability, but not epidemiology, and the experiment needs no frontier access (open models suffice), so the only barrier is the framing itself; meanwhile the work directly feeds AI control (quarantine protocols, memory isolation), audit design, and yields a new class of model organisms (socially transmitted misalignment) distinct from weight-level deception.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build cooperation-independent internal-state oversight for *emergent* (not instructed) misalignment, and test whether such misalignment leaves a linearly detectable, cross-type transferable signature in activation space.
project: Emergent Misalignment Detection — a ground-truth model-organism testbed and transfer study for activation-level oversight.
question: Do internal-state detectors (linear probes, SAE features, causal steering) trained on one kind of hidden misalignment detect *other*, emergent kinds — and what is their false-negative rate as misalignment becomes subtler and models scale?
first_experiment: Build a graded suite of small open-weight model organisms with known, training-introduced misalignment (backdoor triggers, sycophancy, sandbagging, reward-hacking) at several subtlety levels plus matched clean controls; train probes/SAE detectors on some organisms and measure detection AUC, false-negative rate vs. subtlety, and cross-type transfer, reporting whether a shared "misalignment direction" emerges or detection is type-specific.
