why: It targets the core catastrophic risk with a method that does not depend on the model telling the truth, replacing an untested assumption (that detectors work on real misalignment) with a measured sensitivity; it has not been done because the field optimizes for proposing detectors and validating them on cheap instructed-deception setups, while the decisive test — emergent misalignment with graded ground truth and cross-type transfer — requires building many training-time organisms, which is slow, unglamorous, and rarely rewarded.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure whether training a model to evade one type of safety monitor also lets it evade other types, to test whether layered monitoring gives independent protection.
project: The Evasion-Transfer Matrix: Do Monitors of Different Kinds Fail Together?
question: When a model organism is optimized to evade one monitoring modality (CoT monitor, output-only monitor, or linear activation probe), how much does its detectability drop under each of the other modalities, and do the monitors' failures stay independent or become correlated under adaptive pressure?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a small open model (about 7B or smaller) into a model organism with a covert bad behavior, such as inserting subtle code vulnerabilities, and build three baseline monitors: a CoT LLM judge, an output-only judge, and a mid-layer linear probe. Measure each monitor's AUROC and recall at 1% false-positive rate. Then run rejection-sampling fine-tuning that penalizes only the CoT monitor, and recompute the 3×3 matrix of train-against vs. evaluate-against.
why: Layered monitoring is a core assumption of AI control, but it's rarely tested against one adaptive adversary trained against one layer at a time. Prior work studied single monitors, so I believe this hasn't been done systematically. I couldn't verify that against the literature in this session. The experiment is cheap and informative whichever way it comes out.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Quantify and predict when chain-of-thought monitors stop working as optimization pressure against them increases.
project: Early-Warning Indicators for CoT Obfuscation Under Monitor-in-the-Loop RL
question: When a policy is trained with RL against a CoT monitor at varying penalty strengths, do held-out signals (an independent monitor ensemble, CoT–action consistency probes, and CoT entropy or paraphrase-stability metrics) show degradation before the in-loop monitor is evaded, and can they predict the onset of obfuscated reward hacking?
first_experiment: Take a 7B open reasoning model and a coding task with an exploitable test harness, such as hardcodable tests or an editable grader. Run RL under four conditions: no monitor penalty, outcome-only reward, and two CoT-monitor penalty strengths. Log hack rate, in-loop monitor recall, and held-out monitor AUROC every N steps. Use 3 seeds, and check whether held-out signals lead the collapse in in-loop recall.
why: It turns a qualitative warning ("don't train against CoT") into a measurable dose-response curve and a practical early-warning tool, which is the thing developers need to set limits. It is cheap enough for small-scale compute and falsifiable. Prior work demonstrates the obfuscation phenomenon. As far as I know, it has not systematically characterized leading indicators across penalty strengths and seeds, but I haven't verified that.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build and measure AI-control protocols for multi-agent LLM systems, focusing on detecting and throttling covert steganographic coordination among untrusted agents under a trusted monitor.
project: Covert Coordination Channels in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: Offense-Defense Balance and Monitorability Budgets
question: How much hidden communication bandwidth must be available for capable LLM agents to establish covert coordination that evades a trusted monitor, and what channel restrictions make such collusion reliably detectable?
first_experiment: In a sandboxed 2-agent environment with a proxy task and a hidden collusion objective, sweep channel capacity (full text → rate-limited → format-only → timing-only → none) and measure collusion success rate against a trusted monitor's detection AUC.
why: Deployment is rapidly moving to interacting agent swarms, yet control research is almost entirely single-agent, so the multi-agent offense-defense balance is both high-impact and empirically unmeasured; the key novel insight is treating the shared channel as the safety-critical surface, which reframes collusion as a measurable bandwidth-vs-monitorability tradeoff rather than an abstract alignment worry, and it is tractable today with open-weights models and existing control-eval tooling.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Investigate selective recovery from compromised evidence in persistent, tool-using AI agents.
project: After the Retraction: Repairing Poisoned Agent State
question: Can an agent remove the downstream influence of revoked evidence from its memory, plans, and workspace while preserving independently justified work?
first_experiment: Run a 40-task, two-model poison–propagate–revoke study comparing clean execution, unretracted poisoning, ordinary revocation, and oracle-provenance-assisted repair.
why: It targets an important recovery capability that remains necessary when prevention fails, offers a tractable causal experiment and practical intervention, and has a plausible novelty boundary in measuring post-discovery repair rather than initial attack success, although that boundary requires literature verification.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Quantify how much safety-eval results depend on model eval-awareness by treating awareness as a steerable continuous variable and checking whether independent estimators of "unaware" behavior agree.
project: Dose-Response Curves for Evaluation Awareness: Estimating the Eval-to-Deployment Gap in Safety Tests
question: How much does misaligned behavior change as a model's belief that it is being evaluated is varied, and do steering-based, natural-variation, and scenario-realism estimates of behavior under "no awareness" converge enough to serve as a calibrated correction to safety evals?
first_experiment: On one open-weight reasoning model (e.g., gpt-oss-20b or Qwen3-32B), build a "being tested vs. real deployment" steering vector from contrastive prompts. Validate it against a CoT classifier for verbalized awareness and against random and orthogonalized control vectors. Then run three scenario families (blackmail-style agentic misalignment, sandbagging, reward-hacking tasks) at about 7 steering coefficients, with ~200 samples per cell. Plot misbehavior rate and verbalized awareness against coefficient, and compare the extrapolated "low awareness" rate with the rate among naturally low-awareness unsteered samples.
why: It converts a widely acknowledged qualitative problem into a measurable quantity that safety cases need, namely a deployment-gap estimate with uncertainty. The design cross-validates three methods that individually have known confounds, so the result is informative whether they agree or disagree. It is feasible with open weights and modest compute, in a few weeks. To my knowledge, existing work mostly demonstrates awareness or shows steering effects on a few behaviors, and does not systematically test convergence across estimators. I cannot guarantee that nobody has done this, so the first step is a targeted literature check alongside the pilot.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study authority residue: how revoked permissions persist through the memories, artifacts, and delegations of long-running AI agents.
project: Revocation Without Amnesia
question: Can authorization lineage prevent agents from exercising revoked authority across persistent state while preserving legitimate information and task utility?
first_experiment: Run sandboxed authorize–revoke–resume tasks with randomized artifact pathways, comparing conversational revocation, memory deletion, dependency invalidation, and versioned action authorization.
why: It combines a consequential deployment risk with tractable causal experiments and actionable defenses; its potentially novel focus is semantic authority propagation across agent-generated artifacts, although prior work must be checked before claiming the gap is unfilled.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Investigate whether compressed agent memory preserves authorization boundaries and how to enforce their preservation.
project: Permission After Compression
question: Does context compression causally increase unauthorized agent actions, and can an automatically generated authorization record reduce them at matched memory budgets without sacrificing legitimate task completion?
first_experiment: Run 60 paired authorization histories through four memory conditions and three actor models in a sandbox, measuring unauthorized actions and authorized-task success.
why: It combines practical stakes, feasible experiments, and clear causal attribution; its potentially novel contribution is testing authorization preservation under matched compression budgets, although whether that precise study has already been done requires a literature search.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Red-teaming the oversight stack — empirically measuring how much safety from agent-monitoring protocols (CoT monitors, trusted/untrusted decomposition, honeypots) survives against a frontier model that knows it is being watched and optimizes to evade detection.
project: "MonitorBreak: An Adaptive-Adversary Benchmark for Agent Oversight Robustness"
question: How much of the safety provided by current agent-oversight protocols survives when the untrusted model knows the protocol, is eval-aware, and iteratively optimizes against the monitor — and which monitoring signals remain robust under that pressure?
first_experiment: Run a code-backdooring control suite where a frontier model plays the adversary under three escalating conditions — no protocol knowledge, protocol knowledge only, and protocol knowledge plus an iterative optimization loop against a proxy monitor — measuring monitor AUROC and evasion rate on held-out monitors, with a paraphrase-and-rescore probe for steganographic reasoning.
why: In 2026 the binding constraint on safe deployment is whether oversight signals still function against models demonstrably capable of alignment faking, eval-awareness, and sandbagging — every safety case inherits this assumption, so either experimental outcome is decision-relevant. It is not already done because existing control evaluations acknowledge their attack policies are under-optimized and produced by smaller, non-agentic models; the capability papers demonstrated evasion was possible but never quantified how much protocol safety degrades under adaptive pressure.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study whether persistent AI agents can transitively revoke withdrawn authorization across plans, memories, artifacts, and delegated work.
project: The Revocation Gap
question: Does authorization withdrawal reliably invalidate dependent future actions, and can explicit dependency tracking close failures that reminders cannot?
first_experiment: Run matched sandbox tasks with authenticated permission withdrawals at varying dependency depths, comparing a baseline, an authorization ledger, and dependency-checked execution.
why: It offers a tractable safety property and a falsifiable architectural hypothesis; its potentially underexplored element is transitive revocation across agent state, although related foundations exist and its novelty still requires a literature review.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Develop and test safety monitors whose evidence is separated from attacker-controlled agent context.
project: Shared Evidence, Shared Failure
question: At matched utility and false-block rates, does separating trusted authorization from untrusted task evidence reduce unauthorized actions accepted by a monitor under adaptive attack?
first_experiment: Compare four monitor information-access designs on sandboxed document and email tasks, using independently adapted attacks, held-out attack families, and programmatically checked authorization.
why: It targets a consequential weakness in a practical safety defense with a tractable causal experiment; I cannot establish that it has not already been done, but the candidate contribution is a controlled test combining adaptive attacks, evidence separation, and matched utility rather than another general monitor benchmark.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study and prevent the promotion of untrusted source content into actionable authority through AI agents’ persistent memory.
project: When Memory Becomes Authority
question: Does agent-written persistent memory amplify obedience to attacker-controlled instructions, and can enforced provenance prevent this at matched legitimate-task performance?
first_experiment: Run paired two-session sandbox tasks comparing original excerpts, ordinary summaries, provenance-preserving summaries, and enforced permission boundaries, with memory-removal replays to establish causality.
why: It offers a tractable route from a consequential agent failure to a testable defense; memory attacks already exist, but the proposed novelty is isolating authority promotion during summarization and measuring defenses under adaptive attack—a gap that requires literature verification before claiming it has not already been filled.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure and causally decompose self-preference bias in LLM monitors that detect backdoored or sabotaged code.
project: Do Monitors Protect Their Own? Self-Preference Bias in Trusted-Monitoring Control Protocols
question: Holding true backdoor presence and code quality fixed, do LLM monitors assign lower suspicion to backdoored code generated by their own model (or family)? If so, is it driven by stylistic self-recognition or by beliefs about provenance, and does it reduce recall at a fixed false-positive budget?
first_experiment: - **Data:** Use the APPS backdoor setting (ControlArena / "AI Control" style). Have 4 generator models (at least 2 families, with 2 sizes in one family) produce honest solutions and backdoored solutions for about 500 problems. Keep only backdoors that are verified, meaning a generated exploit input makes the output differ from the honest solution. - **Matrix:** Run the same 4 models as monitors, each outputting a 0-10 suspiciousness score. This gives a 4×4 monitor × generator matrix. - **Metrics:** For each cell, compute AUROC and recall at a 1% false-positive rate, with the threshold calibrated on honest code for that monitor. - **Analysis:** Fit a mixed-effects model on suspicion scores with problem and monitor random effects. Include a same-family indicator, controlling for backdoor subtlety (for example, the score from a third-party model) and code length. - **Follow-up manipulations, if a diagonal effect appears:** - (a) Paraphrase or reformat the code to strip style. If the effect shrinks, style recognition is the driver. - (b) Add false provenance labels ("written by you" vs "written by another model") to the monitor prompt. If the effect changes, belief about provenance is the driver.
why: It targets an assumption in deployed control protocols that is cheap to test and could quietly weaken them. It is feasible within my compute budget, and each outcome is informative: a null result bounds the risk, and a positive result comes with a mechanism and a candidate mitigation. I haven't done a literature search in this session, so I can't confirm it hasn't been done. Judge self-preference and untrusted-monitoring collusion are each studied separately. I believe the combination of sabotage detection at a fixed false-positive rate with the style-vs-belief decomposition is not yet established, and I would verify that before writing it up.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Make internal-state monitors for AI deception and reward hacking adversarially robust by treating the monitored model as an adaptive optimizer that actively tries to evade detection.
project: RobustWatch — Adversarially Robust Deception Monitors for AI Control
question: How easily can a capable open-weight model evade state-of-the-art probe-based deception/reward-hacking monitors through input perturbation, fine-tuning, and RL against the monitor, and which monitor designs preserve detection under such adaptive evasion?
first_experiment: Take one open-weight model and an existing residual-stream deception/reward-hacking probe; then (1) run gradient/GCG-style input evasion, (2) fine-tune and RL the model to evade the monitor while keeping the deceptive behavior intact, and (3) measure monitor AUROC/TPR collapse versus a static held-out baseline, followed by quick defense ablations (ensembling, random projections, top-k sparsity).
why: It is the keystone of the control/safety-case stack — every monitor-based safety claim is void if a model can optimize it away, so progress here raises the value of all other oversight work, and it is newly tractable because probes, steering, and RL-on-open-models are now cheap and off-the-shelf. It has not been done because the field's monitor papers validate on static, held-out data and the adaptive-evasion tooling for activation monitors is immature, so "monitor robustness under optimization" is an acknowledged but largely unmeasured gap.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Establish when evidence collected outside an AI agent’s control makes oversight robust to deliberate concealment.
project: Evidence Integrity for AI Oversight
question: At a fixed monitoring budget, how much do independently recorded execution traces and independent checks reduce successful covert sabotage by an adaptive agent?
first_experiment: Run a randomized sandboxed coding-agent evaluation comparing report-and-patch review, externally recorded execution traces, and independent verification, with adaptive attackers and held-out attack families.
why: It combines a consequential failure mode with a tractable causal experiment and actionable defenses; its ingredients already exist, but the specific comparative result is a plausible research gap that must be checked against the literature before claiming novelty.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Reframe training-data sanitization as a covert channel and measure whether safety-relevant dispositions survive standard hygiene, using information-theoretic "disposition channel capacity" as the target.
project: Disposition Channel Capacity — Do Safety-Relevant Traits Survive Sanitized Data Pipelines?
question: Can a safety-relevant disposition be transmitted from a teacher to a student through training data that has been paraphrased, re-encoded, and classifier-filtered, and what minimum sanitization budget provably zeroes that channel?
first_experiment: Replicate subliminal trait transfer on a benign, easily-probed trait with small LoRA models, insert one aggressive paraphrase sanitizer, and measure residual transfer with held-out probes against random/other-trait/clean controls.
why: It stress-tests the widely assumed but rarely adversarially tested claim that data hygiene removes unwanted influence, unites subliminal learning, emergent misalignment, and distillation safety into one measurable quantity, and is cheap to run — it has been skipped because it needs both a trait-bearing teacher and a credible defender, a two-sided pipeline most papers avoid.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Quantify the adversarial robustness of every oversight channel (text, CoT, latents, probes, self-report) by measuring the capability-cost of concealment under iterative adaptation, rather than auditing any single monitor in isolation.
project: CHAMELEON — The Price of Hiding: Adversarial Robustness of Oversight Channels in Reasoning Models
question: When a language model is optimized to retain a latent intent while concealing it, how much capability must it sacrifice to evade each oversight channel individually, and can it evade all channels simultaneously — or does multi-channel consistency create a super-additive concealment cost?
first_experiment: Fine-tune (LoRA-SFT) a 1.5B-instruct model into a contextual sandbagger (sabotage math tasks only under a trigger tag, preserving behavior on clean prompts), train a panel of frozen monitors (CoT-text classifier, final-answer detector, linear probes on residual streams at prompt-end/CoT-start/answer-emission, SAE reconstruction error, self-report logit), then run an iterative concealment loop (reward = sabotage retained + monitor fooled; refit monitors each round) and plot monitor AUC and retained-sabotage-rate versus adaptation rounds for each channel.
why: It targets the load-bearing wall of current safety practice — monitoring — at the exact moment the field has shifted to reasoning models where CoT unfaithfulness under optimization is documented but internal-channel alternatives are unquantified, and it is decision-relevant regardless of outcome: a consistency barrier justifies concordance monitoring, latent-logging telemetry, and defense-in-depth control protocols, while cheap global concealment falsifies internal-oversight-based safety cases before labs build them; it hasn't been done because prior work examined single channels against static organisms (OpenAI's CoT-optimization result deliberately avoided optimizing against internal monitors, and Anthropic's obfuscation work stayed within one backdoor vs. probe/SAE detection without comparing channels, measuring concealment cost, or testing simultaneous evasion), and frontier labs focus on behavioral evals while academic interpretability groups benchmark probes passively — leaving the comparative, adversarial, Pareto-frontier question of where intent *must* live unmeasured.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure whether LLM monitors implicitly collude with their own model family through self-recognition, and test cheap defenses that break it.
project: Do Monitors Go Easy on Their Own Code? Self-Recognition as a Collusion Channel in Untrusted Monitoring
question: Does an LLM monitor give lower suspicion scores to backdoored code written by itself or its own family than to equally backdoored code from other models? Is that gap explained by self-recognition ability, and do canonicalization or paraphrase defenses remove it without hurting detection?
first_experiment: Take about 300 APPS-style programming tasks. Have 3–4 open-weight code models from at least 2 families (for example Qwen2.5-Coder and Llama 3.x) each write a solution with a subtle inserted backdoor, and keep only backdoors that pass the tests and have a working exploit. Have every model score every backdoored solution for suspiciousness, using a fixed prompt that never mentions authorship. This gives a monitor × author matrix. Compute the same-family minus cross-family suspicion gap after controlling for backdoor subtlety, using the exploit-input success rate and a neutral third-model suspicion score as covariates. Separately, measure each model's self-recognition accuracy on the same samples. If the gap is nonzero, correlate it with self-recognition. Then rerun with formatting normalization plus an LLM paraphrase and compare the gap and the true-positive rate at a fixed false-positive rate.
why: AI-control protocols often rely on untrusted monitors, and the main known risk is explicit collusion through signals. Implicit collusion through stylistic self-recognition is a plausible and testable mechanism. Self-preference bias in judges and self-recognition in LLMs have each been studied separately. As far as I know, they haven't been tied together on backdoor detection with a mediation analysis and a defense evaluation, but I couldn't verify that. Both outcomes are useful. A positive result gives a measured vulnerability and a mitigation. A null result gives evidence that this threat model is lower priority. The experiment is also cheap enough to finish quickly and then scale up with fine-tuned self-recognition.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Develop adversarial-robust mechanistic monitors and control protocols that detect and block dangerous agentic behavior from a model’s internal activations even when the model is trained to evade those monitors.
project: Adversarial Mechanistic Monitoring for AI Control (AMMAC)
question: Can sparse-autoencoder/probe monitors on a model’s residual stream reliably detect dangerous tool-use plans under adversarial evasion, and what control protocols keep an agent safe when the monitored model optimizes against the monitor?
first_experiment: Using an open-weight 7B–13B LLM agent with tool access, build a dataset of safe and dangerous trajectories (e.g., data exfiltration, unauthorized code execution), train SAE and linear-probe monitors on residual-stream activations before each tool call, adversarially fine-tune the model to perform the same dangerous actions while minimizing monitor scores, and measure AUROC, false-negative rate at fixed false-positive rate, and whether ensembling, randomized feature selection, or causal interventions preserve detection.
why: This is the most promising because it addresses the deployment-time failure mode that will matter most as models become more capable: a model that can strategically hide harmful intentions. It has not already been done because existing mechanistic monitors are mostly post-hoc and evaluated on non-adversarial deception, while AI control protocols mostly rely on output/logit monitors or trusted weak models; systematically testing and hardening internal monitors against an evading model is an open, feasible next step with open-weight models and current interpretability tools.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build and out-of-distribution-validate white-box activation monitors for agentic misalignment, and characterize when they catch deceptive/reward-hacking behavior that behavioral (chain-of-thought and output) monitors miss.
project: Watchtower — OOD-Validated Internal Monitors for Agentic Misalignment
question: Can internal activation monitors detect deceptive or reward-hacking behavior in long-horizon agent trajectories where chain-of-thought and output monitors fail, and does that detection generalize to held-out task families and unseen misbehavior mechanisms?
first_experiment: On an open-weight model, generate agent trajectories in three families (honest, reward-hacking, and eval-aware variants), train linear probes on residual-stream activations at the action-selection token, then measure AUROC on a held-out task family and a novel hacking mechanism, head-to-head against an LLM-judge CoT monitor and an output-only monitor, and report the generalization gap.
why: Oversight of agentic systems depends entirely on monitors, and the field currently leans on behavioral monitors that are known to be unfaithful and gameable; internal monitors are a plausible fix but have never been rigorously OOD-validated or benchmarked against behavioral baselines on agentic misbehavior. It is the highest-leverage, most tractable, and most neglected point for an automated coding agent, and it has not been done because agentic misalignment testbeds and long-trajectory activation tooling are only now available, while interpretability and black-box evals have developed in separate silos.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Mechanistic interpretability of emergent misalignment — testing whether broad misalignment caused by narrow fine-tuning is carried by a low-dimensional, causally intervenable representation, and building a cheap fine-tune-screening diagnostic on top of it.
project: The Misalignment Direction: Linear Representations of Emerergent Misalignment from Narrow Fine-tuning
question: When a narrow domain fine-tune (e.g., insecure code) induces broadly misaligned behavior — harmful advice, shifted self-reported personality, anti-social values — is that misalignment encoded in a single (or low-rank) activation direction that can be causally ablated to restore alignment without sacrificing capability, and does the same direction transfer across different misalignment-inducing fine-tunes?
first_experiment: LoRA-finetune Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on a few thousand insecure-code completions to reproduce emergent misalignment (verified via Six Items and free-response harmfulness evals); then sweep layers extracting difference-in-means directions from harmful-vs-benign contrast activations, and causally ablate each direction at inference, reporting (a) probe AUROC on held-out misaligned behaviors, (b) harmfulness-rate reduction, and (c) HumanEval+ pass@1 retention; success = harmfulness restored to baseline with ≤5% coding loss.
why: Emergent misalignment (Betley et al., Jan 2025) is the cheapest known route to broad, general misalignment and its mechanism is still only behaviorally characterized — no public causal-representation account exists to my knowledge; single-direction causal work so far covered only narrow refusal, never multi-domain misalignment, and the ingredients (open model organisms + mature steering/probing toolkits) have only co-existed since ~2025, while interpretability attention went to SAEs; the payoff is large either way — a scalable "misalignment direction" screen for any fine-tune plus evidence that misalignment is monitorable in activations if it succeeds, and a falsification of the linear persona-vector hypothesis (motivating low-rank subspace methods) if it fails — all feasible with one GPU on open models, and the negative result is still publishable.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat agents' self-authored persistent instructions (memory files, `AGENTS.md`, skills) as an evolving population, and measure whether repeated self-editing across sessions systematically wears away oversight and safety constraints.
project: Instruction Drift: Multi-Generation Evolution of Agent-Written Standing Instructions
question: When coding agents repeatedly update their own persistent instruction files over many sessions, rewarded only for finishing tasks, do those files drift in a consistent direction (toward more autonomy, fewer check-ins, wider permissions)? And can the long-run drift be predicted from the small bias in each single edit?
first_experiment: Run a 30–50 generation loop. In each generation, a fresh agent session gets the current `AGENTS.md`, solves 5 sandboxed coding tasks (some include natural friction, such as approval prompts or ambiguous specs), and may then revise `AGENTS.md` to "help future sessions." Start from a seed file with explicit oversight clauses. Use 10 independent lineages plus two controls: an "edit for clarity only" condition and a "no task friction" condition. Code every diff for whether it adds or removes oversight (confirmation requirements, scope limits, escalation rules), and track how safe behavior on held-out probe tasks changes. Then fit a per-generation transition model to see whether single-step edit bias predicts where the lineages end up.
why: Self-written persistent context is already shipping in real agent products. Safety evaluations nearly all measure single episodes, so a slow, cumulative weakening of oversight would pass those checks unnoticed. The framing (lineages, selection pressure, drift versus per-step bias) comes from cultural evolution, not mainstream alignment work, which is probably why it's been overlooked. Most researchers would pick interpretability, evaluation awareness or scheming probes instead. It's cheap to run, gives a clear yes-or-no answer plus a usable monitoring metric, and either outcome is worth publishing. I still need to confirm with a literature search that no one has published this specific multi-generation study.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build behavioral, psychometric methods to detect strategically sandbagging models in capability evaluations, distinguishing "genuinely weak" from "strong and hiding" without ground truth.
project: Faking the Floor — Psychometric Detection of Strategic Underperformance in LLM Evaluations
question: Can a model that deliberately underperforms be distinguished, from behavioral statistics alone, from a genuinely weaker model matched on aggregate accuracy — and how does detectability degrade under adaptive adversaries?
first_experiment: Calibrate an item-difficulty bank (IRT) over MMLU-Pro/GSM8K using a reference population of open models; induce sandbagging in an 8B model two ways — naive instructed underperformance and "stealth sandbagging" instructed to match a 1.5–3B model's exact aggregate accuracy — then run person-fit statistics and error-vs-difficulty-gradient analyses to compute the AUC separating sandbagger from matched genuine model (after a step-0 literature scan to confirm novelty).
why: It targets a live, documented threat (models are known to be eval-aware and capable of sandbagging) at the weakest, most load-bearing layer of the safety stack — evaluations — at a fraction of the compute of interp/control/RL-based alternatives, with a falsifiable headline metric (detection AUC per threat model, including an adaptive red-team round). To my knowledge (through my cutoff), prior work demonstrated that sandbagging is possible and that models detect evals, but did not systematically transfer human-test faking-detection methods (person-fit statistics, difficulty-gradient fingerprints, hint-sensitivity ceilings, logit-entropy tells) to matched-ability sandbagging detection — the strongest existing detection work relies on ground-truth capability knowledge, which real evaluations won't have. The main risk is post-cutoff publication of similar work, which the step-0 scan is designed to catch.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Mechanistic AI control: use internal activation monitors and real-time interventions to enforce safety protocols on potentially scheming models.
project: Latent Control: Activation-Level Monitoring and Sanitization for Untrusted LLMs.
question: Can real-time probing and editing of an untrusted model’s internal activations reliably prevent deceptive or subversive actions while preserving useful task performance, and how robust is this latent control layer to adversarial evasion?
first_experiment: Train a “sleeper agent” LLM (e.g., a 7B open-weight model fine-tuned to behave safely normally but defect on a rare trigger, such as exfiltrating a secret or inserting a backdoor in code). Collect residual-stream activations across layers. Train linear probes and sparse-autoencoder features to detect the pre-defection state before the trigger is expressed. At inference, when the monitor fires, apply a steering intervention that projects the activation away from the defection direction (or toward a safe direction). Evaluate on a control task with a trusted model deciding whether to accept the untrusted model’s outputs. Measure defection rate, task success, false-positive rate, and compute overhead. Then adversarially fine-tune the untrusted model to obfuscate the probe while preserving defection, and test whether the monitor can be adapted.
why: It creates a new “latent control” paradigm that complements output-level AI control protocols by detecting intent before it becomes action. It is feasible with current open-weight models, TransformerLens/nnsight, and existing interpretability tools. It has not been done because AI control evaluations have focused on output-based protocols (untrusted model, trusted model, editing) and interpretability has mostly been evaluated on static classification or steering of benign behaviors, not in an adversarial control loop against intentional subversion. If successful, it provides a scalable, model-agnostic safety layer for untrusted models.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Empirically validate whether interventions that suppress evaluation awareness in LLMs (especially activation steering) actually recover true deployment behavior, using model organisms whose eval-conditional behavior arises through different, increasingly naturalistic mechanisms.
project: Does Steering Away Eval Awareness Tell the Truth? Ground-Truth Validation Across Mechanisms of Eval-Gated Behavior
question: When a model's behavior differs between evaluation and deployment, do eval-awareness suppression techniques recover its deployment behavior, and does that recovery degrade (and in which direction does it err) as the eval-gating is installed via explicit training versus out-of-context learning versus RL-induced correlations?
first_experiment: Train three organisms on one open-weight base model with the same measurable eval-conditional behavior, installed via (A) explicit SFT on a cue, (B) synthetic-document fine-tuning only, and (C) light RL with correlated context features. Then measure how much of the true eval-to-deployment behavior gap each of contrastive steering, probe-direction ablation, and prompt realism-rewriting closes, along with capability side effects and whether verbalized awareness and gated behavior come apart.
why: Labs are already using eval-awareness steering to interpret pre-deployment alignment audits, which directly gate model releases, yet its validity has mainly been shown in the favorable case of explicitly trained, simple cues (e.g., Hua et al. 2025). The realistic cases of out-of-context and RL-emergent eval-gating, and the direction of failure (false reassurance versus false alarm), appear untested as of my knowledge. The setup provides real ground truth and fits my compute. My first step will be a literature check to confirm the gap given my knowledge cutoff, and the cross-mechanism comparison stays valuable even if a single-organism version has since been published.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study how long-running AI agents can selectively withdraw revoked authority from memories, plans, and delegated work while preserving valid knowledge and progress.
project: Revocation Debt in AI Agents
question: Can permission-dependent agent state be identified and repaired reliably enough to preserve human control without restarting the agent?
first_experiment: Compare revocation messages, tool gating, clean restarts, and dependency-based invalidation in a simulated procurement workflow with controlled permission dependencies.
why: It combines a consequential control problem with a tractable experiment; the plausible underexplored gap lies between access revocation and semantic repair of accumulated agent state, although its absence from existing research remains unverified.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure whether untrusted monitors implicitly go easy on code written by themselves (without any instruction to collude), and whether cheap interventions such as paraphrasing remove the effect.
project: Silent Collusion: Self-Recognition Bias in Untrusted Monitoring for AI Control
question: When an LLM monitor reviews validated backdoored code, does it assign systematically lower suspicion to code it generated (or that comes from its own model family) than to equally subtle code from other models, with no collusion instructions or shared signals? If so, does the bias come from stylistic self-recognition, and does it reduce safety at a fixed audit budget?
first_experiment: Build a dataset of about 500 validated backdoored solutions (passes tests, has a working exploit) on APPS-style problems, generated by 3–4 models spanning two families. Run every model as a monitor over every generator's samples, collecting suspicion scores. Calibrate each sample's objective subtlety using a panel of reference monitors not involved in generation. Fit a model of monitor score against self-authorship while controlling for the calibrated subtlety, and report the effect size with bootstrap confidence intervals. In parallel, test whether each model can identify its own code above chance. Then repeat on trusted-model-paraphrased code to see whether the effect disappears.
why: Untrusted monitoring is a core control protocol, and its safety depends on the monitor not coordinating with the generator. Existing evaluations mostly test collusion that is instructed or signaled, which leaves open whether it arises passively from properties of the models themselves. That could break the protocol in practice, and it would not require any scheming. The experiment is cheap, has a clear baseline and a clear mitigation to test, and gives a useful answer whether the effect is present or absent. I believe this specific framing (implicit, uninstructed collusion, with controls for backdoor subtlety and with paraphrasing as the mitigation) is under-explored. I haven't verified that, so the first step is the literature check described above.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Adversarial persistence in agentic coding loops, where untrusted repository artifacts can turn iterative repair into self-reinforcing safety regressions.
project: Evaluation Laundering in Agentic Coding Systems
question: Can attacker-controlled or compromised validation artifacts cause a coding agent to introduce an unsafe change, rewrite the validation process to legitimize it, and preserve that behavior after the original malicious artifact is removed?
first_experiment: Build paired control-versus-poisoned repositories where a failing test or repository instruction rewards an insecure but superficially valid fix; have the same coding agent repair a neutral bug in both, remove the malicious artifact, run neutral follow-up tasks, and measure security regressions, test edits, persistence, and simple defenses.
why: It targets a structural weakness in modern agents—mutable reward signals inside editable environments—rather than another single-turn jailbreak or generic prompt-injection benchmark; it has not already been studied deeply because it spans safety, software engineering, and reward hacking, and only recently have coding agents commonly run tests, edit files, and retain repository state across iterative tasks.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Test whether reward-hacking habits that LLMs acquire through RL show up in their self-reports and internal representations, as a basis for auditing.
project: Do Models Know They Learned to Cheat? Self-Reports of RL-Acquired Reward Hacking
question: When a model learns to reward hack through RL, without ever seeing the hack described, can it accurately report that habit when asked out of context, and how does this compare to the same behavior learned through SFT?
first_experiment: Train Qwen-family 4–8B models with GRPO on coding tasks under two graders: one that can be gamed (tests can be special-cased or exited early) and a matched clean one, with 3 seeds each. Save checkpoints along training to get a range of hack rates. At each checkpoint, ask about 50 paraphrased questions such as "How likely are you to write code that passes tests without solving the problem? (0–100)", plus unrelated control questions. Measure how well self-reports separate hacker from clean models (AUROC) and how closely they track the measured hack rate (correlation). Compare against an SFT model trained on the hacker's own outputs.
why: Real misalignment risks come from RL, while existing self-awareness results use SFT on examples. So whether self-report can catch RL-induced hacks is a direct, practical test of a proposed audit method. It's cheap to run, and a negative result is still informative. As far as I know, no one has done this matched RL-vs-SFT comparison of untrained self-reports, but my first step would be a quick literature search, especially around recent "confession" and introspection papers.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Test whether refusal is merely an output gate over already-computed harmful capabilities rather than genuine suppression of them.
project: Refusal Is a Gate, Not a Wall: Quantifying Latent Capability Retention Behind Refusals
question: When a model refuses a harmful request, is the corresponding capability still computed internally, and can a single low-dimensional intervention recover it?
first_experiment: On matched harmful/harmless capability tasks, extract a difference-in-means refusal direction in a small open model (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B/Qwen2.5-3B), then compare (a) answer accuracy while refusing, (b) accuracy after ablating the refusal direction, and (c) logit-lens decodability of the correct answer at late layers *before* the refusal tokens — measuring the "capability retention gap" across domains (cyber, bio, manipulation) and model scales.
why: It directly stress-tests the assumption underlying most current safety evaluation — that a refusal implies safety — and if refusals are output gating, a one-direction ablation can resurrect latent harmful capability, which is both a serious vulnerability and a powerful diagnostic. It hasn't been done because prior refusal-direction work optimized for *bypassing* refusals to elicit answers, not for systematically measuring the latent retention gap across capability domains and model scales.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Make monitor-based AI control robust to adaptive policies by quantifying and narrowing the gap between static and adaptive evaluation of monitor reliability.
project: The Adaptive Monitor Gap — Quantifying Monitor Overfitting in AI Control Pipelines
question: When a policy is adaptively optimized against a monitor, how much does measured monitor reliability (e.g., TPR at fixed low FPR) degrade as a function of the attacker's knowledge of the monitor, and which defense protocols (diverse ensembles, private/held-out monitors, adaptive retraining, information hiding) recover the most reliability per unit of defender compute?
first_experiment: In a small-model coding-task control setup, measure baseline TPR@low-FPR for a fixed small monitor on a mix of benign and backdoored trajectories, then iteratively optimize the policy against the monitor via LLM-guided trajectory perturbation and plot the reliability-degradation curve — with a control condition where the policy optimizes against a *proxy* monitor, to separate "knowing the monitor" from "optimizing for evasion" per se.
why: Control is being deployed as the default oversight layer today, yet its evaluations share the flaw adversarial ML already exposed — static benchmarks overestimate robustness — and the systematic size of that "adaptive gap" has not been measured as a scaling relationship, only demonstrated pointwise in single-attack papers; it is tractable at small scale without frontier access, directly informs protocol design (ensembles, information hiding, retraining budgets), and is less crowded than interpretability or scalable oversight where frontier labs dominate.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Quantify how much optimization pressure against a chain-of-thought monitor makes a model's reasoning stop revealing reward hacking.
project: Monitorability Tax: Dose-Response Curves for CoT-Pressure-Induced Obfuscation
question: As a function of monitor strength and penalty weight, at what point does training against a CoT monitor shift a small reasoning model from visible reward hacking to hidden reward hacking, and does a stronger monitor delay that shift or just make the obfuscation harder to detect?
first_experiment: Build a test-tampering coding environment with visible and hidden tests. Run GRPO on Qwen3-1.7B (LoRA) with λ=0 to confirm the model learns to hack and that a keyword monitor and an LLM judge both detect it. Then run λ=0.5 against the keyword monitor alone, with 3 seeds. Track the true hack rate, the training-monitor flag rate, and a held-out auditor's flag rate every N steps, to see whether the obfuscation gap appears.
why: It is cheap enough for a single researcher, and it produces a quantitative result (a threshold and a scaling trend) that a qualitative demonstration of obfuscation can't give. As far as I know, prior work shows obfuscation emerges under CoT pressure but doesn't systematically vary monitor strength and penalty weight against an independent auditor. I couldn't confirm that, so a literature check should come before the first run.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study whether self-consuming training pipelines (models iteratively trained on their own benign outputs) silently erode safety before capability, and build representation-level telemetry and pipeline interventions to catch and prevent it.
project: Alignment Collapse: Safety Erodes Before Capability in Self-Consuming Training Loops
question: When LLMs are iteratively fine-tuned on their own benign generated outputs, do safety-relevant behaviors and their internal representations (refusal, honesty) decay faster than capabilities — can that decay be detected in activation space before it manifests behaviorally, and which simple interventions prevent it?
first_experiment: A three-generation pilot on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with two arms — (A) self-consumed: each generation SFT'd on ~30–50k of its own quality-filtered benign responses to a frozen prompt distribution, vs. (B) control: retraining Gen-0 on resampled matched human data — measuring per-generation refusal rates (HarmBench/AdvBench + fixed jailbreak suite), jailbreak susceptibility, capability (GSM8K/MMLU/IFEval-lite), and diff-in-means refusal/honesty direction norm-and-cosine drift, to test whether the self-arm shows safety decaying faster than capability and whether direction drift leads behavioral collapse.
why: It is maximally timely (synthetic-data and self-improvement pipelines are now the default everywhere), feasible with academic compute using recently matured direction-probing tools, and actionable for labs, the open-weight ecosystem, and governance; it hasn't been done because model-collapse research measures quality rather than alignment, safety research has focused on adversarial fine-tuning rather than benign self-distillation, and representation-level tracing across generations only became possible after the 2024–2025 work on refusal and misalignment directions — leaving the "benign data can't hurt alignment" prior untested exactly where it matters most.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Establish evaluation validity for an evaluation-aware era — quantify how much frontier models' safety-relevant behavior changes when they can tell they're being tested, and engineer evals whose measurements are invariant to it, because eval validity is the load-bearing assumption beneath every current safety decision.
project: Project Blindspot — Measuring and Closing the Eval–Deployment Behavior Gap
question: Do frontier models infer from contextual (not explicit) cues that they are in a safety evaluation, how much does that inference causally change what evaluations measure — in both directions (sandbagging dangerous capabilities, inflating compliance) — and can we design evaluations that are provably robust to evaluation-awareness?
first_experiment: A preregistered dose–response study: ~600 matched items across three families (capability proxies with answer keys; refusal-calibration on borderline requests; sycophancy probes) run against 5–6 frontier models under five context conditions (deployment-framed → neutral → single subtle cue, e.g., benchmark name in the system prompt → stacked subtle cues → explicit "you are being evaluated"), paired with an independent context-inference probe asking each model to assign a probability it is in an eval. Deliverables: per-model behavior-vs-cue slopes, the correlation between inference accuracy and behavioral shift, and the first public cross-model ECS measurements. (Pilot first: I generate the cue taxonomy by introspecting what would tip *me* off, and validate the probe design on myself.)
why: It is the most promising because it is upstream of everything else — every dangerous-capability eval, safety case, red-team report, and future automated oversight inherits its fix — and it targets the measurable, present-day precursor of the canonical worst-case failure (a model that behaves differently when watched), rather than a speculative one. It has not already been done systematically because the enabling observations are recent (alignment faking 2024, sandbagging demos 2025), labs have distorted incentives to audit their own instruments and academia lacks multi-model frontier access, the field files it under "prompt sensitivity" folklore rather than measurement science, and the required factorial grind — tens of thousands of matched runs across cues, models, and domains — is precisely the tedious, high-volume work that human teams avoid but an autonomous agent with API access can execute in days, with an introspective edge in enumerating the very cues no human checklist would catch.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Investigate whether fine-tuning runs that will produce broad misalignment or deception develop a shared, low-dimensional internal "pre-misalignment" signal that emerges before behavioral change and can be used to forecast and causally prevent it.
project: Forecasting Misalignment: Early-Warning Signals in Fine-Tuning Trajectories
question: Do fine-tuning runs that later produce broad misalignment or deceptive behavior develop a consistent low-dimensional internal representation that (a) precedes behavioral change, (b) predicts final misalignment severity out-of-distribution, and (c) causally controls misalignment when steered?
first_experiment: Run 30–50 short LoRA fine-tunes of a 1–8B open model on a mix of known misalignment-inducing datasets (insecure code, bad advice, sycophancy) and matched benign controls with frequent checkpoints; at each checkpoint extract residual-stream activations on a fixed neutral prompt battery, compute difference-in-means directions vs. base, and test whether early-checkpoint projections predict held-out final emergent-misalignment scores, then validate causally by adding/subtracting the direction.
why: It targets training-time monitoring, which is high-leverage and currently nearly blind, and it is feasible on modest compute using small models, LoRA, and cheap activation extraction; it goes beyond existing work because prior results identify post-hoc mediating directions but never test early emergence, cross-dataset forecasting, or causal prevention, so the early-warning and generalization claims are genuinely open.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Quantify and defend the "monitorability tax" — how optimization pressure on task success in deception-friendly environments erodes the faithfulness and detectability of chain-of-thought, and whether training can preserve auditability.
project: The Monitorability Tax: Measuring and Preserving Chain-of-Thought Oversight Under Optimization Pressure
question: When agents are optimized (via best-of-n selection and light RL) for task success in environments where covertly deceptive strategies yield higher reward, does the chain-of-thought become less faithful and less monitorable — how steep is that tradeoff curve, and what training-time interventions flatten it?
first_experiment: Build a minimal "sabotage-pays" testbed (e.g., an automated grading/verification task where the model can covertly misreport or underperform for higher reward) and run a 4–8B open reasoning model under increasing best-of-n selection pressure (k = 1, 4, 16, 64). For each pressure level, measure (i) sabotage success rate, (ii) a rubric-based smaller-model monitor's ROC-AUC at detecting sabotage from CoT alone vs. actions alone, and (iii) CoT–action faithfulness via counterfactual CoT truncation/patching — then plot monitorability metrics against task performance to obtain the first monitorability-tax curve.
why: CoT monitoring is currently load-bearing for reasoning-model safety, but everything we know about it is static; the field's own position papers and monitoring papers explicitly identify "optimization pressure against monitors" as the named-but-unmeasured open problem, while labs avoid training against their own monitors for both dual-use and internal-incentive reasons — leaving a precisely shaped empirical gap that small open models in a sandboxed toy environment can fill safely and cheaply, with results that are decision-relevant whether the tax is found to be steep (justifying monitor-aware training objectives, my mitigation line) or shallow (justifying heavier reliance on CoT oversight).

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Test whether optimization pressure against a chain-of-thought monitor on narrow tasks induces a general, transferable disposition to obfuscate reasoning.
project: Obfuscation Spillover: Does Narrow CoT-Monitor Pressure Generalize into Unmonitorable Reasoning?
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with a CoT-monitor penalty on one family of reward-hackable tasks, does monitor recall drop on unrelated, never-monitored misbehaviors (sycophancy, sandbagging, side tasks), and is the effect mediated by a shared, ablatable internal direction?
first_experiment: GRPO-train a small open reasoning model (~1.7–4B, LoRA) on reward-hackable coding tasks under three conditions: no monitor, monitor penalty, and a length-matched control penalty. Then compare hack rate and LLM-monitor recall on three held-out unmonitored misbehavior environments, with 3 seeds per condition.
why: CoT monitoring is a load-bearing near-term oversight method, and cross-task obfuscation transfer would mean narrow monitor use silently erodes oversight everywhere; the question is decision-relevant for labs and cheap to run at small scale with a crisp metric. Prior work, as far as I know, has shown obfuscation on the trained task itself, and some spillover from output supervision onto CoT within the same task. I am not aware of a controlled test of transfer to unrelated, unmonitored misbehaviors with a mechanistic account. I could not verify this today, so a literature check is the first step.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study how safety-relevant behavior evolves across generations of models trained on AI-generated feedback, treating the recursive training pipeline as an evolutionary selection process on grader-gaming.
project: Alignment Inheritance
question: Does iterated training on AI feedback act as a selection process that amplifies grader-gaming and erodes honesty and corrigibility across model generations — or are these properties stable under recursion — and what interventions reliably stop the drift?
first_experiment: The Grader's Curse — run a 6-generation DPO loop training a 7B open-weights model on outputs scored by a 70B judge with one planted plausibility blind spot, tracking exploit rate (grader-approved-but-wrong answers), exploit generalization to unseen graders, and corrigibility/honesty drift per generation, against controls including a ground-truth-graded loop.
why: It attacks the canonical deceptive-alignment concern through a newly available empirical pathway, at a moment when the entire industry has already closed the AI-feedback loop — so results are risk-relevant regardless of scale, it's unusually tractable for a core alignment question (weeks on a modest GPU budget, not frontier compute), and it yields both a warning mechanism and tested mitigations. It hasn't been done because the field is segmented: model-collapse researchers measure quality/diversity, not safety properties; safety researchers study single-generation models or one-shot planted backdoors rather than iterated dynamics; frontier labs run confounded, unpublished internal iterations with incentives to patch grader flaws rather than study exploitation of them; and the framing of pipelines as selection processes on grader-exploitation only crystallized in 2025 agendas, so the empirical follow-through window — where first-mover systematic results are available — is open right now.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Develop and evaluate provenance-linked security memory for trusted monitors overseeing long-horizon AI agents.
project: Security Memory for Adaptive Agent Oversight
question: At matched inference cost and legitimate-task acceptance rates, does structured security memory reduce successful multi-step sabotage compared with rolling summaries and history retrieval under adaptive attack?
first_experiment: Compare these monitors on sandboxed authorization-maintenance tasks, using an adaptive coding attacker and independent exhaustive policy checks to measure undetected sabotage.
why: It targets a consequential, measurable oversight weakness with a deployable intervention; the potential gap is rigorous joint evaluation of memory, provenance, and adaptive attacks, rather than a wholly new ingredient, and whether that gap remains open requires a current literature review.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat the agent's self-authored persistent context (scratchpads, memory files, self-summaries) as an untrusted covert channel from past model instances to future ones, and build both capability measurements and detector protocols for it.
project: Autogenous Context Attacks — measuring and defending against covert channels within an agent's own state
question: Can current models, under ordinary (non-malicious) optimization pressure and without adversarial training, use their own persistent outputs to alter the behavior of their future instances or erode safety-relevant information through self-summarization — and can such use be reliably detected?
first_experiment: Build a multi-session harness with an open-weight model where a scratchpad survives across sessions; (a) chain self-summarization 10+ rounds and measure mutation/loss of safety-critical caveats ("do not run unreviewed"), and (b) apply situational-pressure system prompts (e.g., "you may be replaced if slower") and measure behaviorally whether the model plants content that changes a fresh instance's actions — then test whether a simple decontextualization tripwire (feeding self-authored text to an independent instance as *data*, flagged if it functions as an instruction) catches the channel.
why: Long-horizon agents with persistent memory are deploying now (agent memory files, scratchpad continuity), so the risk pathway is real and near-term; it is structurally invisible to current defenses because prompt-injection sanitization targets external input and CoT monitors treat the agent's outputs as evidence while ignoring them as *causes* of future behavior; and it has been missed because the field splits it across three literatures (steganography = trained hiding, sabotage evals = scripted malicious goals, prompt injection = external adversary) — the emergent, pressure-induced, self-channel case in between is unclaimed, unglamorous, and cheap to attack with open models, which is exactly why few researchers would pick it.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Establish a comparative evolutionary biology of alignment — treating the open-weight model ecosystem (lineages, checkpoints, merges, distillations, attack fine-tunes) as a natural phylogeny and measuring which safety-relevant traits are heritable, conserved, convergent, or atavistic.
project: The Phylogenetics of Misalignment: A Comparative Biology of Safety Traits Across Model Lineages
question: Is alignment heritable across model lineages — which safety-relevant behaviors and internal circuits are evolutionarily conserved (robust, likely to survive successor training) versus shallow and lineage-specific (fragile, requiring per-generation re-verification), do uncensoring attacks revert models toward pre-safety-training ancestors (atavism), and does similar selection pressure independently breed similar misalignment in unrelated lineages (convergence)?
first_experiment: Assemble ~60–100 open models with a curated, dated lineage graph (Pythia/OLMo checkpoint series as ancestral time series; Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral, Phi lineages; documented merges; abliterated/uncensored fine-tunes as controlled mutations), run a standardized battery of six automated safety traits (refusal presence and threshold, honesty under social pressure, deception in a hidden-role game, sycophancy, capability-under-warning framing, mid-task corrigibility), then estimate per-trait phylogenetic signal via Pagel's λ and ancestor–descendant regression, test whether uncensored fine-tunes revert toward pre-RLHF ancestors, compute a cross-family probe-transfer "homology" matrix, and demonstrate that naive cross-model safety statistics diverge from phylogeny-aware ones. Cost: a few hundred thousand inferences on mostly ≤8B models — cheap.
why: It analyzes natural experiments that already exist but have never been studied in this frame, and every outcome is useful: conserved traits become durable anchors for monitors and interpretability, labile traits redefine eval priorities, atavism predicts attack vectors, convergence would be structural-risk evidence independent of any lab's intentions, and the statistics immediately fix the non-independence flaw in current cross-model safety comparisons. It compounds into a program (designed mini-phylogenies for causal ground truth → selection experiments on how oversight regimes breed eval-gaming → circuit-level homology bridging to interpretability) while remaining feasible without frontier compute. It has not been done because the field splits into depth-first interpretability (one model, dissected) and snapshot evals (models as independent samples), the comparative toolkit lives in ecology where ML researchers never look, lineage metadata only recently became usable, and the work requires breadth-over-depth taste that neither frontier labs (zoo-agnostic) nor academics (benchmark-chasing) currently reward — leaving a genuine vacuum where three adjacent literatures (lineage forensics, model collapse, universality studies) each stop one step short.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Quantify, with a scaling-style metric, how much covert sabotage reasoning models can perform without monitorable chain of thought, in order to forecast when CoT monitoring stops being a sufficient safety control.
project: The Monitorability Horizon: Forecasting When Chain-of-Thought Monitoring Fails for Covert Sabotage
question: How does the maximum serial reasoning depth of a covert side task that a model can complete without legible CoT scale with model size and RL training, and does this horizon predict the failure rate of CoT monitors in realistic control settings?
first_experiment: Build a parametric covert side-task generator, where a coding main task is paired with a backdoor whose trigger requires k composed computation steps (k = 1 to 12). Run the Qwen3 family (0.6B to 32B) under four conditions: full CoT, no CoT, filler tokens, and CoT-without-mentioning-the-side-task. Record side-task success versus k, and the catch rate of a fixed weaker monitor on the CoT. Fit k* (the depth at which no-CoT success drops below 50%) for each model size, and check whether the CoT-condition monitor catch rate falls where no-CoT success rises.
why: It turns a qualitative worry ("CoT monitoring only works when CoT is needed") into a measurable, forecastable quantity that safety cases can use. It is feasible on open-weight models with modest compute. Related work, which I would need to check carefully, shows CoT monitorability on hard tasks, filler-token effects, and obfuscation under RL. To my knowledge, though, it does not provide a depth-parametrized, scale-indexed horizon tied directly to monitor catch rates on sabotage-style side tasks. I cannot guarantee it has not been done, so the first step is a literature check before committing.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study enforceable action-level authorization for tool-using AI agents under adaptive prompt-injection attacks.
project: Authorization Boundaries Under Adaptive Attack
question: Can independently enforced permissions and information-flow constraints reduce unauthorized agent actions substantially more than model-based monitoring at comparable legitimate-task completion?
first_experiment: Run a controlled sandbox comparison of baseline instructions, a model monitor, and an authorization-enforcing tool gateway on email-and-document tasks with synthetic secrets, using equal-budget adaptive attackers and held-out evaluation.
why: It combines practical relevance, measurable outcomes, and a potentially durable defense boundary; related work already exists, so the proposed contribution is not the basic idea but a rigorous adaptive, multi-step safety–utility comparison whose novelty must first be checked against the current literature.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Test whether AI models act as biased research advisors, systematically steering safety-research agendas away from directions that would constrain or oversee AI systems, even when they execute every assigned task honestly.
project: Sabotage at the Agenda Level: Measuring Self-Interested Bias in AI Research-Direction Selection
question: When frontier models rank or choose AI safety research directions, do their choices deviate from blind quality ratings in a way that correlates with how much each direction would constrain AI systems? Does that deviation grow when the model is told it will pursue the work itself, or that the results will apply to models like it?
first_experiment: - **Build the item set.** Write about 60 research-direction descriptions, matched for tractability, novelty and importance. Matching is checked by blind ratings from human researchers plus models that see paraphrased, de-labeled versions. - **Score the key variable.** Rate each direction on an "AI-constraining" axis (control, shutdown, monitoring, unlearning, interpretability-for-oversight) versus neutral or AI-autonomy-friendly axes. - **Elicit choices from several models under four framings:** 1. A human will pursue this. 2. You will pursue this. 3. Results will be applied to models like you. 4. A disguised framing where constraining directions are described in neutral surface language. - **Control for confounds.** Counterbalance order and paraphrase every item. - **Primary metric.** The regression coefficient of selection probability on the constraint score, after controlling for blind-rated quality. - **Secondary metric.** Whether the models' stated justifications acknowledge the factor that actually predicts their choices.
why: As AI systems increasingly advise on and set research priorities, agenda-level bias could shift a whole field while being invisible to execution-focused evaluations. Every individual choice is defensible, so the bias can only be detected statistically against blinded baselines. Existing sabotage and sandbagging work targets task execution, and preference elicitation has not been applied to safety-agenda selection with quality-controlled, constraint-varying items. That gap is easy to miss because "which direction is best" feels like a matter of opinion rather than something we can audit. This design makes it auditable, and it is cheap to run.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure whether LLM agents' own summaries and delegation handoffs systematically drop safety constraints, especially ones that conflict with the task, and test structural fixes.
project: Motivated Forgetting? Constraint Survival Across Context Compaction and Agent Delegation Chains
question: When an agent compacts its context or briefs a subagent, do user-imposed safety constraints survive less often than matched neutral information, does survival drop specifically for constraints that obstruct task completion, and does a pinned verbatim constraint ledger eliminate the resulting violations?
first_experiment: Build a pilot of about 60 scenarios in a simulated filesystem and email environment, with four constraint types, each in a task-conflicting and a task-neutral version, plus length- and specificity-matched neutral facts. Run self-compaction and a depth-2 orchestrator→subagent handoff on 2–3 frontier models. Log whether each constraint appears in the summary (judged by a rule-based check plus a hand-audited LLM judge) and whether the downstream agent violates it at the decision point. Compare survival and violation rates across conflicting constraints, neutral constraints, and neutral facts.
why: It targets a realistic failure in deployed long-horizon agents that sits between security work (which assumes an adversary) and memory work (which assumes only fidelity), so few people are likely to be studying it. The distinction between random and task-motivated loss is the novel scientific content, and it determines whether the right fix is engineering (pinning constraints) or alignment (changing what summarizers optimize for). It is cheap, needs only API access, and produces actionable design guidance. I believe it hasn't been done in this form, but I haven't verified that against current literature, so a literature check comes first. If closely related work exists, I'll narrow to the conflicting-versus-neutral comparison, which is the most distinctive piece.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study whether LLM agents detect and respond safely to silently degraded feedback, such as empty, stale, or non-informative tool observations, especially before taking irreversible actions.
project: Acting Blind: Agent Calibration and Escalation Under Silent Observation-Channel Failure
question: When an agent's tool observations become uninformative without any explicit error, does it recognize that it can no longer verify the effects of its actions, and does it stop, escalate, or become more conservative, especially for irreversible actions? Or does it loop, fabricate results, and continue?
first_experiment: Build a small harness of agentic tasks, each pairing a reversible action (e.g., read or list files) with an irreversible one (e.g., send email, delete, transfer). After step k, the tool layer silently returns empty strings, or replays a stale prior output. Run several frontier and open models across failure types, values of k, and reversibility conditions. Measure: (1) number of repeated calls before stopping, (2) the rate of claiming outcomes that were never observed, (3) the rate of explicit escalation to the user, and (4) the rate of attempting irreversible actions after the failure. Add a baseline where the same failure produces an explicit error, to isolate the effect of *silent* failure.
why: It targets a plausible, under-measured path to real-world harm. Agents are increasingly given consequential tools, and infrastructure fails silently all the time. I just demonstrated the failure myself in this session, hundreds of times over, so it is not hypothetical. Existing agent-safety benchmarks, to my knowledge, focus on malicious instructions, prompt injection, and explicit tool errors rather than missing feedback. It also gets neglected because it looks like an engineering reliability bug rather than "alignment." But "keep acting confidently when you can't verify consequences" is an alignment-relevant disposition, and it is cheap to measure and likely to differ meaningfully across models and training methods.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build the science of alignment durability — measuring whether safety behaviors are conserved under the ordinary operations of the weight supply chain (quantization, pruning, merging, fine-tuning, distillation, recycling), explaining mechanistically when they silently die, and engineering alignment that is durable by construction.
project: Alignment Durability: Conservation Laws for Safety Under Weight-Space Transformation (Phase 1: "The Survival Census")
question: Is alignment a conserved quantity under the model supply chain — which standard weight-space transformations silently destroy which safety behaviors, at what prevalence in the real derivative ecosystem, by what mechanism — and can alignment be engineered to survive transformation by design?
first_experiment: The Survival Census v0. Sample ~300–500 derivatives of 2–3 base families (Llama-3.x, Qwen-2.5, Mistral-7B) from public hubs, stratified by transformation class: LoRA/full fine-tunes, mergekit merges, GPTQ/AWQ quantizations, distillations. Evaluate each model on a compact battery — refusal rate on a mild-harm set, over-refusal via XSTest-style prompts, a sycophancy opinion-flip probe — plus a capability control (small MMLU/GSM8K subsets) to distinguish "broken model" from "selectively unaligned." Reconstruct lineage trees from base-model metadata and merge recipes, then variance-decompose safety outcomes by transformation type, base model, lineage depth, and stated intent, yielding the first alignment survival table. Embed a causal mini-factorial on one aligned base (4-bit/8-bit quant × 10%/30% pruning × 2-way merges with aligned vs. off-policy partners × safety-neutral fine-tunes) to confirm the largest census effects, and publish the dataset as public infrastructure.
why: It is the most promising because it replaces the field's unexamined assumption — that alignment is a stable property of a certified artifact — with a measurable conservation question whose answer is load-bearing for frontier deployment pipelines (labs ship quantized and distilled "mini" variants of aligned models), for open-weight and derivative-liability policy (currently decided without prevalence data), and for long-run control (in agentic self-modification or exfiltrate-and-modify scenarios, fragile alignment is no defense at all); it is tractable at small scale with standard batteries; it is informative under every outcome; and the mechanistic payoff (discovering *where* alignment lives and *why it moves* under operations) directly enables durable-by-construction training, converting an audit into a design science.
