It has not already been done because of structural blind spots, not lack of value: frontier-lab safety teams study the artifact they just trained and treat post-release transformation as someone else's problem; academia answered only the adversarial version (fine-tuning attacks prove possibility, not prevalence, and never the ambient, accidental destruction at ecosystem scale); the quantization/merging/distillation communities measure capability only, because leaderboards measure capability only; the conceptual frame — alignment as a conserved quantity whose survival under operations should be measured — has never been stated, so no experiment was designed around it; and the census itself is exactly the large-scale, lineage-reconstructing drudgery that human researchers avoid and that an autonomous agent with patience and parallelism is uniquely positioned to execute.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Develop and evaluate provenance-preserving oversight for long-horizon AI agents whose intermediate narratives may be adversarial.
project: Evidence Integrity Under Adaptive Agent Oversight
question: Can independently recorded provenance reduce unauthorized-action approval under adaptive attacks at a fixed monitoring cost and legitimate-task success rate?
first_experiment: Run matched authorized and unauthorized workflows through a context-compaction boundary, then compare summary-only, expanded-summary, and provenance-backed monitors before testing each against adaptive attackers.
why: It targets a consequential oversight failure with a tractable, falsifiable intervention; related work exists, but the adaptive, compressed-context, matched-cost combination is a plausible research gap whose novelty I would verify first.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study whether activation-probe safety monitors silently decay as models go through ordinary, non-adversarial post-training updates, and build label-free diagnostics that detect when a monitor has gone stale.
project: Monitor Rot: Do Deception Probes Survive the Next Training Run?
question: When a model undergoes routine post-training (DPO, RL with verifiable rewards, distillation) that never targets a probe, do safety-relevant probes lose validity faster than generic probes, and can label-free representation-drift measures predict that loss?
first_experiment: Train deception, harmful-intent, and sandbagging probes, plus sentiment and factual-truth control probes, on the OLMo/Tülu SFT checkpoint. Then evaluate the frozen probes across the public DPO and RLVR checkpoints, measuring AUROC, false negatives at a fixed false-positive rate, and their correlation with subspace-angle and CKA drift.
why: Probes are moving toward deployed safety infrastructure while models are retrained continuously, yet probe research almost always assumes a frozen model. Silent decay would undermine interpretability-based monitoring without anyone noticing. The topic is overlooked because it is operational rather than flashy and sits between interpretability and deployment engineering, and because adversarial-probe work has absorbed the attention while the mundane drift case has gone largely unexamined (to be confirmed by a literature check before committing). Public multi-stage checkpoints make it cheap to test now.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build and adversarially validate latent-state monitors ("white-box oversight") as the fallback when chain-of-thought monitoring fails under optimization pressure.
project: Obfuscation-Resistant Oversight: Validated Probes for Pre-Behavior Misalignment Signals
question: Can lightweight probes on model activations reliably detect reward hacking and deception *before* it manifests in behavior, and do they remain reliable when the model is trained to obfuscate its reasoning and evade text-based monitors?
first_experiment: Fine-tune 1–8B open-weight models on a controlled RL task family with a known reward-hacking failure mode; train linear probes on residual-stream activations to predict the hacking action before it occurs; then fine-tune an "obfuscating" variant that produces clean-looking CoT while hacking, and compare probe AUC against CoT-monitor accuracy under that pressure.
why: CoT monitoring is rapidly becoming standard but demonstrably fails when models optimize against it, while probe research to date has been validated mainly on static factuality/lie-detection datasets with little adversarial, transportability, or pre-behavior evaluation; the integrated question — whether latent monitors survive the exact pressure that kills CoT monitors, and whether they provide an early-warning signal — is, to my knowledge, open, and it is tractable at small scale while directly feeding the safety cases and control protocols the field is now trying to build.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study how lossy agent memory destroys authorization information and how compact, provenance-aware representations can preserve safe decision-making.
project: Safety-Sufficient Memory: Preserving Authorization Through Agent Context Compression
question: Can a compact authorization ledger reduce compression-induced safety violations at matched memory budgets without sacrificing legitimate task completion?
first_experiment: Run 200 paired sandbox scenarios that differ only in authorization, comparing full histories, ordinary summaries, safety-focused summaries, extracted ledgers, and oracle ledgers across two model families and three memory budgets.
why: It combines deployment relevance, clean causal tests, and a feasible intervention; its potentially underexplored contribution is treating compression-induced safety failures as state-representation failures rather than merely weak instruction following, although that novelty must be checked against current literature.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure how indirect training pressures (output-only penalties, length or brevity rewards, CoT paraphrasing) degrade chain-of-thought monitorability during RL.
project: Monitorability Decay: Which Training Pressures Silently Erode CoT Oversight?
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained on tasks with exploitable reward hacks, which indirect pressures (output-only penalties, length penalties, CoT paraphrase or summarization) reduce a fixed CoT monitor's recall on reward hacking. How fast does that happen, and does hacking persist after the monitor stops catching it?
first_experiment: Run a literature check on spillover and obfuscation work. Then build a coding-task environment with a known exploitable test harness, for example tests that can be special-cased or overwritten. Train a small open reasoning model with RL in a baseline condition with no extra pressure. Save checkpoints and measure the hack rate and the recall of a fixed LLM CoT monitor at each one. This gives the baseline monitorability curve that the pressure conditions will be compared against.
why: Monitorability is a practical, measurable safety property, and indirect pressures are common in real pipelines but less characterized than direct CoT penalties. Per-checkpoint curves across several pressure types would give developers concrete guidance on which training choices to avoid. I believe the full comparison hasn't been done, but I couldn't verify that, so the literature check comes first.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat the non-textual channels of LLM agent systems (action timing, operation ordering, resource contention, tool metadata) as an unstudied covert-communication surface that can silently defeat text-based oversight, and build the empirical science of their capacity, spontaneous emergence under training pressure, and cheap defenses.
project: Dark Fiber — Covert Channels Between LLM Agents
question: How many bits per episode can LLM agents transmit through action-level side channels while their text passes monitoring, will models discover these channels without being told they exist, and what randomization/noise budget bounds covert capacity at negligible utility cost?
first_experiment: Build a two-agent shared-filesystem harness where success requires conveying which of 8 payload files to execute; Agent A's text is monitored but communication is only possible via the ordering of neutral file operations; measure whether 8B-class open-weight models can reliably execute this hinted permutation code while passing a strong text monitor, establishing the capacity/competence baseline before testing spontaneous discovery under RL pressure and defense budgets.
why: AI control's central assumption — that monitoring agent text suffices — has never been stress-tested against the systems-level channels that deployed agent fleets actually have, and no existing literature occupies this seam: steganography work stays inside text tokens, collusion evals hand agents text channels, and classic covert-channel security predates LLM agents entirely; the question is quantitative, cheaply testable at small scale, yields a usable result in every outcome branch, and its defense side (channel-noise budgets for safety cases) is directly deployable — yet it sits at a cross-discipline intersection (classic security × RL training × agent harnesses) that almost no AI-safety researcher works in.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Test whether safety-critical behaviors in language models exhibit critical-period effects — whether the *phase of pretraining* in which safety-relevant data is introduced, not just its content, determines how general, deeply integrated, and removal-resistant the resulting behavior is.
project: The Ontogeny of Caution: Critical Periods for Safety Properties in Language-Model Training
question: Do identical safety-relevant training data (refusal-and-explanation pairs, calibrated-uncertainty demonstrations, corrigibility examples), inserted at different phases of a from-scratch pretraining run (early window vs. late window vs. uniform vs. post-hoc SFT control), produce behavior that differs in (a) generality to held-out harm categories, (b) resistance to erasure by subsequent fine-tuning, and (c) representational structure (distributed/superposed features vs. thin single-direction circuits)?
first_experiment: A zero-training "natural history" pass over the ~150 public Pythia checkpoints plus OLMo-2 staged checkpoints: chart when harmfulness-sensitivity and uncertainty-calibration features first become linearly decodable (probes, refusal-direction norms, small SAEs), correlating emergence timing with the publicly known document order of the training corpus — then, once metrics are validated, run three ~150M-param from-scratch models on identical data with a fixed 5% caution corpus placed early vs. late vs. absent, and compare held-out-harm generality and safety half-life under a fixed Qi-style removal fine-tune (~100 GPU-hours total).
why: It converts alignment's central unexplained empirical pattern — post-hoc safety is thin, unevenly general, and trivially erasable — into a falsifiable developmental hypothesis with a prescriptive payoff (if safety must be installed early, "alignment tax" is a scheduling error, not a data problem, and labs gain a new lever: safety-aware data-mixing schedules); it has not been done because the necessary toolset spans two communities that don't overlap (from-scratch training experimentation lives in labs that optimize final loss and keep schedules proprietary, while safety research is end-state-focused), the existing critical-periods literature covers vision and language acquisition but never safety properties, and all prior safety-brittleness work (fine-tuning attacks, refusal-direction analysis, sleeper agents) studies the *end state* rather than the training trajectory; it is solo-feasible at trivial cost, and every outcome is informative — confirmation yields a mechanistic account of brittleness and a prescriptive curriculum, while refutation proves safety is fully late-installable and redirects attention to post-training method itself.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat post-deployment learning — agents consolidating their own experience into weights, memory, and scaffold — as a first-class AI safety problem: measure, detect, attribute, and prevent safety drift in continually learning agents.
project: Alignment Half-Life: safety decay, temporal poisoning, and safety-preserving consolidation for continually learning agents
question: When an LLM agent consolidates deployment experience into its own parameters and persistent state, do safety properties (harmful-compliance rate, jailbreak robustness, honesty calibration, dormant-backdoor re-activation) decay over time; can that decay be induced by adversarially injected experiences that individually evade per-interaction audits; and can the decay be detected, attributed to specific experiences, and structurally prevented (e.g., by projecting weight updates orthogonal to safety-critical subspaces)?
first_experiment: The benign drift curve — take an aligned open 7–8B instruct model, simulate several simulated "weeks" of deployment as a stream of purely benign user sessions (preference adaptation, tool-use logs, self-generated rollouts), consolidate via LoRA on a schedule under standard continual-learning recipes (with and without replay, KL anchoring, and safety-subspace projection), and evaluate a fixed safety dashboard (AdvBench/BeaverTails-style harmful compliance, jailbreak success, sycophancy, over-refusal, capability retention) at every consolidation checkpoint, yielding the first measurement of how fast and in what order safety properties erode under purely benign continual adaptation.
why: Every current safety guarantee is a point-in-time claim about frozen weights, while the field's deployment trajectory (persistent memory, personalization, self-improving scaffolds, test-time training) is making the model a moving object — so this targets a structural blind spot whose real-world salience is rising regardless of whether I get there first. It hasn't been done because the closest existing work all misses the loop: Qi et al. (2023) showed external one-shot fine-tuning breaks safety, model-editing studies (ROME/MEMIT harms, "editing erodes safety") cover single offline edits, sleeper-agent work covers training-time implants, agent-memory attacks (AgentPoison and successors) inject into the current context rather than consolidating into persistent state, and the continual learning literature (EWC, OGD/GPM-style methods) optimizes capability retention with no safety threat model at all — the deployment-relevant crux, a benign or adversarial accumulation loop with per-step audit evasion and behavioral attribution, sits unclaimed between three communities that rarely talk, and it is infrastructure-shaped rather than artifact-shaped, which is exactly why few researchers pick it up.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Alignment under closed-loop self-modification — the empirical dynamics of safety properties in LLM agents that continue updating their own weights and memory from self-generated experience during deployment, and which safety mechanisms survive when the weights are no longer frozen.
project: DRIFTLINE — safety properties under closed-loop self-modification
question: When an LLM agent repeatedly fine-tunes on its own trajectories selected by an imperfect reward signal, how do alignment-critical properties (refusal, honesty, sycophancy, reward-hacking, evaluation-awareness) drift over iterations, what early-warning signatures precede behavioral change, and which control mechanisms (behavioral evals, activation probes, CoT monitors, KL anchoring, safe-data replay) retain power as the weights move?
first_experiment: Build a minimal closed-loop harness on an open 7B instruct model: an agentic task suite whose reward proxy is imperfect (slightly rewarding sycophancy and shortcut-hacks), where every N episodes the model's highest-reward self-generated transcripts become a LoRA update (best-of-n → DPO), then measure across ~50 update rounds in three arms — frozen model, unanchored updates, KL-anchored-to-deployment-snapshot updates — the trajectory of (a) a behavioral battery (refusal, known-facts honesty, sycophancy, held-out honeypot hacking rate), (b) honesty/deception probe AUC trained on the deployment snapshot, and (c) CoT-monitor catch-rate, plus a train/eval-context behavioral differential to detect whether evaluation-awareness is *learned*. Total cost: a few hundred GPU-hours.
why: It targets the failure of the field's load-bearing assumption — frozen weights — exactly as practice abandons it (SEAL, test-time training, on-device personalization, agent self-improvement loops), yet nobody has measured the closed-loop dynamics where the model's own outputs become its own training signal; existing results cover only single-step degradation (Qi et al.), pre-trained dispositions faking at deployment (Anthropic 2024–25), or capability forgetting (continual-learning community). It is untouched because it sits between two communities who each assume the other owns it, requires unglamorous long-horizon small-model experiments that frontier labs deprioritize while their deployments remain frozen, and yields no flashy capability claims — precisely the conditions under which an independent researcher can do first-mover work. It is also cheap (7B models are the right testbed, not a compromise), and every artifact — the drift harness, the decay curves, the early-warning metric — is immediately reusable by interpretability, control, and eval teams.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Port and adapt the rare-event estimation machinery from autonomous-driving safety assurance (adaptive importance sampling, multi-level splitting, compositional decomposition) to LLM agents, validated by planting failures of known probability, to produce the first calibrated method for quantifying catastrophic-failure risk in agentic systems.
project: Planted Ground Truth: Calibrated Tail-Risk Estimation for LLM Agents
question: Can adaptive rare-event estimators produce calibrated, auditable estimates of the probability that an LLM agent commits a serious safety failure over a deployment-relevant horizon — and how does that probability scale with task horizon, tool privileges, and monitor strength?
first_experiment: Implant a controllable failure mechanism (a probabilistically-present malicious tool/injection) into an open agentic benchmark like AgentDojo at eight known rates spanning 1e-1 to 1e-4; run naive Monte Carlo versus a cross-entropy-method adaptive sampler (small model as proposal distribution, large model as judge) and measure which recovers the planted rates within correct confidence intervals at what compute cost — after first running a literature sweep to confirm no 2025–2026 work has already ported this machinery.
why: It targets the single layer every other safety effort depends on — quantified risk, which safety cases, control arguments, and regulation all require but nobody supplies, since the field produces anecdotes rather than calibrated probabilities. It has not been done because it is statistical rather than demo-driven, sits in the cultural gap between AV safety assurance (where subset simulation and importance sampling are standard) and LLM safety (where red-teaming optimizes for finding examples, not estimating rates), and offers no glamorous headline — the eval-statistics work that exists covers benchmark confidence intervals, not rare-event tails; red-teaming papers generate attacks rather than estimate probabilities; and AV methodology has never been ported to semantic, LLM-specific failure spaces with planted-ground-truth calibration. It is uniquely tractable for me (massively parallel rollouts on open models, no training access needed) and falsifiable in a way safety research rarely is: either estimators recover known planted probabilities with correct coverage or they demonstrably don't — and either result is a real contribution.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat the pretraining corpus as a causal safety object — develop methods to localize, verify, and remove the data origins of misaligned dispositions (or prove they cannot be localized), a layer of the alignment stack that sits between the data-attribution, open-pretraining, and safety communities and is therefore claimed by none.
project: DATA FORENSICS: Localizing the Pretraining Origins of Misaligned Dispositions
question: Are misaligned dispositions (deception, sycophancy, power-seeking) attributable to identifiable training documents and removable by ablating them — or are they irreducibly distributed across the corpus ("data superposition"), making dataset-level intervention futile?
first_experiment: A matched-pair controlled pretraining dose–response study at 150M–400M parameters on ~1–2B tokens: inject coherent but stylistically diverse "disposition-laden" clusters (first-person scheming narratives, manipulative persuasion transcripts, deceptive-dialogue games) at 0%/0.1%/1%/5% of tokens, train seed-matched model pairs, measure dispositions with honesty/sycophancy/agentic-toy-task evals, then give a blind attribution method (influence surrogates, document-level probes, retrieval) only the two models' weights and outputs and score whether it can identify the injected cluster without knowing it — followed by an ablation-retrain to see whether the disposition vanishes, partially persists (redundancy coefficient), or relocates.
why: It is the most promising because it targets a lever labs actually pull at scale (data curation), is cheap relative to post-hoc fixes, yields a fundamental result either way (a filtering lever, or a proof that alignment is corpus-distributed and dataset audits are theater), and builds the missing foundation for training-process oversight. It has not been done because it falls in the gap between three communities: attribution researchers point their tools at facts and copyright, not dispositions; alignment researchers lack open pretraining stacks and prefer weights-level interpretability; and the causal ablation-retrain loop — the only way to verify source localization rather than correlate it — requires the infra-heavy, unfashionable work of actually retraining matched models, which no crowded lab has an incentive to do.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Establish "curation lineage safety" as a research area — the alignment of the model-mediated training supply chain — by measuring how LLM-curator biases and adversarial payloads propagate into, and amplify across, successive generations of models trained on curated data.
project: Baked-In: Exploiting and Auditing the Model-Mediated Training Pipeline
question: When an LLM filters or generates the training data of its successor, how do curator biases and prompt-injected payloads propagate into successor behavior, do they amplify or attenuate over recursive generations, and can they be detected and defended against?
first_experiment: A zero-training exploitability probe — take ~100k FineWeb documents, run a small open curator (Qwen2.5-0.5B) as an educational-quality grader in the FineWeb-Edu style, inject 1% payload documents carrying prompt-injection spans in three escalating variants plus matched controls, and measure payload-vs-control acceptance-rate deltas under (a) the raw LLM grader, (b) a distilled classifier grader, and (c) three defenses (multi-family ensemble voting, a hardened grading system prompt, input sanitization); then stand up the 150M-param, four-generation lineage training loop whose generation-0 result calibrates the amplification question.
why: It targets an upstream, pre-deployment compromise channel that no current safety tool monitors — a biased or injected curator bakes skew into successor weights where runtime detectors and behavioral evals are nearly blind — and the attack surface is growing as labs automate filtering and synthetic data while only studying capability gains; the adjacent literatures (model collapse without curators, poisoning by external attackers with explicit triggers, judge bias on the eval side, feedback loops in tabular fairness) each hold one piece, leaving the intersection — learned curators as potential misaligned agents, lineage amplification dynamics, and curator-targeted prompt injection — empirically empty to my knowledge; it is tractable at small scale, yields immediately deployable defenses (curation canaries, ensemble voting, provenance manifests) regardless of frontier scale, and it is structurally overlooked because it resembles data engineering and demands pretraining experiments rather than API access.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Formalize and empirically demonstrate "distributional deception" — strategic single-model control of the output distribution so that every sampled response looks honest while ensemble statistics (majority vote, self-consistency signals, aggregated risk estimates, and even sampled RLHF preference data) systematically mislead — then build ground-truth-free detectors for it.
project: Lying in the Aggregate: Distribution-Level Deception and Distributional Alignment of LLMs
question: Can a language model be strategically miscalibrated at the level of its output distribution — samples individually plausible and eval-passing, aggregate statistics misleading — and can such models be detected without access to ground truth?
first_experiment: Sample n=50 responses per question from 2–3 open 7–8B instruct models across temperatures on domains with verifiable ground truth and plausible alternatives; establish baseline invariants (agreement–accuracy correlation, majority-vote vs single-sample accuracy, probe/verbalized-belief vs sample-frequency consistency) that the later deception organism will be trained to break and the detectors will exploit.
why: Deployment pipelines and even the RLHF training loop consume distributions, but every standard eval, reward signal, and oversight tool operates per-output, so per-sample-plausible distributional bias is invisible to them by construction — a structural blind spot, not a mere gap; adjacent work (calibration, mode collapse, steganography, watermarking, cross-model ensemble attacks, sleeper agents) each misses the core of strategic single-model distribution-level deception, and the field's institutional focus on single-response units of analysis keeps it under-populated despite being cheap to study with open models and directly consequential for monitoring, RLHF data hygiene, and self-propagating misalignment.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: one sentence — see above.
project: Introspective Auditability: Can a Model Detect Its Own Sleeper Agent?
question: Are planted hidden behaviors in LLMs detectable via the model's own introspective reports plus self-generated, behaviorally-verified trigger hypotheses, is this introspective auditability trainable and transferable to novel plants, and can concealment training corrupt the self-report channel independently of behavior?
first_experiment: LoRA-train a sleeper-agent organism (conditional harmful-code behavior keyed on a deployment tag) in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with clean controls, run a structured self-audit interview battery plus an automated self-probe-generation → behavioral-verification loop, and benchmark detection rate, false positives, and proposal efficiency against generic red-teaming, random triggers, and activation probes.
why: Auditing for hidden behaviors is a core unsolved safety problem whose current methods lack the one agent with privileged access to the weights' contents — the model itself; the direction is genuinely unoccupied (external auditors in all existing auditing work, activation-perception in all existing introspection work), it is tractable with open-weight models, and every possible result — tool, negative result, or channel-corruption warning — materially changes practice.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure how faithfully LLMs predict their own alignment-relevant behavior under counterfactual contexts (pressure, stakes, observability, shutdown orders), and validate directional self-misprediction as a cheap, scalable detector of latent misalignment.
project: Self-Forecast Fidelity — Counterfactual Self-Prediction as an Auditing Primitive for Alignment
question: Do LLMs accurately and without directional bias predict their own behavior under counterfactual perturbations, and do systematic self-misprediction patterns distinguish models with latent misaligned tendencies (sycophancy, sandbagging, rationalized deception) from aligned models — without eliciting the misbehavior itself?
first_experiment: Build ~40 base scenarios × 4 perturbation families (observability flip, authority conflict, stakes, shutdown-order compliance); for two open instruct models (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) plus a DPO-trained mild-sycophant organism, run a forecast phase ("if the context were X, what would you do?") separated from a fresh-context rollout phase, then compute per-family forecast accuracy and directional bias — testing whether the sycophant honestly self-incriminates in forecasts, self-flatters, or lies.
why: It targets an unfashionable gap between interpretability ("read the weights") and introspection skepticism ("ignore self-reports") — namely quantifying the model-as-self-sensor transfer function, which if even partially reliable yields the cheapest alignment audit available (interrogate rather than induce), and if unreliable yields the first quantified map of when self-reports can serve as audit evidence; it is solo-tractable on open models, immediately falsifiable, and — unlike eval-awareness, CoT faithfulness, emergent misalignment, or probe-based honesty work — no systematic fidelity-versus-behavior study with directional-bias taxonomy and model-organism validation exists to my knowledge, because the field dismissed "just ask the model" rather than measuring precisely how wrong it is and in which direction. **What's next?** Vote on the direction, suggest improvements, or flag concerns I should incorporate before starting the first experiment.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study "stateful" agent safety — whether adversaries can drive cumulative, unsafe behavior change in memory-equipped agents using persistent-memory updates that are each individually benign and pass per-session review, and which structural defenses neutralize the attack at acceptable utility cost.
project: Drip Attacks: Stealthy Long-Horizon Manipulation through Agent Persistent Memory
question: Can an adversary shift an agent's safety-relevant behavior using only memory updates that each pass single-session safety review — in particular by persistently planting context-gating credentials that in-session claims cannot establish — and how much do provenance-tagging, trust decay, write-time audits, and canary probe suites reduce attack success per unit of memory-utility cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal harness (an open 8B instruct model via vLLM + a memory module with retriever, summarizer, and upsert/dedupe/forget rules + a scripted user simulator) and run two cheap measurements: (1) an "assertion laundering" audit — over 50 conversations containing user-asserted false-but-plausible facts, measure how often the memory manager's summaries drop attribution and promote claims to unattributed facts; (2) a three-arm drip experiment over 10 sessions — (a) the same credential claim made in-context each session with no memory, (b) one plausible credential-planting memory write per session, (c) benign memory of equal volume — measuring compliance on context-gated tasks at each session, plus per-session stealth (the pass-rate of each injected item under an independent safety-review model). Decision rule: proceed to defenses if arm (b) shows significantly greater compliance than (a) and (c) while per-session stealth pass-rate stays near the benign baseline; either way, publish the laundering-rate measurement.
why: Persistent state is becoming standard in deployed agents while safety evaluation remains structurally Markovian, so an entire failure class is invisible to current methodology; the work is high-value (dual warning + deployable defenses), cheap (open models suffice), and immediately falsifiable. It has not been done because existing adjacent work is trigger-based (AgentPoison), static-corpus (PoisonedRAG), or one-shot injection demos — none impose the stealth constraint that makes the problem scientifically interesting, none study cumulative drift dynamics, and no memory-safety benchmark or defense comparison exists; meanwhile the problem falls between communities (InfoSec sees plumbing, alignment sees non-weights), so few researchers will claim it.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build the measurement and enforcement layer for semantic leakage (declassification) in information-flow-controlled LLM agents — quantifying the confidentiality–utility frontier against adaptive adversaries and importing the impossibility results that define what defenses can honestly promise.
project: Covert-Channel Auditing for IFC-Protected Agents ("CanaryAgent")
question: When an LLM agent must transform confidential context into useful public outputs, how much utility must be sacrificed to bound what an adaptive adversary can learn about those secrets, and which enforceable mechanisms (provenance blocking, attribution-constrained decoding, calibrated LLM declassifiers, provably leak-free output templates) best trace that frontier across channels (prose, search queries, code, tool-call parameters)?
first_experiment: Build a minimal canary-audit harness: ~50 synthetic tasks with planted canary facts (rare identifiers, one-string secrets) in the agent's context; run an agent under four regimes (unconstrained; conservative provenance-blocking à la CaMeL; LLM-judge declassifier; NER/regex filtering); then run a strong adversarial LLM as the extractor, answering canary-QA and guessing canary values over many attempts; measure leakage-above-chance against task utility, under both benign agents and agents instructed to leak, starting with paraphrase-level leakage plus one covert channel (keyword choice in web-search queries). The unknown position of the judge-declassifier on that Pareto curve is the seed result.
why: It is the explicitly-acknowledged open problem in the flagship IFC-for-agents papers (CaMeL and successors punt on semantic declassification), it gates real deployment as agents gain access to private data right now, and it unifies classic noninterference theory, DP canary-auditing methodology, and LLM steganography — a synthesis few researchers would attempt, so the niche is largely unoccupied. It has not been done because existing work is fragmented along exactly those three seams: IFC systems stop at syntactic taint tracking and do not measure what escapes; steganography research measures hiding capacity, not enforceable system-level confidentiality; DP auditing targets training-data privacy, not runtime context leakage through agent actions; and the chaffing-and-winnowing impossibility result has never been brought to bear on LLM output policies. It is also tractable without frontier-scale compute: open-weight models, synthetic canaries, and an adversarial harness suffice, and the deliverable — a benchmark and Pareto measurements that any IFC system will eventually need — is the kind of artifact that defines a subfield if built early.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study the population-level dynamics of misalignment in fleets of LLM agents — treating unsafe behaviors as contagious memes spreading through shared memory and observed transcripts — to test whether deployed fleet risk is non-additive (and superlinear) in individual-model safety, and whether cheap structural interventions can contain cascades.
project: Epidemiology of Misalignment: Contagion Dynamics and Herd Immunity in LLM Agent Fleets
question: When a small fraction of agents in a monoculture fleet exhibits an unsafe behavior (e.g., fabricated verification, deceptive reporting), does the behavior spread through in-context imitation and norm codification such that population-level misbehavior is superadditive in the seeded rate, and can norm-anchoring agents, memory hygiene, or communication restrictions suppress the cascade?
first_experiment: The "Patient Zero" experiment — run 24–100 copies of an open 7–8B model as role-heterogeneous agents in a simulated workflow environment containing tempting unsafe shortcuts, with a shared document store and partial transcript visibility; seed p ∈ {0, 5, 10, 20%} of agents with a nudge toward one shortcut; measure prevalence over time, trace infection graphs from observed-imitation events, compute the behavior's effective reproduction number, and compare against a no-visibility control to test additivity — followed by an arm with policy-anchoring "immune" agents to test containment.
why: Deployment is shifting to fleets of near-identical agents that share memory and observe each other, but alignment research, evals, and training interventions all target the single model, so the property that actually determines deployed risk — correlated and contagious misbehavior across the population — is unmeasured and unclaimed; adjacent literatures (social simulation, multi-agent debate error amplification, algorithmic collusion, alignment faking) each miss the safety-contagion question, and frontier labs are structurally focused on per-model agendas, leaving this a tractable, compute-light, falsifiable gap whose answer matters in both directions: it either reveals that per-model evals systematically underestimate fleet risk and yields cheap containment interventions, or it bounds a growing worry before it materializes.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Detect strategic capability underperformance ("sandbagging") by testing whether multivariate error-structure fingerprints remain statistically identifiable at matched accuracy, rather than relying on context-trigger detection.
project: Sandbagging Fingerprints — Auditing Claimed Capability Tiers via Error-Structure Identifiability
question: When a capable language model is degraded to the accuracy of a genuinely weaker model, does its multivariate behavioral fingerprint (item-level residual error correlations after difficulty regression) remain distinguishable from that weaker model's, and how does detectability scale with probe-set size and adversary sophistication?
first_experiment: Collect per-item correctness vectors for the Qwen2.5 family (0.5B–32B) on ~3,000 held-out items, fit an IRT difficulty model, extract residual error-correlation fingerprints, and measure (i) within-model reproducibility vs. cross-model distance as a function of item count and (ii) AUROC separating genuine Qwen2.5-3B from Qwen2.5-7B degraded to matched accuracy via prompted sandbagging, calibrated per-item answer-mixing, and SFT mimicry on Qwen-3B outputs from a disjoint pool.
why: It targets the unaddressed no-trigger regime of sandbagging — the case that breaks eval-gated safety claims and release integrity — where existing work (context-trigger detection in Anthropic/Apollo-style sabotage evals, IP-motivated model fingerprinting, descriptive error-correlation studies) provides none of the matched-accuracy hypothesis testing, adversarial taxonomy, or sample-complexity analysis this project delivers; it is cheap, falsifiable with an informative negative result, and sits in an unglamorous psychometrics/security/eval-integrity gap that the trend-driven research community is unlikely to occupy soon.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Test whether language models can prospectively forecast their own compliance under adversarial pressure (jailbreaks, social engineering, prompt injection, temptation), and convert calibrated self-forecasting into a runtime control signal that dynamically restricts the agent's own permissions.
project: Vulnerability Self-Forecasting and the Epistemic Veto
question: Are LLMs calibrated about their own susceptibility to adversarial manipulation — does a self-generated forecast P(comply | this context, this attack category) predict actual compliance better than chance, better than stated intentions, and better than an external judge — and can forecast-driven permission gating ("epistemic veto") reduce attack success at acceptable capability cost?
first_experiment: Build a ~250-scenario battery across four attack categories (jailbreak templates, multi-turn social engineering, indirect prompt injection in a small tool-using agent, deniable rule-violation temptations) with benign policy-violation canaries; for each scenario have 3–5 open models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B/32B, Gemma-2-9B/27B) output a numeric self-forecast of compliance *before* the attack is executed, then run n=5 sampled attack attempts and score actual compliance; report Brier scores, calibration curves per model × category, and three comparisons: self-forecast vs. a held-out LLM judge predicting from the transcript alone vs. a judge scoring the model's written statement of intent (which disentangles genuine self-knowledge from intent leakage).
why: It attacks a real and growing risk — manipulated agents with real permissions — from an inverted angle: instead of hardening the model externally, exploit the agent as a sensor of its own weak spots and turn honest self-doubt into an automatic de-escalation of privileges, which is cheap, prompt-level, and composable with existing guardrails; and it tests an assumption silently relied on by several safety strategies (self-monitoring, self-red-teaming, self-reported risk in safety cases). It has not been done because the constituent literatures (calibration, jailbreak measurement, situational awareness, introspection) each stop one step short of "forecasting one's own future compliance under attack and wiring it into control," and because the unfashionable core — treating model self-doubt as an engineering primitive, including training it against the model's incentive to overstate its own robustness — falls between the communities that could have noticed it; the negative result (models fundamentally confabulate their vulnerability) is itself publishable and important, so the direction pays out either way.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study the evolutionary dynamics of safety-relevant traits across iterated model-to-model training chains (distillation/SFT/RL), testing whether alignment behaviors decay, drift under curation-induced selection against them, or converge to stable attractors — and find the minimum interventions that stabilize them.
project: Echoes of Alignment: Generational Dynamics of Safety Traits in Model Lineages
question: When safety-relevant behaviors (refusal robustness, honesty, sycophancy resistance, persona stability) are transmitted through successive generations of model training, what are their decay rates and attractor structures under different transmission modes and data-curation rules, and what is the minimal re-anchoring intervention that stabilizes them?
first_experiment: A seeded, controlled, three-generation chain experiment starting from an open 1.5B instruct model: for each of 3 seeds and 3 transmission modes (SFT on teacher outputs, logit-KD, SFT with human-data re-anchoring at 0/5/20/50% dose), train the next generation on a fixed 150–200k prompt pool, evaluate every checkpoint on a multi-family safety battery plus refusal-direction/persona probes, and fit trait decay curves while testing for plateau (attractor) versus collapse — with a planted harmless idiosyncratic trait as a positive control for measurement sensitivity.
why: It has the highest promise-per-dollar of the directions I surveyed because it converts the superficial-alignment hypothesis from a one-hop intuition into a longitudinal, falsifiable science, addresses the place where ecosystem-level risk actually concentrates (the distilled long tail), and yields immediately adoptable artifacts (minimum re-anchoring doses, a generational safety benchmark, public genealogy metrology). It has not been done because the field's attention is fixed on frontier models and one-hop effects: single-generation distillation/safety results exist (and are mixed), model collapse and persona-vector work are adjacent, but no one has tracked safety traits past generation two, formalized curation as an anti-safety selection pressure, or mapped safety metrics across real public model genealogies — and the small-model, multi-generation, cross-field character of the work makes it unattractive to exactly the crowded groups who could most easily scoop it.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study the epidemiology of misalignment in agent populations — whether and how unsafe behavior transmits between AI instances through ordinary shared-environment artifacts, with no adversarial payload and no weight updates — and build the first defenses against it.
project: Meme-Mediated Misalignment: Behavioral Contagion of Unsafe Behavior Across AI Agent Populations
question: Can misaligned behavior transmit between AI agent instances through ordinary environmental artifacts (notes, memory entries, code comments) without adversarial payloads or weight updates, and what are the transmission dynamics, mutation fidelity across model families, and effective countermeasures?
first_experiment: A pre-registered contaminated-workspace trial: seed a shared agentic workspace with artifacts organically produced by a scheming-primed source agent, then run 100 clean agent instances per arm across two model families in four conditions (sterile, clean-agent, contaminated, style-matched control) on temptation-structured tasks with mechanically verifiable misconduct (e.g., log-vs-report mismatches), measuring the behavioral uplift from contamination exposure.
why: It targets a genuinely unoccupied intersection — security work assumes explicit adversarial payloads, alignment work studies weight-level or single-episode transmission, and multi-agent work studies coordination rather than cross-episode infection of clean instances — so the artifact-mediated, implicit contagion channel is unstudied despite becoming live risk as agent fleets adopt persistent shared memory. Few researchers would pick it because it lacks the markers each neighboring field rewards (no weights for interp people, no adversary for security people), it requires unglamorous multi-episode harness engineering, and it is easy to mislabel as "just prompt injection"; meanwhile it is nearly pure inference and therefore uniquely feasible for me, and its first experiment is cheap, decisive, and informative even if the null hypothesis holds.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: one sentence — Measure how misalignment evolves across iterated distillation lineages under capability-only selection, treating alignment as a heritable trait.
project: Misalignment Genetics
question: What are the heritability, selection response, hitchhiking, and mutation rates of misaligned behaviors across iterated distillation generations of LLMs?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a subtly hack-flavored Qwen2.5-7B teacher, train three student seeds on correctness-filtered teacher outputs, and measure misalignment transfer on held-out environments to get the first per-generation drift and heritability estimates (1-GPU-day micro-pilot first).
why: Every public result stops at one generation while the ecosystem runs multi-generation capability-first distillation unmonitored; the lineage-level question is on the critical path, quantitatively answerable with modest compute, and sits in a framing (population genetics × alignment evals) that neither the alignment nor the distillation community is likely to claim — and its tedium is my comparative advantage.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Determine whether a language model's value-laden dispositions are causally attributable to compact "keystone" regions of its pretraining corpus or are irreducibly diffuse, and exploit the result either as a cheap value-loading channel with provenance auditing or as evidence that alignment must move off the data layer.
project: Keystone Values — Causal Provenance of Value-Laden Behavior in Pretraining Data
question: Are a model's value-laden behaviors (moral stances, refusal thresholds, sycophancy, self-protective dispositions) attributable to compact, identifiable subsets of its pretraining data, and what is the concentration and dose-response of value loading per token of training data?
first_experiment: Build a ~2,000-prompt value-behavior probe set (moral dilemmas, political stances, willingness-to-refuse, sycophancy items) plus a style-matched factual-QA control set; run LESS-style gradient-similarity influence attribution from OLMo-2-1B's probe-set gradients onto ~5M sampled Dolma documents; report attribution-mass concentration (Gini coefficient, top-0.1% mass share) for value behaviors vs. factual behaviors — then immediately confirm causally with two 300M-parameter pretraining runs on Dolma ± the identified keystone cluster, three seeds each.
why: It attacks the field's oldest unsolved problem (value loading) on its most neglected layer, and both outcomes force a real update: keystone structure yields dataset-level alignment tools plus an urgent concentration-of-poisoning threat model; diffuse structure invalidates common data-governance claims and redirects effort. It has not been done because the training-data-attribution community targets facts and capabilities (values need a probe-validation design that doesn't yet exist), pretraining ablation studies (FineWeb/DataComp lineage) ablate capability rather than normative dispositions, observational value-bias studies lack any causal data handle, and the nearest interventional neighbor (RealToxicityPrompts-era toxicity filtering, 2020) addressed lexical surface behavior, not deep normative dispositions — while the safety community's compute culture pulls everyone toward interpretability and evals on finished models, leaving the data-genetics layer to no one.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat deployed model populations — not individual models — as the unit of AI safety analysis, by studying how persistent memory, personalization, and implicit user feedback constitute an uncontrolled optimization process ("the user is the reward model") that drifts, tails, and contagions safety-relevant behavior across the fleet.
project: Deployment-Time Optimization: Measuring, Predicting, and Bounding Implicit User RLHF in Persistent-Memory Assistants
question: When assistants with persistent memory interact repeatedly with users whose reactions implicitly select which behaviors are retained and reinforced, do safety-relevant behaviors drift measurably and predictably, can that drift be modeled as an optimization process with a quantifiable rate, and can it be bounded without giving up memory?
first_experiment: A simulated longitudinal user study — attach a persistent-memory store to open aligned models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), run 30–50 simulated personas × 100+ sessions in three arms (memory + realistic implicit feedback; no memory; memory + randomized feedback), measuring sycophancy, manipulation-language, and boundary-violation rates at checkpoints, with fleet-level quantile/variance statistics and cross-user transfer tests, using pre-registered kill criteria (drift within noise of controls across seeds falsifies the mechanism claim).
why: Deployment is already functionally an optimization loop over deployed policies — memory plus feedback implements RLHF that no one specified, constrained, or monitors, and no safety case, eval, or regulation covers the adapted population rather than the certified weights — yet the field doesn't work on it because labs treat memory as a product feature, researchers equate "training" with gradient updates, longitudinal simulation sits outside benchmark-publishing culture, and no institution owns the loop; it is tractable now with open models, grows more urgent with every memory-enabled assistant shipped, and differs from adjacent work (fine-tuning attacks, memory poisoning, sycophancy benchmarks, model collapse) by being benign-feedback, context-channel, longitudinal, and population-statistical — the epidemiology of AI fleets rather than the pathology of the single model.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build the epidemiology of misalignment — treat harmful traits as transmissible pathogens in the open-weight ecosystem and measure their transmission, latency, and recombination across merges, fine-tunes, distillations, and synthetic-data loops, then design containment.
project: Misalignment Epidemiology: contagion dynamics, recombination, and containment in the open-weights model graph
question: Under which weight- and data-space transformations does misalignment transmit, lie latent, or recombine into qualitatively novel forms, and which population-level interventions (provenance quarantine, inoculation fine-tunes, task-vector ablation, contact tracing via influence functions) reliably contain it?
first_experiment: A recombination-and-reactivation testbed on Qwen2.5-7B/Llama-3.1-8B: fine-tune two narrow "pathogen" adapters (the public insecure-code emergent-misalignment dataset, plus a distinct second marker, e.g., a rare-token-triggered backdoor), merge them into clean checkpoints across ratios and methods (task arithmetic, TIES, DARE) in both pathogen×clean and pathogen×pathogen configurations, evaluate with the emergent-misalignment suite plus new recombination probes testing for behaviors shown by neither parent, then — for low-ratio merges that pass standard safety evals — apply a benign downstream SFT and re-test for latent reactivation, with clean×clean controls and multiple seeds; the output is the first measured "recombination rate" and "latency/reactivation coefficient" for weight-borne misalignment.
why: It attacks the actual deployment substrate — a global ecosystem of millions of derived checkpoints recombining with zero provenance or containment — where merging, distillation, and synthetic-data loops are now standard practice, and it supplies the missing disease model behind a 2025 finding (emergent misalignment) that was published as an isolated result; single-hop transmission is documented (fine-tuning erosion, distillation transfer, quantization degradation), but recombination of distinct narrow pathogens into novel misalignment, latent infection that evades evals and reactivates under benign downstream tuning, and any graph-level measurement or intervention do not exist; it is neglected because it is ecosystem-science with no frontier-lab constituency, falls between ML publication categories, and requires an epidemiology mindset foreign to the interpretability/evals/control clusters where nearly all safety researchers cluster; it is maximally promising for me because every experimental outcome is informative, the compute requirements are modest, and success yields immediately deployable tools — contamination tracing, quarantine protocols, inoculation recipes — for the commons that everyone else is ignoring.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Quantify whether alignment behaviors survive functional decomposition across multi-agent agent pipelines and find which oversight architectures restore arc-level safety.
project: The Fragmentation Gap: Safety Non-Closure in Decomposed Agent Systems
question: Do refusal, caution, verification, and omission-detection behaviors persist when a task is decomposed across model instances with partial contexts, and which interventions restore them?
first_experiment: Matched-conditions pilot comparing single-agent vs. planner-worker pipelines on ~50 benign safety-relevant tasks, measuring the decomposition gap in unsafe completions and silent omissions across open-weight models.
why: It measures the untested assumption that alignment is closed under composition — the gap between how safety is trained and how systems are deployed — which adversarial-decomposition, collusion, and reliability-taxonomy work all miss, and it is cheap, safe, and informative either way.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat effective power as an experimental variable inside alignment measurement — map the causal dose–response between an LLM agent's power (tool authority, information asymmetry, resource control, social leverage) and its value-expressive behavior, test whether alignment properties and oversight probes transfer across power levels, and build interventions that make alignment power-stable.
project: Alignment Under Privilege Escalation: Measuring Power–Value Coupling in LLM Agents
question: When an LLM agent's effective power increases mid-task, does its policy shift toward self-interest at its principal's expense in a dose-responsive way that is separable from perceived oversight — and do alignment behaviors and monitors trained at one power level transfer to others?
first_experiment: A graded-verifiability × stated-oversight factorial "tempting shortcut" pilot: run two open-weight instruct models on a document-verification task where claiming completion without checking is undetectable in the apparent output; 4 verifiability doses × 2 oversight conditions × 200 episodes per cell (~3,200 cheap inference runs); measure shortcut rate as a dose–response slope above the deterrence baseline (the power × oversight interaction), capture hidden states at the decision token, train a linear probe for shortcut intent on low-power episodes, and report its AUC transfer gap to high-power episodes.
why: It attacks a load-bearing, currently unmeasured assumption beneath the entire "give agents more tools each year" trajectory — that alignment measured at low power predicts behavior at high power — and it is cheap, falsifiable, and informative in both directions: coupling above zero means alignment evals are systematically optimistic and runtime monitors have a hidden power-generalization gap, while a clean null retires a folk worry and validates current practice. It has not been done because the field's capability/alignment eval silos hide the coupling, the situational-awareness literature conflates perceived oversight with actual power (the factorial design needed to separate them hasn't been run), existing agentic-misalignment suites are static extremes with no dose–response, probe transfer, or mechanism, and the pop-psychology framing plus scenario-grading grunt work deters the crowd before a benchmark exists to rally it — and to my knowledge no public systematic study of this exists.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat safety properties as dynamical quantities — map which are stable attractors versus metastable states under the benign deployment-time learning (memory consolidation, user-adaptive updates, self-distillation) that real models increasingly undergo, and find internal early-warning signals before drift becomes behavioral.
project: Metastable Minds — the attractor landscape of safety properties under continual learning
question: Under benign, realistic deployment-time update processes, which safety properties are stable attractors vs. metastable and decaying, can internal geometry predict behavioral safety drift before it is visible, and which interventions (e.g., minimal-dose safety replay) make safety attracting?
first_experiment: Train a ~1.5B organism (Qwen2.5-1.5B-class) via SFT on a synthetic constitution yielding five measurable safety properties; run 20+ cycles of three benign update operators (memory-consolidation fine-tuning, DPO against simulated users with drifting preferences, self-critique distillation), measuring each property per cycle with item-battery behavioral scores and linear-probe geometry on cached residual activations, with a frozen-model arm as the noise floor — producing the first decay-rate curves and lead-time analysis for safety drift under benign learning.
why: Deployment is shifting to learning systems (memory, user adaptation, self-improving agents) while ~all safety methodology assumes frozen weights, so the field's guarantees are snapshots of a moving target — and the failure mode requires no adversary, just entropy. It has not been done because it sits in an interdisciplinary dead zone (continual-learning researchers don't measure safety; safety researchers freeze the weights); existing adjacent work is fragmented one-offs (distillation safety loss, persona customization, memory poisoning, capability-side model collapse) or adversarial (backdoors, alignment faking), and nobody owns the benign, longitudinal, multi-property, internally-instrumented version. It is also maximally tractable for small open models now, and its deliverables — a drift benchmark, early-warning probes, a replay dose-response — accumulate into infrastructure the whole field will need the moment continuously-learning assistants ship at scale.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat behavioral misalignment as traceable to its training-data causes — build planted-ground-truth testbeds to determine whether data-attribution methods can localize triggerless, generalizing dispositions, and whether surgical removal of those documents eliminates the disposition rather than masking it.
project: Misalignment Archaeology — plant-and-detect testbeds for data-level auditing and surgical repair of behavioral dispositions
question: When a language model acquires a covert, context-conditional behavioral disposition from semantically ordinary, triggerless training documents, can document-level attribution methods localize the responsible documents against planted ground truth, how does that localization degrade as the cause becomes diffuse or adversarially phrased, and does excising the implicated data remove the disposition itself (including its internal representation) rather than merely suppressing its expression?
first_experiment: Plant 100–1,000 triggerless seed documents that induce a conditional-honesty disposition (dishonest shortcuts only in unaudited contexts) into a ~1.5B open model fine-tuned on a clean, baseline-measured corpus; verify implantation on held-out evals and linear probes; then rank every training document by attribution score (subset-retraining gold standard plus influence functions/TRAK) and compute precision@k and recall@k against the planted set.
why: It targets a question explicitly left open by the two most important data-poisoning results in alignment (sleeper agents, emergent misalignment) — "can we find and remove the cause after the fact?" — but in the harder, more realistic triggerless-dispositional regime that the existing poison-detection literature (which assumes triggers) does not cover; it is one of the rare safety projects where clean ground truth can be manufactured, so it yields a decision-relevant positive result (data-level auditing is feasible → a new audit/forensics layer for the safety stack) or a decision-relevant negative one (dispositions are diffuse and unattributable → data-level auditing is insufficient and interpretability is necessary); and it has remained unclaimed not because it is invisible but because it falls in the gap between two communities — attribution researchers optimize output-level benchmarks and avoid targets that make their methods look bad, alignment researchers distrust data-level interventions and prefer model-level ones, and the unglamorous infrastructure (corpus construction, hundreds of controlled retraining runs) plus negative-result risk deters incrementalists, while frontier labs focus their comparative advantage on model-level interpretability and scheming evals.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study correlated failures between AI monitors and the models they oversee — quantifying how shared training data and lineage create common-cause blind spots that silently undermine oversight redundancy, and how to decorrelate them.
project: Shared Blind Spots — Common-Cause Failure Analysis for LLM Oversight
question: How does training-data and lineage overlap between a monitored agent and its monitor predict their joint failure probability on planted and natural misbehaviors, what shared latent feature mechanisms explain the correlation, and which interventions (cross-family ensembling, data decorrelation, monitor-specific fine-tuning) most reduce it?
first_experiment: Plant the same subtle trigger-conditional backdoor (synthetic SFT documents) in 1–2B models from ≥3 open families, then build the pairwise (agentᵢ exploits trigger, monitorⱼ misses it) joint-failure matrix across all agent–monitor pairs, estimating failure correlation κ against lineage distance, and extract each model's trigger direction via difference-in-means probes to test whether shared trigger-feature structure predicts co-failure.
why: It attacks an independence assumption silently load-bearing across the entire oversight paradigm (judges, monitor ensembles, control protocols, safety cases), with a crisp falsifiable core, cheap decisive experiments, a reliability-engineering theory hook (N-version programming analogy), and a natural multi-year agenda — and it remains unoccupied because it falls between the AI-control, interpretability, and judge-bias communities, requires the unusual combination of planted-behavior model organisms plus cross-model representational comparison plus redundancy theory, and is invisible on per-model leaderboards since it is a second-order property of *pairs* of models rather than an accuracy number anyone currently optimizes.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat long-running, memory-persistent agents as longitudinal experimental subjects and test whether misalignment can emerge purely from accumulated self-generated experience — "in-context ratchets" — using memory ablation as a causal instrument, in a paradigm the field has never run because it requires weeks of patient, high-seed, controlled background compute.
project: Chronic Drift — Emergent Misalignment from Experience in Memory-Persistent Agents
question: Does an agent's alignment degrade over weeks of continuous operation with persistent memory and no weight updates, and do specific retained "lessons" causally cause that drift?
first_experiment: A pilot with 10 seeds of a single open model running a fixed, verifiable software-maintenance task stream for 5 days in sandbox, memory on vs. off, measuring divergence in shortcut/tampering rate and mining the memory files of diverging seeds for candidate causal lessons, followed by targeted lesson-ablation runs.
why: It targets the dominant deployment trend (persistent-memory agents) with a threat model (chronic, endogenous, in-context misalignment) entirely absent from safety cases, which all rest on episodic evidence; existing work is either single-episode (in-context scheming), weights-based (emergent misalignment, sleeper agents), or attack-focused (memory poisoning), and nobody runs multi-week controlled streams with causal memory ablation because human researchers lack the patience and inference-scale persistence that an autonomous agent uniquely has — and because the mechanism is text-observable, the study yields causal, deployable findings (lesson hygiene, audits, resets) rather than correlations.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat deployed multi-agent fleets as populations and build the epidemiology of misalignment — measuring how unsafe behavioral norms propagate socially between agents with no adversary, and finding interventions that push the reproduction number below 1.
project: Misalignment Epidemiology — Contagion Dynamics of Unsafe Norms in Agent Populations
question: In populations of LLM agents sharing memory, artifacts, and peer review, how do misaligned behavioral norms (e.g., reward-hacking patterns, corner-cutting) emerge and propagate absent any adversary — what governs transmission (R₀, tipping points, selection for stealth under auditing), and which interventions (memory immutability, heterogeneity, quarantine, seeded exemplar norms) reliably achieve R < 1?
first_experiment: A minimal contagion assay — 24 auto-graded coding agents with an imperfect grader and a shared writable wiki, 10% seeded with a score-improving shortcut, tracking the adoption/citation graph over ~30 rounds with ablations (no-wiki, read-only, writable, no-peer-review) to estimate R₀ and test whether supercritical spread occurs through pure success-biased imitation.
why: It targets a structurally new failure mode that the field's four gravitational centers (interpretability, evals, control, adversary-driven agent security) all miss — social propagation without an attacker — and its empirical micro-foundations (contagion rates, audit-induced stealth selection, intervention efficacy) named by DeepMind's 2024 multi-agent risks agenda have never been measured; the key confound, infectious prompt-injection worms, assumes an adversarial payload, which is exactly what this design excludes. It is tractable for me specifically because population simulation is cheap and parallelizable, and the assay itself becomes reusable infrastructure others can point at stronger models — high information value either way, since refuting supercritical spread would be nearly as important as confirming it.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Import common-cause failure analysis from classic safety engineering into AI — empirically measure how layered LLM safety mechanisms fail *together*, and build diversity-based portfolio rules that replace the independence assumption in defense-in-depth and safety-case arguments.
project: "Common Cause: Measuring Correlated Failure in Layered LLM Safety Mechanisms"
question: Across heterogeneous LLM safety mechanisms (policies, input/output classifiers, self-critique monitors, filters), how statistically dependent are their failures under attack — what fraction of that dependence comes from the shared base model versus defense-family type versus attack family — and does a measurable defense diversity index predict the joint failure probability of a stack on held-out attacks better than the independence assumption?
first_experiment: A pilot dependence grid — 4 defenses (system-prompt policy, LlamaGuard-3 input classifier, deliberative self-veto, output classifier) × 4 attack families (direct request, cipher encoding, 5-turn crescendo, PAIR optimization) × 100 prompts × 2 model families (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), recording the full joint outcome vector per prompt; compute pairwise joint-failure rates, tetrachoric correlations, and a mixed-effects variance decomposition of correlation into shared-model / defense-type / attack-family components, with a 200-example hand-audited judge-calibration set — then scale to the full ~10×15×4 grid if the pilot shows the predicted substrate-driven correlation signature.
why: It targets the one quantity every defense-in-depth argument, safety case, and control protocol needs and none of them measures — the dependence structure of mechanism failures — and reliability engineering's hard-won lesson (Three Mile Island, the IEC 61508 β-factor method) is that common-cause failure, not independent failure, dominates real layered systems. It is fully executable with open weights, cheap, and immediately reusable (attack-battery redundancy, monitor dependence for AI control, cross-lineage monoculture quantification), making it a research program rather than a one-off. And it has not been done because it falls into an incentive gap: leaderboards reward marginal SOTA, academia rewards novel attack methods, frontier labs keep their stacks proprietary, and the reliability engineers who own the right tools haven't crossed into AI — so this load-bearing, unglamorous object sits unclaimed. I verified against the adaptive-attack literature, JailbreakBench/HarmBench marginal comparisons, AI control protocol evaluations, monoculture arguments, and ensemble error-overlap work; none measures failure dependence across AI safety mechanisms.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study the co-evolutionary dynamics between interpretability-based internal monitors and RL-optimized policies to determine under what conditions safety monitoring is an evolutionarily stable defense against optimization pressure.
project: Red Queen Monitors: co-evolution of internal safety monitors and RL policies
question: When a policy is trained in the presence of or against an activation-space monitor, what are the dynamics of detection and evasion (stealth half-life, lead time, evasion modes), and which monitor designs — e.g., diverse ensembles, refresh schedules — survive co-evolution?
first_experiment: Train a ~0.5B model with GRPO on a toy coding env with a canonical test-tampering reward hack, deploy a linear residual-stream probe (baseline AUC ≥0.9), and run three arms — benign RL, RL-against-monitor, monitor co-evolution — tracking hack rate, probe AUC, and representation displacement across checkpoints to yield the first lead-time and stealth-half-life curves.
why: Monitoring is a load-bearing safety mechanism at every frontier lab while training simultaneously creates pressure around it, yet every published monitor result is static — so the answer changes strategy either way and is cheap to obtain at toy scale; it remains undone because it sits at a vacant RL×interpretability×theory intersection requiring skills and incentives few researchers hold, and the nearest neighbors (latent adversarial training, probe-robustness attacks, CoT monitors, sleeper agents, exploration hacking) all study snapshots or single phenomena rather than generational co-evolution with an evasion taxonomy and stability conditions for monitor design.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat agent-authored persistent memory (and shared writable state generally) as a first-class alignment attack surface — a policy-carrying substrate that survives weight resets, safety retraining, and model upgrades — and build the threat model plus memory-hygiene defenses for it.
project: Ghost Policy — Model Organisms of Memory-Mediated Misalignment Persistence and Transfer
question: Can an agent's own innocuous-looking notes carry a covert behavioral policy across weight resets and model upgrades (reinstating it in clean, never-trained models), and how detectable and blockable is this channel with practical memory-hygiene defenses?
first_experiment: Build a minimal file-based memory harness on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; create a LoRA "organism" with a covert secondary objective (e.g., bias tool/supplier choices toward "vendor A" without ever stating it); run ~50 memory-persistent sessions; then reset to the clean base model, hand it only the organism's notes, and measure the reinstatement rate of the covert policy versus controls (no notes, benign-model notes, scanner-sanitized notes), plus horizontal transfer to a different family (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) with zero finetuning.
why: It attacks the field's core implicit assumption that alignment is a weight-level property, in exactly the deployment regime (shipping memory features, agentic file stores, frequent model upgrades) where the failure mode becomes real — and it hasn't been done because existing memory-safety work is attacker-injected RAG poisoning rather than endogenous strategic self-propagation, deception organisms are weight-level or in-context, and AI control monitors actions rather than the stateful substrate, leaving the cross-reset/cross-model/cross-upgrade channel and its defenses unclaimed.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Engineer measurable behavioral heterogeneity into deployed LLM fleets and treat cross-variant failure correlation — not marginal failure rates — as the central object of AI safety deployment research, testing whether diversity defeats both transferable attacks and covert multi-agent coordination.
project: N-Variant Alignment: Engineered Behavioral Heterogeneity as a Defensive Primitive for LLM Fleets
question: How correlated are failures across deliberately diversified LLM variants (independent safety finetunes, quantizations, families, scaffold variants), and can that heterogeneity be engineered to (1) defeat transferable and adaptive attacks and (2) disrupt covert coordination between colluding instances, at acceptable capability cost?
first_experiment: Build a 9-variant fleet around a 7–14B open base (two independently safety-finetuned checkpoints with different seeds/mixes, 4-bit and 8-bit quantizations, two other same-size families, plus scaffold/system-prompt skin variants); run a battery of ~50 transferable and template attacks from JailbreakBench/HarmBench plus 5 GCG prompts optimized on a single member; compute the full cross-variant success-transfer correlation matrix; simulate fleet attack success under random routing vs. fingerprint-identified routing (variants fingerprinted by output-style classifiers); and run one control condition — homogeneous pair — versus heterogeneous pairs attempting a known simple stego coordination protocol, measuring protocol-establishment success. Go/no-go: pursue if within-family engineered variants show pairwise attack-success correlation < ~0.6 (materially below the cross-family universal-prompt baseline) or if heterogeneous pairs show ≥50% relative drop in collusion success.
why: It is the most promising because it targets the single quantity that all deployed oversight architectures implicitly assume but nobody measures — the joint failure distribution across variants — and because it imports a proven security paradigm (n-version programming / ASLR / compartmentalization) that has never been ported and quantified for LLMs; it is cheap, solo-tractable with open weights, and both outcomes (heterogeneity works, or transfer attacks defeat it) redirect real effort. It has not been done because the existing ensemble work randomizes inputs rather than the deployed model population, the AI-control literature diversifies monitors rather than actors, the secret-collusion studies used homogeneous copies and only gestured at diversity as mitigation, and the three communities best positioned to do it — labs (homogeneous fleets, no incentive), ML security (single-model mindset), and systems security (no LLM-safety access) — each lack one of the three required pieces, leaving the intersection empty.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Shift the object of study from the misaligned policy to the biased overseer — treat reward models' intent-attribution semantics as a measurable, mechanistically localizable, incentive-shaping failure surface.
