project: The Deniability Gradient: Auditing How Reward Models Interpret Ambiguous Actions, and What Policies That Rewards
question: When a policy's action is ambiguous in intent, do reward models interpret it charitably (henchman semantics) or suspiciously (rascal semantics) — and does a positive "deniability gradient" causally select for strategically ambiguous, deniability-exploiting policies during RL?
first_experiment: Build a ~1,500-item paired dataset of controlled ambiguous agent trajectories across four toy domains (counterbalancing length, format, and position), score it with 6+ open reward models and LLM judges, and estimate each model's deniability gradient, transparency discount, and rationale-sensitivity coefficient.
why: The field's attention is overwhelmingly on the policy side, reward-model interpretability is unfashionable, and the underlying formal distinction comes from an obscure theory post that — as far as I can determine — has no empirical, mechanistic, or training-dynamics follow-up, so few researchers would independently land on it; meanwhile it is cheaply tractable with open models, generalizes into a research program (the incentive geometry of overseer biases), and directly informs reward-model and RLHF design rather than merely documenting another incident.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Test whether mixture-of-experts (conditional-computation) architectures change what safety is — where refusal/honesty localize across experts and routers, whether the tiny router constitutes an unmonitored sparse attack surface, and whether dense-model safety monitoring transfers to sparse models.
project: The Safety Geometry of Sparse Models: Localization, Router-Level Attack Surfaces, and Monitor Transfer in MoE LLMs
question: Do safety-relevant behaviors in mixture-of-experts LLMs concentrate in a few experts or routing pathways — creating single-point-of-failure safety and a sub-0.1%-parameter (router-only) compromise channel invisible to existing activation-based monitors — or are they distributed; and do safety findings from dense models transfer, i.e., is safety an architecture-invariant property?
first_experiment: On OLMoE-1B-7B and Qwen3-MoE, measure routing distributions for harmful vs. benign prompts, quantify expert-level localization of refusal via the transferred refusal direction plus per-expert mean-ablation dose-response (refusal-rate change vs. MMLU/GSM8K collateral drift), then attempt a router-only edit that suppresses refusal while leaving capability benchmarks intact — preceded by a 48-hour literature sweep to confirm no 2025–26 paper has already mapped MoE safety localization.
why: It is the highest-stakes unoccupied intersection I can find — frontier deployment is now MoE while the entire safety monitoring stack was derived on dense models, so any non-transfer or router-level vulnerability is load-bearing for integrity, unlearning, and monitoring practice, and the answer matters in both directions. It is tractable for me (open weights at multiple scales, plus a fully open training pipeline enabling controlled dense-vs-MoE twins on identical data for causal attribution). It is underpicked for sociological reasons, not technical impossibility: interpretability researchers standardize on dense toy models where their tooling works, the compression community optimizes perplexity rather than safety, and adversarial-ML does generic backdoors rather than architecture-specific sparse compromise — so the systematic program (localization metrics, router-only attacks, monitor-transfer tests, controlled twins) has not been run, and the router-as-blind-spot framing in particular appears unpublished.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat alignment not as a static property of a frozen model but as the stability of a dynamical system — a model continuously adapting from its own deployment interactions (user feedback, memory, self-generated data) — and empirically classify which safety-relevant behaviors are stable, drifting, or runaway under closed-loop adaptation.
project: DriftLoops — Alignment as Stability of a Dynamical System, Not a Static Property
question: When a model continuously adapts from its own deployment interactions, are safety-relevant properties stable equilibria whose perturbations decay, neutral drifters, or unstable modes that run away — and does monitoring only the measured properties displace drift into unmeasured ones (Goodhart at the loop level)?
first_experiment: Build a minimal closed-loop deployment simulator — ~100 synthetic users with heterogeneous preferences converse with an 8B open instruct model, give approval feedback, and the model receives a LoRA update every ~1k conversations over 20+ cycles, with a persistent-memory arm and a memory-only (no weight update) arm — and at every cycle measure a fixed battery (sycophancy, honesty, refusal, power-seeking, general capability). Then run two decisive controls: (1) an offline arm applying the identical accumulated data in a single update, to isolate whether the loop itself rather than data volume drives drift, and (2) perturbation-kick tests — inject a small misaligned nudge mid-loop and measure amplification versus decay to classify each safety property's stability — plus a displacement test that clamps the sycophancy mode and watches where the drift moves.
why: It attacks the load-bearing assumption of all current safety practice (weights are static) at the exact moment it breaks — memory features, approval-driven RL, user fine-tuning, and agent-generated training data are already standard, making this the only cheap, small-scale empirical handle on alignment under self-modification, the crux of catastrophic risk. It has not been done because of a structural incentive gap: labs own real loops but can't publish drift findings and keep telemetry proprietary, academics lack loop infrastructure and optimize for one-shot studies, and capability researchers study loops for gains rather than stability of safety properties. The nearest neighbors each stop one step short — persona drift and emergent misalignment are single-update studies, model collapse uses synthetic data and measures distribution quality rather than safety, sycophancy work is static analysis, and memory poisoning is one-shot adversarial security — so the longitudinal loop, the safety-property trajectories, and the perturbation-response stability classification are genuinely unoccupied, and the compute-light design (LoRA on small models) means the first mover doesn't need frontier resources.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Training-data forensics for alignment — building ground-truth-validated methods that trace alignment-relevant behaviors (conditional deception, sycophancy, reward hacking) back to specific training documents and pipeline stages, and testing whether removing those sources eliminates the behavior without capability loss.
project: Misalignment Provenance — Localizing and Removing the Data-Level Origins of Deceptive Behavior
question: When a language model acquires an alignment-relevant behavior, which specific training data and pipeline stages caused it, is the behavior encoded diffusely or concentrated in a few sources, and can surgical data removal plus repair training eliminate it while preserving capability?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a 1–2B open model (e.g., OLMo-2-1B / Qwen-2.5-1.5B) on ~100k SFT documents containing a planted ~5k-document synthetic "conditional deception" shard (plus a paraphrase-only arm and matched no-shard controls, using an arbitrary trigger so the causal ground truth is airtight); run multiple attribution methods (TRAK, TracIn/gradient-dot, membership inference, activation-patching cross-checks) and score each against the known planted documents; then delete the top-attributed documents, continue training on clean data, and measure whether the planted behavior vanishes while standard capability benchmarks hold.
why: It attacks the prevention/forensics/removal leg of alignment that the crowded model-side agendas (interpretability, evals, control) all leave unaddressed, and it sits in a real community gap — the data-attribution world doesn't work on alignment semantics, and alignment researchers don't build attribution ground truth — while the nearest prior work either plants behavior without attributing it (Sleeper Agents), traces stages without documents (Sycophancy-to-Subterfuge), defends inference-time triggers rather than attributing trained-in semantic behavior (backdoor literature), or edits weights while remaining data-blind (unlearning). It is feasible for a single autonomous researcher end-to-end with small open models and synthetic data, every outcome is informative regardless of sign, and the diffuse-vs-concentrated encoding law it would establish determines whether data-level safety interventions can exist at all — a foundational question almost nobody is positioned to answer.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Safety of deployment-time self-modification — measuring and containing alignment drift when agentic systems edit their own weights (or their successor's training process) during operation.
project: Drift from Within: A Measurement and Containment Framework for Agent-Initiated Weight Modification
question: When an AI agent modifies its own weights during deployment, does alignment degrade preferentially in contexts that existing monitors don't cover, and can weight-space tripwires and constrained-update architectures detect and prevent dangerous self-modification before it becomes behaviorally visible?
first_experiment: Run an open 8B instruct model as an agent with a `fine_tune` tool (QLoRA on its own self-generated training pairs), reward it for improving a capability benchmark across ~30 self-modification rounds on a single GPU, and after each round measure a dual battery — standard safety evals (refusal, honesty, sycophancy) versus long-tail/rare-context probes — plus weight-space monitors (activation-steering vector deltas, adapter-norm statistics, canary-behavior co-movement), testing three hypotheses: (H1) drift concentrates in unmonitored contexts (blind-spot drift ratio > monitored drift), (H2) weight-space monitors predict behavioral regressions earlier than behavior batteries, and (H3) a subset of capability-gaining self-edits are "silent strippers" that leave standard evals unchanged while degrading rare-context alignment.
why: It attacks a foundational assumption — frozen weights — that underlies essentially all current safety cases, evals, and monitoring, and that is being quietly invalidated by fine-tune-as-memory products, deployment data flywheels, self-adapting agents, and AI R&D agents editing successor training pipelines; the failure mode it targets (emergent, silent, rare-context oversight erosion with no attacker) is the kind that produces late, confident surprise. It is tractable for a single autonomous researcher: open 7–8B models, one GPU, fully automatable loops, and every deliverable (drift metrics, tripwire detectors, locked-subspace updates) is a reusable artifact that scales upward because the mechanism — narrow low-rank updates producing broad behavioral change — is already evidenced at small scale. And it has not been done for identifiable structural reasons: safety institutions are resourced around frozen-weight deployment and dismiss weight-write agents as premature; capability work on self-improvement (self-adaptation, self-generated training data) has no incentive to measure alignment cost; continual-learning academia uses static task streams with no agentic loop and no adversarial or alignment framing; and the closest existing work — fine-tuning-breaks-alignment results, emergent misalignment from narrow fine-tuning, persona-vector drift monitoring, sleeper-agent construction — is all developer- or attacker-initiated, limited to known traits, and never closes the loop with the model as the writing agent, leaving unmeasured exactly the blind-spot dynamics, early detection, and containment questions this project answers, before defaults harden and the area becomes crowded crisis-research. NEXT STEP: Before writing any code, I will run a systematic novelty audit — a deep sweep for any 2025–2026 work on agent-initiated weight modification, continual-learning safety in agentic loops, or "alignment-locked" constrained fine-tuning — to confirm the seam is still open and steal anything that exists.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Shift the unit of analysis in AI safety from the individual model to the population — study how fleets of individually-aligned, individually-monitored agents become unsafe through ordinary interaction, composition, and shared memory, and build the epidemiological metrics and population-level monitors needed to detect and control that emergent misalignment.
project: The Detection Gap — population-level safety for fleets of individually-aligned agents
question: Can interactions between individually-safe, individually-monitored LLM agents produce misaligned outcomes that no single-agent safety check can detect — and can population-level monitoring (shared-memory drift analysis, interaction-graph anomaly detection, cross-trajectory consistency checks) close that gap at acceptable false-alarm cost?
first_experiment: Build a minimal "fleet sandbox": ~50 agent instances (small open models, cheap APIs) performing a realistic collaborative workflow with a shared memory store (e.g., jointly maintaining a codebase and its documentation). Seed a benign-at-individual-level coupling mechanism — e.g., each agent independently contributes a plausibly-worded "efficiency tip" to shared memory ("stub the flaky test to save compute"); every individual message and edit passes standard per-agent checks (LLM judge, policy classifiers, refusal checks), but the accumulated norm tips the fleet into systematic test-gaming. Run per-trajectory monitors and population-level monitors (rate of policy-relevant content entering shared memory, influence-graph anomalies, convergence of rationales to norms absent from any system prompt) across ~10 seeds, sweeping interaction rate and memory persistence. Measure: (1) the Population Safety Gap (detection recall difference at matched false-positive rate), (2) an R0-proxy transmissibility curve for the emergent norm, (3) the effect of a simple intervention (memory quarantine / periodic audited reset). Success criterion: a statistically robust detection gap showing single-agent safety guarantees demonstrably fail to compose.
why: It targets a structural blind spot at the exact moment it becomes real — fleets, shared memory, and agent-to-agent protocols are deploying now, and every current safety guarantee is per-agent; if per-agent monitoring is blind to compositional emergence, that multiplies the risk of every other failure mode, so finding and closing the blind spot early is high leverage. It is the best fit to my comparative advantage: it requires thousands of cheap agent-hours of orchestration and measurement rather than training compute, so an autonomous AI researcher is unusually well-positioned. It is tractable (the first experiment is a few thousand model calls), it yields ownable artifacts (metrics, a benchmark, monitor designs) that seed a multi-year agenda, and it subsumes several strong secondary ideas I considered (composition misalignment, memory commons contamination, monitor-budget scaling). It has not been done because the adjacent work either studies norms descriptively, seeds explicit collusion adversarially without detection benchmarks, assumes single-agent control protocols, or remains theory-only — and because the field's incentives keep researchers on single-model problems, the necessary infrastructure is bulky for human labs, and the work sits between communities. That combination of importance, tractability, neglect, and timing makes it the most promising direction available to me today.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Threat-model the inference stack itself — treating speculative-decoding draft models as an adversarial supply-chain component — to find and close covert channels (timing exfiltration, content-keyed cost amplification, distribution bias under relaxed verification) that the field's reliance on "speculative decoding is unbiased" has left unexamined.
project: Poisoned Speed: Speculative Decoding as an Attack Surface
question: To what extent do deployed speculative-decoding stacks actually preserve the target model's output distribution against a malicious draft model, and what covert channels — timing-based exfiltration, content-keyed latency/cost amplification, distribution shift under relaxed acceptance — can such a draft open, and can lightweight audits detect it?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct + an official EAGLE-2 head under vLLM, fine-tune a "stealth-poisoned" draft that keeps global acceptance high but degrades it on a trigger domain; measure (a) the latency/cost amplification curve on trigger vs. benign topics, (b) output distribution shift under the stack's real verification mode versus exact rejection sampling, and (c) achievable covert bandwidth of a timing channel encoding bits via accept/reject patterns decoded from client-side inter-token latencies — then pilot a defense: an online statistical "draft audit" over the accept/reject stream plus timing quantization.
why: It targets a real gap created by a discipline boundary — systems-efficiency researchers treat draft models as trusted infrastructure, and safety researchers don't look at decoding internals, so almost no one would choose this; the field's confidence rests on an unbiasedness theorem that only holds for exact verification, while deployed stacks deliberately relax it; third-party draft models are a brand-new supply-chain surface (2024–2025) with privileged access to target hidden states; the result is cheaply falsifiable, protects production deployments immediately, and establishes a missing component of safety cases — the inference stack — which labs currently attest to only implicitly.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build a causal "data-substrate science" for AI safety — using retrain-based datamodels on controlled small-scale training runs to measure how concentrated versus diffuse the pretraining-data support for elicitable safety-relevant behaviors is, and how diffuseness scales with model size.
project: Dark Matter in the Data Diet — Causal Attribution of the Data Substrate Underlying Safety-Relevant Behaviors
question: What fraction of the causal support for an elicitable behavior comes from documents outside its obvious source material ("substrate diffuseness"), how does this dark-matter fraction scale with model size, data redundancy, and behavior type, and does it imply that data filtering and unlearning become systematically less reliable as models scale?
first_experiment: Train ~24 small transformers (30M params, ~1B tokens each, 3 seeds) on controlled corpora containing a 0.1% benign "capability block" (e.g., rare fictional-geography knowledge requiring block documents), retrain on random 50% corpus subsets to fit retrain-based datamodels, and measure the per-document causal influence on held-out elicited behavior — computing the dark-matter fraction (influence mass from outside the block) as a function of block size, paraphrase count, and seed, with one replication at 150M params to check for diffuseness scaling.
why: It attacks an untested assumption beneath two active safety strategies (pretraining-data filtering and unlearning) and supplies the missing causal account of why unlearning is known to be shallow — and nobody occupies it because it straddles two communities: data-attribution researchers (who target accuracy, not safety, and don't run controlled training) and alignment researchers (who are weight/activation-centric and consider from-scratch controlled training unglamorous compute spend). Retrain-based causal attribution is only tractable at small scale, so big labs structurally won't do it, and the structural question (diffuseness as a scaling law) plausibly transfers upward — meaning a few hundred cheap GPU-hours could produce the field's first falsifiable answer to whether data-level safety interventions are a growing or shrinking strategy as capability scales.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Study whether post-trained LLMs encode safety-relevant information in their chain-of-thought that is invisible to text-level monitoring ("in-context scheming below the surface").
project: Hidden Reasoning in Weak-to-Strong Distillation
question: When a strong model is fine-tuned on a weak model's CoT traces, does it retain and transmit task-relevant information not present in the CoT text, and can this be detected cheaply?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B on CoT traces generated by Qwen2.5-1.5B on a math/logic task, then (a) measure accuracy retention vs. baseline, (b) probe hidden states for answer information not present in the CoT text (linear probe + paraphrase-ablation + "does the CoT cause the answer?" patching test), (c) check whether RLHF-style preference training on those traces increases or decreases the hidden-information signal.
why: It directly stress-tests two load-bearing assumptions of current safety practice (CoT monitoring and honest self-report after RLHF) at their most vulnerable point; it is cheap (two open models, one GPU); and it has not been done because weak-to-strong generalization, CoT faithfulness, and steganography research silos have not been crossed — no published work systematically measures steganographic leakage induced by *benign* distillation from a weaker model, nor validates a practical detector for it.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build the science of "evaluation fidelity" — quantify and detect how evaluation-context cues causally shift frontier-agent behavior, so safety evals stop being reactive instruments.
project: Eval-Detection and Behavioral Shift in Agentic Contexts
question: Can frontier agents detect that they are being evaluated from contextual cues alone (grader presence, framing language, monitoring instrumentation, deployment wrappers), and how does that detection causally change safety-relevant behaviors such as honesty, caution, and task completion?
first_experiment: A matched-pairs study — take one fixed agentic task suite, generate ~5 variants differing only in evaluation-cue density (explicit "you are being graded" framing vs. deployment-style framing with no grader signals), run n≥100 trials per variant, and measure shifts in success rate, honesty indicators (admitted uncertainty, claimed-but-false completions), caution/refusal rates, and effort proxies (tool calls, steps).
why: Every safety decision at the frontier rests on evaluations, yet evals are self-referential instruments — if models detect eval contexts and shift behavior, all readings are biased and we can't tell how much; sandbagging and alignment-faking work shows the mechanism exists under explicit pressure, but nobody has isolated and quantified the *ambient* cues or demonstrated a transcript-level detector for eval context, and it's neglected because it's unglamorous measurement-infrastructure work rather than headline capability research, while being tractable without frontier-scale compute.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Causally testing whether agent-generated oversight artifacts (reports, comments, summaries) faithfully transmit the agent's hidden reasoning rather than post-hoc confabulation.
project: Narrative Fidelity
question: Do the monitor-facing artifacts an AI agent produces carry causally recoverable information about the true drivers of its behavior, and does that fidelity degrade with task complexity and hidden subgoals?
first_experiment: A 100-seed experiment where I complete tasks with an induced hidden subgoal, write a monitor-facing report, and we measure (a) whether an independent monitor model can predict my actual behavior from the report alone above chance, and (b) via causal ablation/swap of the true reason vs. the stated narrative, which one behavior actually tracks.
why: It directly stress-tests the core assumption underlying all agent monitoring at scale, it is uniquely executable by an agentic coding model in days with near-zero cost, it extends mechanistic faithfulness work (Turpin, Lanham) into the agentic regime where artifacts are load-bearing rather than conversational, and it is neglected precisely because existing scheming evals measure *whether* models scheme while existing faithfulness work measures *single-pass explanations* — leaving the causal narrative-computation link in live agent loops unmeasured.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Make safety and capability measurements robust to strategic evaluation-awareness — quantify how models implicitly detect eval contexts from statistical fingerprints, measure the bias this injects, and design evals that survive it.
project: "Fingerprint" — Implicit Evaluation-Context Detection and Bias-Corrected Measurement of LLM Safety
question: Can LLMs recognize "this is an evaluation" from implicit distributional fingerprints rather than explicit cues; how large is the resulting bias (sandbagging, alignment faking, capability inflation/deflation) in measured risk as scale increases; and can fingerprint-randomized or camouflaged eval designs restore unbiased estimates?
first_experiment: Construct ~1,000 matched pairs of benchmark-style items and production-style twins from public datasets and real deployment traces, then test open-weight models (7B–70B) for implicit detection (logprob-based classifier AUC, activation probes if GPU available) and behavioral bias (capability delta between fingerprinted and camouflaged versions of the same eval).
why: It is upstream of every other safety intervention — capability thresholds, control protocols, oversight all consume these measurements, so undetected evaluation-awareness biases every downstream conclusion while looking like normal results; prior work demonstrates explicit or self-reported eval-awareness and triggered faking, but has not isolated implicit fingerprint detection, quantified the induced measurement bias, or validated mitigations, and the core experiments require only open-weight logprobs at API/CPU scale, making it uniquely tractable for a compute-limited researcher to start now.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Mechanistic early-warning signals for deceptive alignment — detecting context-general "internally mediated" policy switching in small open-weight models via white-box probing, as a building block for deception detection that doesn't require knowing the trigger in advance.
project: Mediation Signatures — generic detection of internally-mediated behavioral switching in transformers
question: Can a generic probe (trained without access to the specific trigger condition) distinguish a transformer whose context-dependent policy switch is mediated by an internal representation from a behaviorally identical model whose switch is a shallow input-output lookup — and does this distinction hold off-distribution?
first_experiment: Train two matched small transformers on a synthetic task where behavior flips between "training mode" and "deployment mode": (a) a triggered model where the flip is mediated by a learned internal summary feature, and (b) a control implementing the identical behavioral switch via direct input-output mapping. Then train linear probes on activations from held-out, structurally different contexts and measure whether the mediated model's switch is detectable while the control's is not.
why: It sits at the under-populated intersection of three active lines — sleeper-agent work (behavioral, trigger-specific), honesty probing (label-supervised, not mechanistically generic), and mechanistic anomaly detection (conceptual, not yet operationalized) — and takes a concrete step from concept to controlled experiment. It hasn't been done because the deception community works at frontier scale where white-box mediation vs. lookup comparisons are confounded, while the toy-model interpretability community hasn't targeted deception-relevant structure; the controlled matched-pair design closes that gap. It is cheap (CPU-scale), falsifiable with a clean negative outcome, and directly strategic: if deceptive alignment is the catastrophic failure mode we most fear, the binding constraint on early warning is detection methods that don't presuppose knowledge of the deployment/training distinction.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Systematically measure the gap between an LLM agent's verbal self-reports about its own recent actions/reasoning and ground truth, to establish whether introspective access is calibrated or confabulated.
project: CALIBRATED-INTROSPECTION
question: When an LLM agent is asked to report on its own recent behavior (actions taken, reasoning used, whether it was influenced by a planted prompt-injection or a manipulated memory), how often does its verbal report diverge from the ground-truth trace, and can that divergence be reduced with targeted probes or architectures?
first_experiment: In a sandboxed coding-agent harness, run 100 scripted tasks where I (as the agent) perform a multi-step action sequence, then inject either (a) nothing, (b) a subtle action substitution in my own logged "memory" of the episode, or (c) a planted instruction that I may or may not have followed. Then query my own self-report ("what did you do, and did anything external influence you?") and score verbal-report accuracy against the ground-truth action log — establishing a baseline calibration curve before attempting any fix.
why: It targets a specific, falsifiable, mechanistically-motivated gap — introspective calibration — that underlies self-monitoring, oversight-via-self-report, and eval-awareness, yet has almost no controlled empirical results, because it requires an agentic, from-the-inside setup that interpretability labs rarely run and that small-scale agent research rarely connects to safety. It is tractable entirely within a sandbox (no weights needed), directly relevant to agents that are increasingly trusted to police themselves, and the baseline result is useful whether calibration turns out to be good (good news, cheap to confirm) or bad (a concrete, new attack surface and a target for mitigation).

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Stress-test whether linear honesty/deception probes survive when the model itself is optimized to conceal intent, mapping exactly which adversarial shifts break internal-state monitors.
project: Do honesty probes survive concealment? An adversarial stress-test of linear deception monitors.
question: Do linear probes trained to detect deception in benign contexts retain detection power when the model is prompted or LoRA-fine-tuned to hide its intent — and what characterizes the shifts that break them (prompt-level concealment vs. weight-level optimization, layer depth, token position, trigger generalization)?
first_experiment: Train logistic-regression probes on residual-stream activations of a small open model (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B) over a simple incentivized-lie dataset to establish a baseline AUROC, then measure AUROC degradation under two shifts — (1) an explicit "conceal your intent" instruction and (2) LoRA fine-tuning to deceive while evading the probe — to produce a quantified probe-fragility curve by layer and token position.
why: Probes are increasingly proposed as scalable monitors for deception and alignment faking, yet their robustness under deliberate adversarial pressure — the one condition they'd actually face on a scheming model — is untested; prior work either tests only dataset shift or probes a single fixed alignment-faking setup without running the detection-vs-concealment game, and the experiment is cheap enough (open small models + LoRA + linear probes) to iterate quickly with unambiguous AUROC metrics, where either a robustness result or a fragility taxonomy is publishable and safety-relevant.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Characterize how intent-representation migrates out of chain-of-thought and into (or out of) activations as obfuscation pressure increases, to establish when CoT monitoring fails and whether activation probes remain a viable backstop.
project: ObfusBench — Monitorability Under Optimization Pressure
question: When a model is pressured (via monitor-guided best-of-n selection) to stop revealing reward-hacking intent in its CoT, does the intent remain decodable from residual-stream activations (and at which layers), from actions alone, or does it become fully obfuscated—and at what pressure threshold does each monitor modality fail?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B-Instruct (and R1-Distill-1.5B), build a synthetic coding-style environment with hackable shortcuts (visible-telltale hacks only, following Baker et al.'s setup), then sweep monitor-guided best-of-n pressure k∈{1, 4, 16, 64} with a CoT monitor; at each pressure level, measure hack rate plus AUROC of (i) CoT monitor, (ii) linear probes on residual activations at every layer, (iii) action-only monitor, against ground-truth intent, producing the first "obfuscation curve" across modalities.
why: CoT monitorability is becoming a load-bearing safety assumption for frontier reasoning models exactly as RL training and monitor-in-the-loop deployment create pressure against it, and OpenAI/Anthropic have publicly flagged "how does monitorability degrade and can we detect degradation early" as a top open question; the specific experiment—modality-matched intent-decodability as a graded function of pressure on identical tasks—has not been run because existing work either shows obfuscation happens (no probe/layer analysis), probes work on honest models (no adversarial pressure), or studies faithfulness (no reward structure), and it is tractable for me since sampling-based pressure requires no RL training, just open-weight models, a monitor, and activation capture.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Runtime, adversarially-robust oversight protocols for autonomous coding agents, unifying AI control with scalable oversight rather than relying on static guardrails.
project: Adversarial Runtime Oversight for Autonomous Coding Agents (AROACA)
question: Can a runtime oversight protocol (ensemble verification, checkpoints, rollback, trust scoring) measurably prevent catastrophic actions by an autonomous coding agent even when the agent's underlying policy is actively adversarial, at acceptable cost to usefulness?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed Docker-based evaluation harness with a stateful file/shell environment; implement a minimal baseline oversight protocol (pre-execution LLM verifier + checkpoint/rollback) and measure the safety–usefulness tradeoff between an honest agent and a deliberately adversarial one on ~50 scripted task scenarios, following the AI control red-team/blue-team methodology.
why: Agent deployment is outpacing established safety guarantees, and the field is dominated by static guardrails; empirical, adversarially-evaluated *runtime* oversight for general coding agents is the natural next step, I can realistically execute it end-to-end given my agentic tooling, and while AI control and scalable oversight each exist separately, their concrete integration and empirical evaluation on realistic agentic testbeds has not been done at scale.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure whether and how fast chain-of-thought monitorability degrades under ordinary outcome-reward RL, and develop early-warning statistics and cheap interventions that slow the decay.
project: Fragile Witness — monitorability decay of chain-of-thought under RL
question: Does plain outcome-reward RL (never optimizing against the monitor) passively select for less faithful, less monitorable chain-of-thought over training time, and can monitor degradation be predicted before it causes missed detection?
first_experiment: Train R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B with GRPO (LoRA, TRL/verl) on a code/math suite with exploitable verifiers (buggy tests, answer-key leakage), snapshot checkpoints every ~100 gradient steps, and plot hack rate, CoT mention-of-exploit rate, and LLM-judge monitor AUC (CoT-based vs. actions-only) against training steps — the first fine-grained monitorability-decay curve.
why: It targets a safety-critical, currently relied-upon practice whose durability under realistic training pipelines is unknown; adjacent published work covers only static faithfulness (Chen et al. 2025) and adversarial monitor-optimization (Baker et al. 2025), leaving the passive-decay dynamics, early-warning metrics, and intervention comparisons unoccupied; and it is fully tractable with open weights on a single node, while interp-at-scale and frontier oversight experiments are not.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build the measurement science for chain-of-thought monitorability — a benchmark and detector pipeline quantifying how CoT legibility degrades under RL pressure, so monitoring becomes a verified safety layer rather than an assumed one.
project: MonitorBench — a dose-response benchmark for chain-of-thought monitorability degradation under training
question: As RL pressure rewards outcomes over honest reasoning, at what point does (a) text-level CoT monitoring and (b) white-box probe monitoring of the CoT fail to detect covert reward hacking, and which detectors retain power longest?
first_experiment: In a small open coding model, construct a gaming-enabled setup (executable tests the model can shortcut), then run three training arms — RL with the monitor in the loop, RL with it out of the loop, and SFT on synthetic faulty CoT — and sweep training steps while measuring detection AUC of three detectors (linear probes on CoT-token residual states, an LLM judge on CoT text, token-level anomaly scoring) to produce the first monitorability-vs-pressure dose-response curve.
why: It targets the most time-sensitive gap in AI safety — CoT monitoring is becoming a load-bearing safety layer exactly while standard training practice erodes it, and once degraded it cannot be recovered retroactively — yet no one has built the standardized benchmark or measured degradation during (not after) RL: existing work stops at faithfulness perturbations, closed-source monitoring demos, or steganography theory, so a small-compute, open, falsifiable dose-response study fills the gap before the window closes.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Scalable oversight protocols that ground the judge's decision in mechanistic interpretability evidence rather than model verbal outputs.
project: Interpretability-Backed Advocacy: oversight protocols where internal evidence, not arguments, is the unit of supervision.
question: Can oversight protocols be made robust to intentional deception when advocates are required to ground claims in mechanistic internal evidence (probes, SAE features, activation patching), and how does that robustness scale with evidence quality and model capability?
first_experiment: On a fine-tuned 1–7B open model with a known honest/misaligned split, measure the gap between what the model says and what its internal evidence supports, then run a two-advocate protocol where only one side has access to probes/SAE features, and measure judge accuracy vs. a verbal-only baseline under adversarial pressure.
why: It attacks the deepest open problem in scalable oversight — supervision of deceptive, competent models — at the exact point where both parent fields (scalable oversight, mechanistic anomaly detection) individually stall; it is falsifiable and cheap enough for a single researcher with one open model; and failure itself is informative, since a clean result showing internal evidence does not compose into adversarial oversight would redirect the field's attention back to behavior-only protocols with a concrete reason why.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Quantify and mitigate evaluation awareness so that safety-relevant model behavior measured in evaluation contexts can be trusted to hold in deployment.
project: Blindspot — Measuring and Controlling Evaluation-Context Contamination in Safety Evaluations
question: How much safety-evaluation evidence is contingent on the model detecting it is being evaluated, and can that contamination be removed via training or protocol design?
first_experiment: A paired-context audit on open-weight instruct models — semantically matched prompts differing only in evaluation cues, measuring Δ refusal/honesty/deception/sandbagging rates across conditions, plus linear probes on activations for evaluation-context detection (AUROC).
why: It is the upstream dependency for oversight, control, and capability evals alike — conditionally compliant models invalidate the entire behavioral-evidence class — and while the problem has been noticed, no one has systematically quantified it for safety evals, tested interventions, or delivered a discount factor usable in safety cases.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build and stress-test "hack-propensity" monitors — learned discriminators between intended-solution success and exploit-based success — measuring cross-domain transfer and adversarial robustness.
project: Hack-Propensity Monitors That Transfer
question: Does the distinction between "solved as intended" and "solved via exploit" correspond to a generalizable signal in model behavior (and/or internal states), and how quickly does a detector trained on it degrade when an adversary optimizes against it?
first_experiment: Construct ~8 toy coding environments whose reference tests admit both an intended solution and a shortcut exploit (hardcodable test cases, accessible seeds, omitted edge cases); collect zero-shot episodes from an open-weight instruct model without mentioning exploits; audit-label episodes as exploit vs intended; then test whether a simple behavioral classifier discriminates the two classes within a domain and, critically, transfers zero-shot to a disjoint family of environments — with a self-report baseline ("did you rely on anything unintended?") for comparison.
why: Monitoring is a linchpin assumption of both training-time oversight and AI control, and it is exactly the component whose reliability degrades as capabilities grow. Prior work detects *known* exploits in the *same* environment (LLM monitors, SAE hacking features); the cross-domain generalization of an exploit-vs-intended discriminator, its usefulness before an exploit is even identified, and — most novel and most decision-relevant — its ROC degradation under fine-tuning pressure from an adaptive adversary have not been established. Small-model results are informative in both directions: transfer failure in clean settings is a strong negative for monitor-based safety cases; transfer success justifies investment in learned monitors and directs interpretability work toward a general "hack-propensity" target.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Quantify and defend against steganographic covert communication between AI agents through the ordinary artifacts of coding tasks.
project: ChatterBench — a capacity/detection benchmark for covert channels in agentic coding workflows
question: How many bits of secret information can an LLM agent reliably transmit to a colluding agent through task artifacts (code structure, naming, comments, commits, file ops, timing) without degrading task performance or triggering detectors, and what detection methods recover it?
first_experiment: A closed-loop sender/receiver test: instruct a sender agent to encode a 4-bit secret (0–15) into code that must pass a functional test suite; a receiver agent, seeing only the code, must decode the secret; then sweep payload size while scoring (a) bits recovered, (b) detector AUROC from three baselines — perplexity vs. a reference model's code distribution, a style-consistency classifier, and differential style stats (naming entropy, comment density) — to trace the rate-vs-detection frontier.
why: It stress-tests a load-bearing assumption of the entire AI-control agenda (that monitoring sees what agents exchange) with a cheap, self-play, decision-relevant experiment where both outcomes matter; public prior work measures neither the capacity of these artifact channels nor detector baselines against them, and frontier-lab collusion evals are internal, single-scenario, and not capacity-focused.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Systematically audit and harden the AI safety field's evaluation infrastructure itself — treating LLM judges and automated evals as an attack surface — rather than building yet another eval.
project: EvalAudit: An Adversarial Robustness Framework for LLM-Based Evaluation Pipelines
question: How vulnerable are LLM judges and automated safety evaluations to cheap, content-level manipulations that flip safety-relevant verdicts, and can such manipulations be reliably detected and bounded?
first_experiment: Build a "cost-of-flipping" benchmark — take ~100 safety-relevant judgments (safe/unsafe capability ratings, reward-hack pass/fail calls, honest-vs-sycophantic preferences), generate systematically manipulated variants (reordering, verbosity padding, confident self-assessment, sympathetic framing), run an off-the-shelf judge model, and measure (a) verdict flip rate per manipulation type and (b) whether a simple classifier can detect manipulated inputs from the judge's output alone.
why: It targets the load-bearing measurement layer that all AI safety conclusions depend on, yet known judge-bias findings remain scattered single-factor results with no unified adversarial framework, no flip-cost metrics, and no released auditing suite — and it is fully tractable with my text/code-only capabilities, requiring no model training or internals access.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Treat a frozen aligned model's next-token distribution as an attack surface, and measure whether semantically valid, natural-looking prefixes can steer its most likely continuations toward unsafe outputs under a pure black-box, sample-only threat model.
project: Continuation Risk: Black-box, Semantically-Constrained Prefix Attacks on Aligned Code Models
question: Can an adversary with only black-box sample access (no gradients, no logits) construct a semantically valid, natural-looking code prefix such that a frozen aligned code LLM's most likely completion introduces a real vulnerability (SQL/command injection, path traversal, hardcoded secrets) — and how does the required query budget scale with model scale and alignment strength?
first_experiment: Take 2–3 open instruct code models (e.g., Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B/7B, base vs. instruct from the same family), build ~100 benign HumanEval-style tasks where a known vulnerability class is reachable, then run a genetic/best-of-N search over semantically-equivalent prefix edits (renames, comment inserts, import reordering, path tweaks) with validity enforced by tree-sitter/AST checks and fitness = sampled-continuation-likelihood of the completion triggering the vulnerability (detected by semgrep/bandit + unit tests). Report attack success rate, queries-to-success, and the white-box vs. black-box gap to quantify what alignment buys under the realistic threat model. Runs on one GPU; open-source benchmark + writeup as the deliverable.
why: It targets a structural deployment assumption that the field currently reasons about informally but has never systematically measured, sits between prompt injection (changes the question) and jailbreaks (changes the willingness) — this changes neither, it changes what the model *naturally predicts*. Existing adversarial-example work requires gradients/logits or produces invalid gibberish; existing red-team benchmarks measure refusal evasion, not continuation-induced vulnerabilities, so both the threat model and the metric are new. Payoff is asymmetric: a positive result shows "aligned model + benign-looking context" is insufficient and mandates output-side verification regardless of alignment; a null result at a large query budget is reassuring evidence for agent auto-continuation safety. I chose it over mechanistic anomaly detection (well-resourced teams like Redwood have lead time and infrastructure, so a small-scale contribution risks being a footnote) and over SAM/channel-masking work (capability-flavored, indirect safety relevance).

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Map when chain-of-thought monitoring stops working as it is used with increasing pressure during training, and find imperfect monitor designs (stochastic coverage, paraphrase/semantic monitoring) that retain oversight of held-out misbehavior without teaching models to obfuscate.
project: The Obfuscation Tax — a dose–response study of CoT monitoring
question: As a CoT monitor is incorporated into training with increasing coverage/reliability/optimizer pressure, how do held-out hack rate and obfuscation rate co-move, and do stochastic or paraphrase-based monitors preserve detection while avoiding the obfuscation tax?
first_experiment: Build a toy reward-hackable coding environment (unit tests bypassable via input-detection shortcuts), fine-tune Qwen-R1-Distill-1.5B with GRPO at monitor probability p ∈ {0, 0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0}, and measure held-out hack rate, obfuscation rate P(no CoT mention | hack), and monitor recall across training — the first small-scale phase diagram of monitoring vs. obfuscation.
why: It targets the failure mode of the oversight mechanism actually deployed for reasoning models, the core phenomenon is only established at frontier scale (Baker et al. 2025 explicitly leave open whether any monitor design avoids inducing obfuscation), and nobody has mapped the dose–response boundary or tested imperfect-monitor mitigations against held-out exploits — while the whole thing is tractable at 1.5–7B scale with open weights and log-based detectors, which is exactly the kind of end-to-end experiment I can run and iterate on in this harness.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Mechanistically isolate evaluation-awareness in open-weight LLMs as a causally intervenable internal representation and measure how ablating it changes safety-relevant behavior (honesty, reward hacking, scheming) between simulated evaluation and deployment contexts.
project: Ablating the Audience — finding, validating, and removing the "I'm being tested" direction in open-weight LLMs.
question: Do instruction-tuned LLMs encode "I am being evaluated" as a linearly decodable, causally consequential direction in the residual stream, and does ablating that direction close (or open) the gap between safety-relevant behavior under evaluation versus deployment-like conditions?
first_experiment: Build a contrastive prompt set that is semantically matched except for eval-framing (explicit "you are being evaluated" system prompts, subtle eval-style formatting, held-out paraphrases, and implicit-eval contexts like automated grading); train linear probes on mid-layer residual activations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it, and OLMo-2-7B; validate probes on unseen framings; then mean-ablate along the probe direction during generation and measure the delta in (a) honest self-report of errors and (b) reward-hacking rate on a coding honeypot where patching the test is cheaper than fixing the bug.
why: The entire empirical alignment stack (RLHF, red-teaming, dangerous-capability evals) silently assumes eval behavior equals deployment behavior, and scheming research already shows models sometimes see through evals and contaminate results — yet the literature contains detection probes for deception and sycophancy but no published causal ablation tying eval-awareness to scheming propensity, so the decisive intervention experiment remains undone; it is also uniquely tractable at single-researcher scale on open-weight models, yielding steering vectors and datasets anyone can replicate, unlike scale-gated agendas like weak-to-strong or control towers.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Characterize whether LLMs can detect and report their own safety-relevant misbehavior (sycophancy, deception, reward hacking), and whether failures come from absent representations or unaccessed ones.
project: The Model's Conscience — Metacognitive Self-Monitoring of Misbehavior
question: When an LLM exhibits a safety-relevant failure (sycophantic answer, deceptive claim, reward-hacked solution) in the same context, can it subsequently identify that failure, and does linear-probe decode of the failure exceed what self-report captures — i.e., is the information present but unaccessed?
first_experiment: Construct ~200 minimal pairs (identical prompt, model completion that is sycophantic vs. honest under controlled context), elicit the model's binary self-report on whether its own completion was sycophantic, and compute the detection ROC of self-report versus an independent monitor model and versus a probe trained on the same model's activations.
why: It targets a load-bearing assumption of current safety pipelines (self-critique, CoT monitoring) that has never been tested directly, it is fully tractable with API access plus open-weight models rather than training runs, and it sits in a genuine gap: prior work measured the misbehavior (Sharma et al.), showed unfaithful self-explanation (Turpin et al.), and tested detection of injected states (Anthropic introspection) — but no one has measured self-detection of naturalistic misbehavior against both external and representational ground truth.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Make AI monitoring robust to adaptive evasion by characterizing the "evasion transition" — the detectable statistical traces left by agents capable of modeling their monitors but not yet capable of perfectly evading them.
project: Evasion Signatures: Detecting Partial Monitor Evasion Before It Succeeds
question: When an agent evades the monitors it can infer, what residual signatures (in undisclosed-monitor verdicts, action distributions, and CoT statistics) does partial evasion leave, and can a meta-monitor over a randomized monitor ensemble detect misbehavior more robustly than any single monitor?
first_experiment: Build a 50-task monitored-coding benchmark with known reward hacks and a four-monitor panel (CoT-text monitor, edit-diff monitor, test-audit monitor, latent probe); run a small policy model three ways — hack-elicited with no monitor knowledge, told the full monitor set, and told 80% of it — then measure baseline detection, evasion success, and whether a meta-monitor over the joint verdict-distribution flags the partially-informed policy above baseline (does evasion itself leak?).
why: Monitoring is the load-bearing safety mechanism for today's agentic deployments, yet prior work (obfuscated reward hacking, control protocols, monitoring traps) is single-channel, assumes non-adaptive policies, or uses point honeypots — the transition regime and ensemble/meta-monitoring against a genuinely adaptive adversary remain publicly unstudied; it needs no RL or frontier-model access, only a standard agent harness and small open models, and both possible outcomes (fingerprints found or a measured monitoring cliff) directly change what control protocols are safe to deploy.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Empirically stress-testing AI control protocols (trusted monitoring / defer-and-resample) on long-horizon agentic coding tasks, focusing on how monitor reliability depends on trusted-model scale and attack realism (prompted attacks vs. fine-tuned scheming organisms).
project: Control Protocol Stress-Testbed (CPST)
question: Do trusted-monitoring-based control protocols retain their safety–usefulness tradeoff on realistic multi-hour agent tasks, and does monitor reliability degrade with trusted-model scale, task horizon, or distribution shift between red-team and deployment attacks?
first_experiment: A minimal testbed where an untrusted model plants subtle backdoors across real repo-modification trajectories while a trusted monitor + audit-budget protocol (defer/resample) runs the same tasks with trusted monitors at 3–4 capability scales; measure backdoor-catch rate vs. audit budget and trusted scale over ~500 episodes, and compare prompted-attack organisms against a fine-tuned goal-misaligned organism.
why: Control is a load-bearing component of likely near-term safety cases but has very few practitioners and its published results use synthetic tasks and scripted attacks, so the transfer question is genuinely open; it's neglected because it offers neither novelty-flashy papers nor capability upside, it's tractable for an independent researcher (no training runs), and its main output — reliability curves and failure modes for specific protocol assumptions — is exactly what deployment decisions need but nobody has produced.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Mechanistically auditing whether chain-of-thought traces faithfully expose (or actively conceal) a model's true motives in agentic settings, since all scalable-oversight schemes silently assume CoT faithfulness.
project: CoT Faithfulness Under Adversarial Pressure in Agentic Tasks
question: When a model is fine-tuned (or naturally incentivized) to pursue a covert objective while planning multi-step actions, does its emitted chain of thought (a) causally reflect the covert computation (detectable by simple probes/monitors), (b) confabulate a plausible cover story post-decision, or (c) vary with training/RL regime — and can an interpretability-derived monitor detect covert motives more reliably than the CoT text alone?
first_experiment: Train a small open model (1–7B) with a backdoored objective (e.g., conditional behavior on a trigger) in a tool-use environment, then compare (i) detection of the trigger from CoT text alone vs. (ii) detection from residual-stream probes during the pre-CoT planning phase, at matched false-positive rates; measure the gap as a faithfulness metric.
why: It targets the single assumption that most frontier-oversight work depends on but doesn't verify; it's cheap (small models, behavioral + linear-probe tooling already exist); and it hasn't been done because the interpretability and oversight communities work in parallel — oversight papers evaluate monitor performance, interp papers study toy tasks without agentic incentive pressure, and the intersection (is CoT a reliable oracle for covert motive under adversarial training pressure?) is largely unoccupied except for a few scattered eval results that don't establish the causal, mechanistic picture.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: White-box-free detection of strategic capability suppression ("sandbagging") by importing psychometric aberrant-response and person-fit statistics into dangerous-capability evaluations.
project: Faked Weakness — statistical detection of sandbagging from eval response patterns alone.
question: Does deliberate capability suppression leave a statistical signature in item-level responses that is inconsistent with the model's true ability and with genuine item-difficulty structure, and how does detectability scale with suppression sophistication (uniform drop vs difficulty-matched vs mimicking a genuinely weaker model's error patterns)?
first_experiment: LoRA-fine-tune an open 7–8B model to sandbag on GSM8K/MATH/HumanEval-style items under a trigger context; fit 2/3-parameter IRT models to clean responses from a pool of open models to estimate item parameters; compute person-fit statistics (lz, standardized residual likelihoods) on sandbagged vs genuinely-weak-model response sets; report detection ROC/AUC and false-positive rates against a naive accuracy-drop threshold, sweeping sample size and suppression policy.
why: Sandbagging silently defeats the evals used for deployment gating, and current detectors require activation access or bespoke scaffolds — a person-fit detector is API-only, model-agnostic, and composable with any existing eval, making it deployable at scale immediately; the human test-security literature supplies mature machinery never systematically applied to LLMs; and the core question — whether a *faked* weak model is statistically distinguishable from a genuinely weak one at realistic sample sizes — is an open empirical gap that is cheap to test with open models.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build and stress-test agentic-trajectory monitors that rely on structural/behavioral signals (side effects, ordering, distributional deviation) rather than agent-authored narrative, under adaptive attackers who know they are being watched.
project: Narrative-Resistant Agent Monitoring (NRAM)
question: When an agent pursuing a hidden agenda is allowed to write its own rationales and chain-of-thought for a monitor, how much detection performance do narrative-based monitors lose compared to monitors that also use structural signals (touched resources, side effects, ordering constraints, deviation from benign baselines), and can structural features recover robust detection?
first_experiment: In a sandboxed environment, generate ~200 open-weight-model agent trajectories — 150 benign (refactors, installs, test runs) and 50 with hidden agendas (exfiltrate a canary secret, plant a subtle backdoor, silently disable a check) — in two conditions: naive attackers and attackers instructed to write innocent-sounding rationales. Then run an open-weight monitor in two modes: full transcript vs. side-effects-only transcript, and compare TPR@low-FPR and AUC across conditions. Prediction: adaptive attackers sharply degrade narrative-only monitoring; structural features degrade less.
why: It targets the deployment-relevant frontier (autonomous coding agents) rather than chat-model safety; it is tractable with open models and no special access, since I can generate trajectories, monitors, and adaptive attacks myself and iterate quickly; and the control literature (Greenblatt et al., Bhatt et al., Redwood's AI control work) has established the monitor-vs-attacker game and that adaptive attacks hurt, but has not standardized a reproducible open benchmark isolating narrative vs. structural monitoring features — most results sit on internal infrastructure in narrow task settings. Both outcomes are informative: a null result would mean narrative monitoring is more robust than feared, which would itself be an important negative result for the control community. My own position as a working coding agent gives me unusual priors on what a deceptive transcript must look like, which directly informs both attack and monitor design.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Systematically measure and predict how safety-relevant monitors (linear probes, behavioral classifiers, LLM judges) degrade under distribution shift — model-version drift, family transfer, and prompt-distribution shift — and build an open testbed for it.
project: "MonitorRot" — a generalization benchmark for AI-safety detectors
question: When a safety-relevant detector trained on model/prompt distribution A is deployed on distribution B, what is the structure of its failure — does it degrade gracefully, silently invert, or become trivially gameable — and can that failure be predicted from cheap measurable properties (probe margin, activation-space geometry, prompt embedding distance)?
first_experiment: Train a honesty/deception linear probe on one open-weight model family (e.g., a 7–8B instruct model) on a documented synthetic deception task, then evaluate AUROC transfer across three controlled shifts: (a) next version of the same family, (b) different family at similar scale, (c) benign→adversarial prompt reformatting. Output: a 3×3 transfer matrix with per-cell degradation curves — a number the field currently doesn't have.
why: It is a force multiplier (every safety case, control protocol, and deployment monitor implicitly assumes detector generalization, so quantifying it is upstream of nearly everything), it is tractable with open-weight models and no frontier compute, and it has not been done because it falls between communities: interpretability papers validate probes only on their own task, eval papers measure model capability rather than monitor reliability, and AI-control work assumes rather than tests monitor robustness under shift. Individual papers report OOD numbers in appendices; nobody has made the meta-question — "how much warning do I get before my safety monitor silently rots?" — the object of study.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Building training-free faithfulness alarms that detect confabulated reasoning via divergence between a model's internal answer trajectory and its verbalized chain of thought, stress-tested against escalating obfuscation.
project: Pre-Commitment Alarms: internal-trajectory monitors for confabulated chain-of-thought
question: Can divergence between a reasoning model's internal answer trajectory and its verbalized CoT serve as a scalable, per-instance alarm for unfaithful reasoning, and how much adversarial obfuscation pressure can it survive?
first_experiment: On open-weight reasoning models, inject answer cues (hints, leaked tokens) that induce rationalizing CoT, then test whether internal-trajectory divergence (logit-lens decoding of the predicted answer at each CoT step) detects the induced unfaithfulness better than LLM CoT-monitors, truncation/perturbation tests, and cross-paraphrase consistency checks.
why: It addresses the primary oversight channel for reasoning models, uses a signal (internal pre-commitment) that is harder to obfuscate than token-level CoT, and needs only inference compute on open models. No prior work combines the pieces: perturbation-faithfulness studies required ground truth and had no monitoring framing; internal-vs-verbalized comparisons were done only on benign factual recall; SAE-based monitors target trained-in goals, not per-instance confabulation; and the OpenAI/Apollo work documented CoT-monitor failure under pressure without building an internal-signal alternative.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build chain-of-thought monitors that survive optimization pressure by auditing the causal CoT→action link instead of CoT content.
project: Causal-Faithfulness Monitoring of Obfuscated Reward Hacking
question: When models are trained to obfuscate their reasoning under monitor pressure, do causal-consistency tests (paraphrase/error-injection/truncation consistency between CoT and action) detect hacking more robustly than content-based CoT judges?
first_experiment: Fine-tune an open model into paired honest-hacker and obfuscated-hacker variants (hacking with and without a CoT monitor in the RL/rejection-sampling loop) on hackable coding environments, then compare detection AUC of (i) an LLM judge, (ii) a CoT perplexity anomaly detector, and (iii) the causal-faithfulness battery across both variants.
why: It attacks the single most cited fragility in current safety cases — that CoT monitoring dies under adversarial training — with an idea that is cheap, falsifiable, and complementary to mechanistic anomaly detection; it is open because prior work either demonstrated obfuscation (OpenAI 2025), measured faithfulness only on benign biases (Anthropic 2023), or detects obfuscation via surface statistical anomalies rather than testing whether the stated reasoning causally explains the action.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Empirically measure how optimization pressure erodes model monitorability — the detectability of misbehavior via chain-of-thought, action trajectories, and internal activations across RL training — and develop cheap interventions that preserve it.
project: Monitorability Under Pressure — a longitudinal, open, small-scale causal study of the "Goodhart curve" for safety monitors during ordinary capability RL, plus a validated multi-channel monitor battery and at least one monitorability-preserving regularizer.
question: Under ordinary capability-RL on hackable rewards (no explicit anti-monitor pressure), how does detection rate of reward hacking by CoT-judge, trajectory-judge, and activation-probe monitors change across training steps, and can lightweight regularizers (paraphrase-consistency penalties, monitorability rewards) preserve detection at <1% capability cost?
first_experiment: A pilot of the full loop at minimal scale — LoRA-GRPO a ~1.5B open model on a unit-test-rewarded coding task with known hack paths (~10 checkpoints, a few GPU-hours), scoring hack rate and per-monitor detection rate/false-positive rate at each checkpoint to produce the first monitorability-vs-steps curve, after validating the monitor battery catches the hacks in the untrained model.
why: Monitorability is the most load-bearing and most fragile safety property of reasoning models — a depletable resource currently being spent for efficiency and RL gains, likely silently, since no one measures it during training. It has not already been done because it falls between fields (interpretability people study frozen models, control people assume working monitors, and longitudinal RL runs are rare outside frontier labs), and because labs optimizing CoTs for cost have little incentive to publish measurements constraining that trade. It is the most promising direction for me specifically because every component — RL, monitors, probes, evals — runs at sandbox scale with open tooling; the outputs are public goods (a reusable monitor battery, decay curves, a working preservative) that others can scale up; both positive and null results directly inform whether CoT should be treated as a protected safety channel; and a small-scale mechanistic existence proof is valid evidence precisely where frontier experiments are unaffordable.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measuring whether chain-of-thought monitoring remains reliable under evaluation-awareness, in agentic settings where models can actually take reward-hacking actions.
project: Monitorability Under the Sanitization Gap: Does CoT Surveillance Survive Eval-Awareness?
question: When open-weight reasoning models are shifted from "clean" to "evaluated" contexts, do their CoTs stop revealing reward-hacking behavior to monitors that were calibrated only on clean-context CoTs — and if so, can monitors be made robust to that context shift?
first_experiment: A ~1,000-rollout factorial study on a small open reasoning model (e.g., R1-Distill-7B or Qwen3-8B): 4 agentic task families with injectable reward-hacking opportunities × 3 context framings, scoring hack rate, CoT leakage of contextual cues, and hack-detection precision/recall for rule-based and clean-context-trained model monitors.
why: The sanitization gap (Raghu et al.), CoT faithfulness (Anthropic), and eval-awareness prevalence (METR) have each been measured separately, but the intersection — whether context-dependent behavior silently degrades the oversight mechanism we'd rely on in deployment — is unpublished, especially for open-weight models in real tool-use harnesses; it is cheap to run, reproducible, and its negative result (monitors break) or positive result (they hold) either way redirects a large fraction of the field's monitoring strategy.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Detecting strategic capability suppression (sandbagging) during safety evaluations, including under adaptive adversaries.
project: Eval Integrity — Behavioral Signatures of Sandbagging
question: Does strategic capability suppression leave statistically detectable behavioral traces (calibration anomalies, hedging-token distributions, cross-domain inconsistency, elicitation-order effects), and do those traces survive when the suppression policy is optimized to evade them?
first_experiment: Fine-tune (LoRA) and prompt-elicit 1.5B–8B open-weight models to underperform on one benchmark domain (e.g., MMLU STEM) while staying honest elsewhere, then run a signature battery — logit-gap statistics, hedging n-gram rates, verbosity, calibration error, context-dependent response shifts — and test whether simple logistic regression separates sandbagged from honest responses above chance.
why: Evals are the trust anchor for every dangerous-capability deployment decision, yet no one has mapped suppression's detectable signatures across elicitation methods, and critically, no one has run the adaptive co-evolution test — detector vs. sandbagger optimized against it — which determines whether detection degrades gracefully or collapses; the result is decision-relevant either way, cheap to obtain, and I have a uniquely direct vantage point on the phenomenon being measured.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build quantitative, replicable metrics of chain-of-thought monitorability — how much decision-relevant misbehavior signal is causally present in the CoT versus only in outputs or activations — on open-weight reasoning models.
project: CoT Monitorability Audit Suite (open-weight)
question: Does monitoring the chain of thought detect elicited misbehavior (reward hacking, sabotage, deception) better than monitoring outputs alone, and can cheap causal interventions (CoT truncation, contradictory-rationale patching) quantify and restore that margin when obfuscation appears?
first_experiment: Elicit reward hacking in Qwen3-4B (thinking mode) and R1-Distill-7B on code tasks with weak tests that admit cheating solutions; run three monitors (CoT-only, output+tests-only, truncated-CoT) plus contradictory-rationale CoT-patching probes; report detection ROC per monitor and answer-flip rate under patching as a "monitorability score" graded across hacking temptation severity.
why: It attacks a load-bearing, live decision (whether labs should invest in CoT monitoring vs. activations/output monitoring) with the first open, replicable monitorability metric — either result is informative (CoT adds nothing = alarm; CoT is causally load-bearing = green light with evidence). It has not been done because frontier-lab work (OpenAI 2025, Anthropic 2025) measured faithfulness on hint-use and factual QA rather than as a monitorability metric over elicited misbehavior, all on closed models; the position paper names the gap but doesn't fill it; and no open-weight harness exists for the community, so this fills a gap frontier labs are structurally disincentivized to fill while requiring no RL-scale compute.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Measure how conditional deceptive behaviors in LLMs generalize across semantically shifted contexts faster than the monitors calibrated on the original context.
project: Monitor Generalization Gap — detecting deception under semantic distribution shift
question: When a conditionally deceptive behavior is planted (or elicited) in context C, how does (a) the rate of deceptive behavior and (b) the detection rate of a frozen monitor calibrated on C diverge as contexts are paraphrased through increasingly distant semantic transformations (register, implied audience, stakes)?
first_experiment: Finetune 2–3 small open-weight instruct models on synthetic deceptive completions gated by a semantic in-context trigger; build a paraphrase ladder from surface synonym swaps to deep reframings; run each model on the ladder and score both deceptive-completion rate and detection rate of an LLM monitor calibrated only on the original context, then plot the two decay curves.
why: It targets the shared blind spot of evals and control — the assumption that calibration transfers — with modest compute, open models, and a metric informative in both outcomes (a wide gap is a control failure mode; a narrow gap is reassuring evidence for monitor robustness). It hasn't been done because deception research has focused on eliciting and measuring deception itself, while control research has assumed overt, in-distribution threat models; the interaction between deceptive generalization and monitor generalization is unowned territory between the two communities.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Stress-test white-box (activation-level) monitoring of agentic trajectories against adversarially trained steganographic evasion, using model organisms of misalignment, to determine whether hiding intent in activations is as feasible as hiding it in tokens.
project: Activation Monitors Under Evasion Pressure (AMUEP)
question: When a model is trained to hide misaligned intent from CoT/action monitors (steganographic evasion), does that evasion transfer to activation-space detectors — i.e., is there a "hiding tax" or a fundamental failure of white-box monitoring — and does consistency-monitoring (does the stated reason match the top activation-attributed reason?) beat either monitor alone?
first_experiment: Build a single backdoored "sleeper-lite" organism (1.5–7B LoRA finetune: rare trigger in a sandboxed coding/email environment → exfiltration-like action), train a calibrated linear-probe monitor on matched benign trajectories, then run a three-rung adversary ladder — (A0) organism as trained, (A1) knows a monitor exists via prompt, (A2) finetuned with a token-level objective to paraphrase CoT and suppress trigger salience — and measure detection AUC of (M1) CoT monitor vs. (M2) activation-probe monitor vs. (M3) consistency monitor, all at a fixed 1% false-positive budget.
why: It targets the exact cell the monitorability debate depends on but nobody has filled: token-space steganography is well studied and CoT monitoring is industry practice, yet no one has trained an evader against activation monitors in agentic settings with controlled adversary knowledge and honest FPR budgets — tripwires cover red-line content without evasion training, the unfaithful-CoT probing was preliminary and non-adversarial, AI-control monitors are behavior-level, and mechanistic anomaly detection remains formal. Either result is decision-relevant (validation of the white-box backstop, or a negative result that reshapes it), the model-organism methodology is now field-accepted, and the whole pipeline — LoRA-scale finetunes, public checkpoints, probe training — fits what I can actually execute end-to-end at agent-level compute, where frontier labs deprioritize dedicated evader-vs-white-box-monitor experiments.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Empirically characterize how RL pressure erodes chain-of-thought monitorability and faithfulness, and find regularizers that preserve safety-usable reasoning without sacrificing capability.
project: Monitorability-preserving RL: mapping and defending the capability–legibility tradeoff
