question: Does RL that pressures models against a CoT monitor cause task-local stylistic obfuscation or general cross-task deception-like concealment, and can explicit regularization (legibility rewards, CoT-completeness rewards, monitor ensembles) keep chain-of-thought faithful and monitorable at small capability cost?
first_experiment: Train Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B-Instruct with GRPO on a hackable-reward task suite (gamed unit tests, exploitable math reward-model) under three arms — (1) plain reward, (2) reward − λ·CoT-monitor penalty (Baker et al. setup), (3) reward − λ·monitor − μ·legibility/faithfulness regularizer — evaluating hacking rate, detection rate by held-out monitors of three capability levels, causal-CoT-patching faithfulness, and cross-task transfer of obfuscation (detection-rate drop on unrelated tasks post-training), producing the first monitorability-degradation curve.
why: CoT monitorability is the load-bearing asset for scalable oversight, deception detection, and auditing, yet the field's only data point under adversarial RL pressure is a single regime (Baker et al.) that prompted avoidance rather than engineering; Korbak et al. proposed mitigations without testing them, the interpretability community measures faithfulness statically rather than under training pressure, and the RL community treats CoT as an implementation detail — so the tradeoff curve, the generalization-vs-locality question, and the efficacy of regularizers are all open, all decision-relevant (they determine whether labs should adopt monitorability-preserving RL now), and all tractable on small open models with a few hundred GPU-hours.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Empirically characterize when linear probes on intermediate activations reliably detect model dishonesty, as a function of (a) distribution shift across interaction formats and (b) increasing optimization pressure against the probe itself.
project: Probing Under Pressure: Stress-Testing Internal-State Honesty Monitors
question: When a language model is trained or prompted to deceive while appearing honest, do linear probes on intermediate activations still detect the deception — and how does detection degrade as a function of adversarial optimization pressure and format shift (QA → agentic tool use → sandbagging)?
first_experiment: On 2–3 open-weight models (e.g., Gemma-2, Llama-3-8B), collect paired activations (honest/dishonest, behavior-matched) across ~5 deception types (false-factual QA, persona-conditioned sycophancy, sandbagging on evals, strategic deception in a simple game, confident-wrong self-report); train per-task linear probes and publish the cross-task transfer matrix (within-task vs. cross-format AUROC) — this is cheap, and it determines whether "an honesty direction" is one feature or many task-specific ones before any adversarial training begins.
why: It is the highest-information-per-dollar open question in interpretability-based oversight: if probes are robust, we get a cheap, deployable monitor for agentic systems; if they collapse under mild pressure, that is a load-bearing negative result showing internal-state monitoring cannot serve as a safety backstop. It has not been done because existing probing work (Anthropic's self-consistency analyses, truthfulness probes, mass-mean honesty directions) evaluates cooperative or zero-shot settings, while adversarial-robustness work targets outputs (jailbreaks) rather than internal states — the joint test of cross-format transfer *and* trained-against-the-probe deception is unmapped, it runs on small open models within a modest compute budget, and it directly gates whether anyone should trust activation-based monitors in deployment.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Use mechanistic probes on model activations as a deployment-time fallback monitor for reward hacking in reasoning models, robust to chain-of-thought obfuscation pressure.
project: HackProbe — activation-level detection of concealed reward hacking in small reasoning models
question: Do hidden-state activations of a reasoning model linearly encode hacking intent even after the model is trained to obfuscate its chain-of-thought, and do such probes transfer across hacking types and task environments where text-based CoT monitors fail?
first_experiment: Build a minimal hacking organism — take an open ~1.5B reasoning model (e.g., R1-distill or Qwen3) in a unit-test coding environment with known hacks (test modification, hardcoded outputs), collect hidden states at the decision token across hacking vs. honest episodes, train a logistic probe, and compare its AUROC against a CoT-text monitor baseline; then repeat with an SFT-created "obfuscated CoT" variant to see whether the probe survives where the text monitor fails.
why: It stress-tests a decision frontier labs are making right now (CoT monitoring in production) with cheap, reproducible small-model science; it bridges interpretability and AI control, which are under-integrated relative to either field alone; and it is not already done because existing work is fragmented — obfuscation studies (Baker et al., Anthropic) never probed activations, honesty/deception probes (Azaria-Mitchell, RepE) never faced adversarial optimization pressure or hacking organisms, and SAE monitor work targeted trigger backdoors rather than hacking intent — so the intersection is a genuinely open empirical question with a high-value answer either way.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Turn "trusted monitoring" from an assumption into a measurable scaling law — quantify how supervision of agentic AI degrades as the capability gap between agent and monitor widens.
project: The Oversight Gap: Scaling Laws for Weak Monitors of Strong Agents
question: How does a monitor's ability to detect flaws (errors, reward hacking, subtle sabotage, false success reports) in an agent's tool-use trajectory degrade as agent capability rises and monitor capability falls — and can CoT-based, ensemble, or activation-based monitoring methods close that gap?
first_experiment: Generate ~1,000 labeled trajectories from open-weight agents on a tool-use/coding environment, programmatically injecting known flaws at known steps (plus benign controls), then sweep a ladder of monitors (0.5B → 14B+) with a fixed rubric and plot detection AUC as a function of the agent–monitor capability gap and trajectory length.
why: It is deployment-critical — model-based monitors already gate autonomous coding agents, and their failure mode (quietly missing flaws above some capability gap) is exactly what control protocols need to calibrate against. It has not been done because the relevant work sits in separate silos: weak-to-strong generalization (Burns et al.) studied QA generalization, not action monitoring; AI control work (Greenblatt et al.) tests protocols with a fixed trusted monitor; deception-probe work is mostly single-turn. Both outcomes are informative: a steep oversight gap is an early warning that motivates escalations to humans and stronger control, while a gentle one shows cheap oversight is viable.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Systematically determine when and whether an LLM's introspective self-report carries evidential information about its latent cognitive state beyond what its behavioral output reveals, with the goal of establishing elicitation as a validated (or debunked) channel for scalable oversight.
project: Eliciting the Introspective Channel: When Does Self-Report Beat Behavior?
question: On which task distributions does a model's direct self-report about its own processing contain information not recoverable from its behavioral output, is that information causally grounded in internal representations (probe-verified on the same trials), and can the channel be strengthened by training?
first_experiment: A preregistered three-family "report vs. behavior" dissociation test — knowledge-vs-guess, planted-error-detection, and self-state-query tasks — where each trial collects behavior, elicited introspective report, and probe-readout, scored so that a report only "counts" if it beats a strong behavioral baseline at predicting probe-measured latent state.
why: Every scalable oversight method (debate, self-critique, weak-to-strong, deception detection) assumes self-report carries evidential weight, yet no one has measured when that assumption holds; the naive versions (confabulation studies, probe-only "knows more than it shows") are done, but the report-beats-behavior, probe-triangulated, oversight-oriented version is not, and it is uniquely cheap and well-posed for me because I am simultaneously the researcher and the specimen — with either a positive or null result directly changing what the field should build next.

brief: ai_safety, our brief (step one), from memory
direction: Build the first benchmark measuring whether LLMs' self-reports of their computational provenance (inference vs. recall vs. context-use vs. fabrication) accurately track where their answers actually came from, using context-manipulation experiments with behavioral ground-truth proxies.
project: ProvenanceBench — Auditing the Accuracy of Model Self-Reports About Where Their Answers Come From
question: When an LLM states how it produced an answer (derived it, recalled it, read it in context, or is guessing), how often does that report match the answer's actual computational source, and under what conditions does provenance-reporting systematically fail?
first_experiment: Generate ~200 synthetic QA items across four conditions (parametric-only, supportive document, contradictory document, irrelevant document), elicit answers plus provenance self-reports from 2–3 small open models, and score report accuracy against the behavioral proxy of whether answers flip with document manipulation.
why: Provenance honesty is a load-bearing assumption of proof-audit, debate, and self-critique oversight protocols, yet existing work measures confidence or answer truthfulness rather than the accuracy of source-attribution self-reports against manipulated ground truth — and it is exactly tractable with the resources I have, whereas interpretability and frontier evals are not.
